lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Which branch of Biology focuses on the study of the structure and function of cells?

(a) Cytology (b) Microbiology (c) Histology (d) Ecology
Correct answer: Cytology

Q: The study of the processes of heredity and variation in living organisms is known as:

(a) Ecology (b) Genetics (c) Anatomy (d) Embryology
Correct answer: Genetics

Q: Insulin made through bacteria is an example of the technique of:

(a) Parasitology (b) Biotechnology (c) Biochemistry (d) Histology
Correct answer: Biotechnology

Q: Heart pumps blood, stomach digests food, and kidneys excrete wastes. The statement comes from.

(a) Physiology (b) Anatomy (c) Morphology (d) Histology
Correct answer: Physiology

Q: Which branch of Biology involves the study of the classification of organisms?

(a) Taxonomy (b) Physiology (c) Palaeontology (d) Biogeography
Correct answer: Taxonomy

Q: Which step comes between making hypothesis and doing experiments?

(a) Making deductions (b) Making observations (c) Summarizing results (d) Analysing data
Correct answer: Making deductions

Q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the scientific method?

(a) It relies on evidence (b) It involves formulating hypotheses (c) Hypothesis will always be correct (d) It requires rigorous testing
Correct answer: Hypothesis will always be correct

Q: Choose the correct sequence of steps of scientific method?

(a) Observations - hypothesis - deduction - experiments (b) Observations - hypothesis - law - theory (c) Hypothesis - observations - deduction - experiments (d) Law - theory - deduction - observations
Correct answer: Observations - hypothesis - deduction - experiments

Q: People who slept near smoky fire had less chance to suffer from malaria. Why?

(a) Smoke kills Plasmodium in their blood (b) Fire increases temperature and Plasmodium are killed in air (c) Mosquitoes cannot tolerate smoke and are repelled (d) Smoke kills Plasmodium present in mosquitoes
Correct answer: Mosquitoes cannot tolerate smoke and are repelled

Q: Experiments are very important in scientific method because a researcher:

(a) Always gets correct results (b) Disproves many hypotheses and gets some hypothesis proved (c) Is sure that he will prove the hypotheses (d) Gets a chance to work in the laboratory
Correct answer: Disproves many hypotheses and gets some hypothesis proved

mcqs.q: Which branch of Biology focuses on the study of the structure and function of cells?
mcqs.why: Cytology is the branch of biology that studies the structure and function of cells; microbiology deals with microorganisms and histology with tissues.

mcqs.q: The study of the processes of heredity and variation in living organisms is known as:
mcqs.why: Genetics is the study of heredity and variation, i.e. how characteristics are transferred from parents to offspring, as this chapter's definitions of the branches state.

mcqs.q: Insulin made through bacteria is an example of the technique of:
mcqs.why: Producing human insulin in bacteria is biotechnology: using living organisms and their processes to make useful products, as explained in this chapter.

mcqs.q: Heart pumps blood, stomach digests food, and kidneys excrete wastes. The statement comes from.
mcqs.why: Physiology studies the functioning of body parts. Pumping blood, digesting food and excreting wastes are functions, not structures, so the statement belongs to physiology.

mcqs.q: Which branch of Biology involves the study of the classification of organisms?
mcqs.why: Taxonomy is the branch of biology concerned with the classification of organisms into groups, as stated in this chapter's list of the branches of biology.

mcqs.q: Which step comes between making hypothesis and doing experiments?
mcqs.why: The scientific method runs: observations, hypothesis, deductions, then experiments. Deductions are the logical 'if... then...' consequences drawn from the hypothesis before it is tested.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the scientific method?
mcqs.why: A hypothesis is only a tentative answer and experiments may prove it wrong. The scientific method relies on evidence and rigorous testing, never on assuming the hypothesis must be correct.

mcqs.q: Choose the correct sequence of steps of scientific method?
mcqs.why: The correct order is observations first, then a hypothesis, then deductions from the hypothesis, and finally experiments to test those deductions, as described in this chapter.

mcqs.q: People who slept near smoky fire had less chance to suffer from malaria. Why?
options: Mosquitoes cannot tolerate smoke and are repelled
Smoke kills Plasmodium in their blood
Fire increases temperature and Plasmodium are killed in air
Smoke kills Plasmodium present in mosquitoes
mcqs.why: Smoke does not kill Plasmodium in the blood or in the air; mosquitoes simply cannot tolerate smoke and are repelled by it, so people near smoky fires were bitten less and escaped malaria.

mcqs.q: Experiments are very important in scientific method because a researcher:
options: Is sure that he will prove the hypotheses
Gets a chance to work in the laboratory
Disproves many hypotheses and gets some hypothesis proved
mcqs.why: Experiments test deductions honestly: many hypotheses are disproved by them and only some are supported. That is how the scientific method reaches reliable conclusions.

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Define the following branches of Biology. Genetics, Anatomy, Palaeontology, Marine Biology, Pathology

Genetics: the study of heredity and variation, i.e. how characteristics are transferred from parents to offspring. Anatomy: the study of the internal physical structure of organisms. Palaeontology: the study of fossils, the preserved remains of organisms of past ages. Marine Biology: the study of life in the oceans. Pathology: the study of diseases, their causes and effects.

Q: Which branch of Biology involves the study of the development of organisms from fertilization to birth or hatching?

Embryology: it is the branch of Biology that studies the development of an organism from the fertilized egg (zygote) to birth or hatching.

Q: How is the profession of medicine and surgery different from animal husbandry?

Medicine and surgery deal with human beings: diagnosing, treating and operating upon human patients to cure diseases. Animal husbandry deals with animals: the breeding, feeding, housing and care of farm animals to obtain milk, meat, eggs and other products and to keep the animals healthy and productive.

Q: Differentiate between Morphology and Physiology

Morphology is the study of the form and external structure of organisms. Physiology is the study of the functioning of body parts, i.e. how the organs and systems work. Morphology tells what a part looks like; physiology tells what it does.

Q: What is Computational Biology?

Computational Biology is the branch in which computers and mathematical models are used to store, process and analyse biological data, for example comparing DNA and protein sequences, predicting protein structures and modelling populations. It works together with bioinformatics.

Q: What is the role of observation and experimentation in the scientific method?

Observation starts the scientific method: careful observation of nature raises the scientific problem and provides the facts from which a hypothesis is made. Experimentation then tests the hypothesis and its deductions under controlled conditions: experiments confirm or reject the hypothesis with evidence, so conclusions rest on proof rather than guesswork.

mcqs.q: Which branch of biology studies fossils, the preserved remains of organisms of past ages?
mcqs.why: As defined in this lesson, palaeontology is the study of fossils, the preserved remains of organisms of past ages. Pathology studies diseases and anatomy studies internal structure.

mcqs.q: Anatomy is the study of:
options: The internal physical structure of organisms
mcqs.why: This lesson defines anatomy as the study of the internal physical structure of organisms; heredity is genetics, diseases are pathology and ocean life is marine biology.

mcqs.q: The branch of biology that studies the development of an organism from the fertilized egg to birth or hatching is:
mcqs.why: Embryology studies the development of an organism from the fertilized egg (zygote) to birth or hatching, as stated in this lesson's answer on development.

mcqs.q: How are medicine and surgery different from animal husbandry?
options: Medicine treats animals, while husbandry treats humans
Medicine and surgery treat human patients, while animal husbandry is the breeding and care of farm animals
Both are concerned only with plants
Animal husbandry means performing surgery on humans
mcqs.why: Medicine and surgery diagnose, treat and operate upon human patients; animal husbandry is the breeding, feeding, housing and care of farm animals for milk, meat and eggs.

mcqs.q: Morphology tells us what a body part looks like, while physiology tells us:
options: The scientific name of the part
What the part does, i.e. how it functions
mcqs.why: Morphology is the study of form and external structure; physiology is the study of the functioning of body parts, i.e. what each part does.

mcqs.q: Computational biology uses computers and mathematical models mainly to:
options: Store, process and analyse biological data such as DNA and protein sequences
mcqs.why: Computational biology applies computers and mathematical models to biological data: comparing DNA and protein sequences, predicting protein structures and modelling populations.

mcqs.q: In the scientific method, careful observation of nature serves to:
options: Raise the scientific problem and provide the facts from which a hypothesis is made
Publish the results to other scientists
mcqs.why: Observation starts the scientific method: it raises the problem and supplies the facts used to frame a hypothesis; experiments, not observations alone, then test the hypothesis.

mcqs.q: Experimentation tests a hypothesis under controlled conditions so that conclusions rest on:
mcqs.why: Experiments confirm or reject the hypothesis with evidence under controlled conditions, so the conclusions of the scientific method rest on proof rather than guesswork.

mcqs.q: Pathology is the branch of biology that studies:
options: The internal structure of the body
mcqs.why: This lesson defines pathology as the study of diseases, their causes and effects; fossils belong to palaeontology and ocean life to marine biology.

mcqs.q: Marine biology is the study of:
options: Life only in rivers and lakes
mcqs.why: Marine biology, as defined in this lesson, is the study of life in the oceans: the plants, animals and microorganisms of the sea.

lessons.title: Detailed Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Link the study of Biology with that of Physics, Chemistry, Statistics, Geography, Economics and Computer Science.

Biology is linked with the other sciences. Physics: the working of sense organs, blood pressure, X-rays, microscopes and other instruments is explained by physics (biophysics). Chemistry: the composition and reactions of carbohydrates, proteins, enzymes and hormones are chemistry applied to life (biochemistry). Statistics: biological data on populations, heredity and experiments are analysed statistically (biostatistics). Geography: the distribution of organisms in different regions of the Earth is studied with geography (biogeography). Economics: crops, livestock, fisheries and forests are economic resources, and their production and trade involve economics. Computer Science: biological data are stored and analysed by computers (computational biology/bioinformatics).

Q: Explain how the study of Biology can lead to different professional studies.

Biology is the basic science for many professions. Its study leads to medicine and surgery (doctors), dentistry, pharmacy and nursing for human health; veterinary science and animal husbandry for livestock; agriculture, horticulture and forestry for plant production and conservation; fisheries for fish farming; biotechnology for industry and research; and forensics, where biological evidence is used in crime investigation. Thus a student of Biology can choose a professional study according to his interest in plants, animals, microbes or man.

Q: Science is a collaborative field in which scientists work together to share knowledge. Prove this statement by giving examples.

Science advances by teamwork and sharing. Example 1: the discovery of the cause of malaria was the combined work of many scientists: Laveran found the parasite Plasmodium in the blood of patients, and Ross later proved that mosquitoes transmit it; neither worked in isolation. Example 2: the structure of DNA was solved by Watson and Crick using the X-ray data of Rosalind Franklin and the findings of other researchers. Example 3: scientists all over the world share results through journals and conferences, repeat each other's experiments and build on them, as in the worldwide effort that produced vaccines against COVID-19. Knowledge is thus a shared, cumulative product.

Q: How a hypothesis is converted to theory, law and principle?

A hypothesis is a tentative answer to a problem. When experiments repeatedly support a hypothesis and its deductions, and other scientists confirm it, the hypothesis becomes an accepted explanation, a theory. A theory that is proved again and again by experiments over a long time, without exception, is elevated to a law or principle: a law is a uniform or constant fact of nature (e.g. the law of inheritance). So the path is: hypothesis -> (repeated experimental confirmation) -> theory -> (universal, exceptionless proof) -> law/principle.

Q: What are the basic steps a scientist adopts in order to solve a scientific problem?

The basic steps of the scientific method are: (1) Recognition of a scientific problem. (2) Observations: collecting facts about the problem from nature, books and previous work. (3) Making a hypothesis, a tentative answer to the problem. (4) Making deductions, the logical consequences ('if... then...') of the hypothesis. (5) Performing experiments to test the deductions. (6) Summarizing and reporting the results, accepting or rejecting the hypothesis and communicating the findings to others.

Q: Describe the work of different scientists in discovering the cause of malaria.

For centuries malaria was blamed on bad air from marshes. In 1880 the French physician Charles Laveran examined the blood of malaria patients and discovered the parasite Plasmodium in their red blood cells, proving that a microorganism causes the disease. The question of how the parasite reaches man remained. Ronald Ross, working in India, showed that the parasite develops in the stomach of the female Anopheles mosquito and is transmitted to healthy persons through its bite. Later workers (such as Grassi) confirmed the complete cycle in man. Together these scientists established the cause and the carrier of malaria.

Q: Write a descriptive note on the experiments performed by Ross.

Ronald Ross (1897-98) tested the hypothesis that mosquitoes transmit malaria. He allowed female Anopheles mosquitoes to feed on the blood of malaria patients and then dissected the mosquitoes after some days; he found the developmental stages of Plasmodium on the stomach wall of the mosquitoes, and later in their salivary glands. Because experiments on man were difficult, he repeated the work with bird malaria: he let mosquitoes that had fed on infected birds bite healthy birds, and the healthy birds developed malaria. These experiments proved that the mosquito is the carrier (vector) that transmits Plasmodium from a patient to a healthy person, for which Ross received the Nobel Prize in 1902.

mcqs.q: The application of statistics to biological data on populations, heredity and experiments is called:
mcqs.why: Biostatistics applies statistical methods to biological data such as populations, heredity and experimental results, as described in this lesson on biology's links with other sciences.

mcqs.q: The working of sense organs, blood pressure, X-rays and microscopes links biology with:
mcqs.why: Biophysics explains the working of sense organs, blood pressure, X-rays and microscopes through the laws of physics, as stated in this lesson.

mcqs.q: Which profession uses biological evidence, such as blood and hair, in crime investigation?
mcqs.why: Forensics applies biological evidence to crime investigation; it is one of the professional fields this lesson lists as growing out of the study of biology.

mcqs.q: A hypothesis becomes a theory when:
options: It is printed in a textbook
A single experiment supports it once
Experiments repeatedly support it and other scientists confirm it
mcqs.why: Only after repeated experimental support and confirmation by other scientists does a hypothesis become an accepted explanation, a theory, as this lesson explains.

mcqs.q: A theory proved again and again over a long time, without exception, is elevated to a:
mcqs.why: A law or principle is a uniform, exceptionless fact of nature; a theory that is universally proved over a long time is raised to that status, as described in this lesson.

mcqs.q: Which step of the scientific method comes immediately after making a hypothesis?
mcqs.why: The steps run: problem, observations, hypothesis, deductions, experiments and results. Deductions, the logical consequences of the hypothesis, come immediately after the hypothesis.

mcqs.q: Charles Laveran discovered that malaria is caused by:
options: The parasite Plasmodium present in the red blood cells of patients
mcqs.why: In 1880 Laveran examined the blood of malaria patients and found the parasite Plasmodium in their red blood cells, proving that a microorganism, not bad marsh air, causes malaria.

mcqs.q: Ronald Ross proved that malaria is transmitted to human beings by:
mcqs.why: Ross found the developmental stages of Plasmodium on the stomach wall and in the salivary glands of female Anopheles mosquitoes and proved that its bite transmits the parasite.

mcqs.q: In Ross's experiments with bird malaria, healthy birds developed malaria after:
options: Mosquitoes that had fed on infected birds bit them
They were kept near infected birds
mcqs.why: Ross allowed mosquitoes that had fed on infected birds to bite healthy birds, and the healthy birds developed malaria, proving that the mosquito is the carrier (vector) of the parasite.

mcqs.q: Watson and Crick solved the structure of DNA using X-ray data produced by:
mcqs.why: Watson and Crick built their DNA model using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data and the findings of other researchers; this lesson gives it as an example of science as collaborative work.

lessons.title: Inquisitive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Why is it important to classify biology into different branches such as botany, zoology, and microbiology? How does specialization benefit scientific research?

Living organisms are so numerous and varied that no scientist can study all of them in depth. Dividing Biology into branches (botany for plants, zoology for animals, microbiology for microorganisms, and sub-branches such as genetics and physiology) lets scientists specialise in one area, master its techniques and explore it deeply. Specialisation produces expert knowledge faster, develops better instruments and methods, and the results of all branches are combined for the benefit of mankind, e.g. in medicine and agriculture.

Q: How can a scientist apply the scientific method to confirm an observation that a certain plant species grows more quickly in shady places than in direct sunlight?

He applies the scientific method step by step. Problem: does the plant grow faster in shade? Observation: record the growth of the plant in both places. Hypothesis: the plant grows more quickly in shade than in direct sunlight. Deduction: if the hypothesis is true, then equal seedlings kept in shade will gain more height in a fixed time than identical seedlings kept in sunlight, all other conditions (water, soil, pot size) being equal. Experiment: grow several seedlings of the same species and age in shade and several in sunlight under otherwise identical conditions, and measure their growth over some weeks. Results: compare the average growth; if the shaded plants grew faster repeatedly, the observation is confirmed and the hypothesis is accepted; otherwise it is rejected or revised.

mcqs.q: Biology is divided into branches such as botany, zoology and microbiology mainly because:
options: Each branch must use a different language
The branches were fixed by government law
Organisms are so numerous and varied that no scientist can study all of them in depth
mcqs.why: Living organisms are too numerous and varied for any one scientist to master; dividing biology into branches lets scientists specialise in one area, as this lesson explains.

mcqs.q: Specialisation in one branch of biology benefits scientific research because it:
options: Produces expert knowledge faster and develops better instruments and methods
Stops scientists from sharing their results
mcqs.why: Specialists master the techniques of one area and explore it deeply, developing better instruments and methods; the results of all branches are then combined for the benefit of mankind.

mcqs.q: Botany is the branch of biology concerned with:
mcqs.why: Botany studies plants, zoology studies animals and microbiology studies microorganisms, as named in this lesson on the branches of biology.

mcqs.q: To test whether a plant grows faster in shade, which conditions must be kept the SAME for both groups of seedlings?
options: The final height of the plants
mcqs.why: The deduction requires all conditions except light, such as water, soil and pot size, to stay equal, so that any difference in growth can be credited to shade alone.

mcqs.q: In the shade experiment described in this lesson, the hypothesis is:
options: The plant grows more quickly in shade than in direct sunlight
mcqs.why: The hypothesis is the tentative answer under test: that this plant species grows more quickly in shady places than in direct sunlight.

mcqs.q: The observation about shade is confirmed only if:
options: Shaded plants grow faster repeatedly under otherwise identical conditions
One shaded plant grows tall a single time
The sunny plants are given less water
Seedlings of different ages are compared
mcqs.why: Confirmation requires repeated faster growth of the shaded plants with all other conditions identical; a single uncontrolled result proves nothing.

mcqs.q: If the shaded plants do NOT grow faster than the sunny ones, the scientist should:
options: Announce the hypothesis as a law
mcqs.why: In the scientific method, a hypothesis contradicted by experimental results is rejected or revised; it is never forced onto the data.

mcqs.q: Zoology is the branch of biology that studies:
mcqs.why: Zoology is the study of animals, just as botany is the study of plants; both are main branches named in this lesson.

mcqs.q: Microbiology is the branch of biology that studies:
mcqs.why: Microbiology deals with microorganisms, organisms too small to be seen with the naked eye; it is one of the main branches named in this lesson.

mcqs.q: Why are several seedlings used in each group of the shade experiment instead of just one?
options: Because a single seedling always dies
So the average growth is reliable and one unusual plant cannot mislead the result
To use up the extra pots
mcqs.why: Repeating the measurement on several seedlings and comparing the averages makes the result dependable; a single plant might be unusual for reasons unrelated to shade.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Which of the following taxonomic ranks represents the broadest rank?

(a) Species (b) Genus (c) Kingdom (d) Domain
Correct answer: Domain

Q: Which characteristics is unique to organisms in the domain Archaea?

(a) Cell walls made of peptidoglycan (b) Presence of a nucleus (c) Ability to live in extreme environments (d) Lack of ribosomes
Correct answer: Ability to live in extreme environments

Q: Which of these statements is NOT related to bacteria?

(a) Do not have a nucleus. (b) Cell wall made of peptidoglycan (c) Most are heterotrophic (d) Have chlorophyll in their chloroplast.
Correct answer: Have chlorophyll in their chloroplast.

Q: Which of these organisms belongs to the domain Eukarya?

(a) Escherichia coli (b) Yeast (c) Coronavirus (d) None of these
Correct answer: Yeast

Q: Which of the following is a key characteristic that distinguishes eukaryotic cells from prokaryotic cells?

(a) Lack of a cell wall (b) Presence of a nucleus (c) Absence of ribosomes (d) Smaller size
Correct answer: Presence of a nucleus

Q: Which kingdom includes organisms that are primarily unicellular, eukaryotic, and often heterotrophic?

(a) Archaea (b) Protista (c) Fungi (d) Plantae
Correct answer: Protista

Q: Why are fungi included in heterotrophic organisms?

(a) Have chitin in cell wall (b) Absorb nutrients (c) Reproduce by spores (d) Cannot prepare food
Correct answer: Absorb nutrients

Q: Why it is impossible to classify viruses within traditional biological kingdoms?

(a) They lack cellular structure and organelles. (b) They cannot perform photosynthesis. (c) They are smaller in size than bacteria. (d) They are parasites.
Correct answer: They lack cellular structure and organelles.

Q: Which of the following is the correct way for writing the scientific name of humans?

(a) Homo sapiens (in italics) (b) Homo sapiens (not in italics) (c) Homo Sapiens (d) homo sapiens
Correct answer: Homo sapiens (in italics)

Q: Which information you can get if you know the scientific name of an organism?

(a) Kingdom and phylum (b) Phylum and genus (c) Genus and species (d) Class and species
Correct answer: Genus and species

mcqs.q: Which of the following taxonomic ranks represents the broadest rank?
mcqs.why: The ranks run from domain (the broadest, highest rank) down through kingdom to species, the narrowest. Domain is broader than kingdom and genus.

mcqs.q: Which characteristics is unique to organisms in the domain Archaea?
options: Ability to live in extreme environments
mcqs.why: Archaea are famous for living in extreme environments such as hot springs and very salty or acidic places; this ability is their unique characteristic among the options given.

mcqs.q: Which of these statements is NOT related to bacteria?
mcqs.why: Bacteria have no chloroplasts at all; photosynthetic bacteria carry their pigments in the cell membrane. The other statements are true of bacteria, so this is the one NOT related to them.

mcqs.q: Which of these organisms belongs to the domain Eukarya?
mcqs.why: Yeast is a fungus, and fungi belong to the domain Eukarya because their cells have a true nucleus. Escherichia coli is a bacterium and coronavirus is a virus, which is not placed in any domain.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a key characteristic that distinguishes eukaryotic cells from prokaryotic cells?
mcqs.why: The key difference is that eukaryotic cells have a true, membrane-bound nucleus, while prokaryotic cells lack one. Both cell types have ribosomes, so that cannot be the distinguishing feature.

mcqs.q: Which kingdom includes organisms that are primarily unicellular, eukaryotic, and often heterotrophic?
mcqs.why: Protista includes organisms that are primarily unicellular and eukaryotic, and many of them, such as protozoa, are heterotrophic. Fungi, plants and archaea do not fit this description.

mcqs.q: Why are fungi included in heterotrophic organisms?
mcqs.why: Fungi cannot make their own food because they lack chlorophyll; they absorb nutrients from dead matter or living hosts, which is exactly what heterotrophic nutrition means.

mcqs.q: Why it is impossible to classify viruses within traditional biological kingdoms?
options: They lack cellular structure and organelles.
They are smaller in size than bacteria.
mcqs.why: Viruses are acellular: they have no cytoplasm, organelles or metabolism of their own and reproduce only inside a host cell, so they cannot be placed in kingdoms built on cellular characters.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the correct way for writing the scientific name of humans?
mcqs.why: In binomial nomenclature the scientific name is written in italics in print, with the genus beginning with a capital letter and the species with a small letter: Homo sapiens.

mcqs.q: Which information you can get if you know the scientific name of an organism?
mcqs.why: A scientific (binomial) name has exactly two parts: the first gives the genus and the second gives the species, so the name tells us the genus and species of the organism.

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: What is the term used to describe the variety of organisms in ecosystems?

Biodiversity (biological diversity): the variety of living organisms present in the different ecosystems of the Earth, including terrestrial, marine and desert ecosystems.

Q: How is the biodiversity crucial for humans and for the planet Earth?

Biodiversity provides us with food, medicines, raw materials and clean air and water, and it keeps ecosystems stable and productive: pollination of crops, purification of water, control of pests and recycling of nutrients all depend on a variety of species. For the planet, rich biodiversity maintains food webs, resists environmental change and keeps the Earth's life-support systems working; its loss threatens both nature and human survival.

Q: What are the seven taxonomic ranks used in the Linnaean system?

From the broadest to the narrowest: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. (Above the kingdom, the domain is now added as the highest rank.) Each rank is called a taxon, and species is the basic, most specific rank.

Q: Write the taxonomic ranks of lion and corn?

Lion: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Carnivora, Family Felidae, Genus Panthera, Species leo (scientific name Panthera leo). Corn: Kingdom Plantae, Phylum Angiospermae (flowering plants), Class Monocotyledons, Order Poales, Family Poaceae (grass family), Genus Zea, Species mays (scientific name Zea mays).

Q: What are the basic differences between archaea and bacteria?

Both are prokaryotes without a nucleus, but: the cell wall of bacteria is made of peptidoglycan, while archaea lack peptidoglycan in their walls; the membrane lipids of archaea are different (branched, ether-linked) from those of bacteria; archaea commonly live in extreme environments (hot springs, very salty or acidic places) while bacteria live almost everywhere; and in gene machinery (ribosomes and RNA polymerase) archaea resemble eukaryotes more than bacteria.

Q: What are the shortcomings of the three-kingdom classification system?

In the three-kingdom system all organisms were forced into Plantae, Animalia and Protista. Its shortcomings: bacteria, which are prokaryotic, were placed with plants; fungi, which lack chlorophyll and absorb food, were also treated as plants; organisms like Euglena, which show both plant and animal characters, could not be placed satisfactorily; and there was no place for viruses. These defects led to the modern domain and multi-kingdom systems.

Q: Which kingdom includes organisms that are multicellular and heterotrophic, and lack cell walls?

Kingdom Animalia: animals are multicellular, heterotrophic and their cells lack cell walls; they ingest food and digest it in specialized cavities.

Q: Enlist the distinguishing characteristics of fungi.

Fungi are eukaryotic organisms; their cell walls are made of chitin; they lack chlorophyll and are heterotrophic, absorbing food from dead matter (saprophytes) or living hosts (parasites); their body is made of thread-like hyphae forming a mycelium (yeasts are unicellular); they reproduce by spores and store food as glycogen.

Q: List the three domains that encompass all living organisms.

Domain Archaea, Domain Bacteria and Domain Eukarya. The domain is the highest level of classification.

Q: Why cannot we classify viruses in any kingdom?

Viruses are not made of cells: they have no cytoplasm, no organelles and no metabolism of their own, and they can reproduce only inside a living host cell. Outside a host they behave like non-living particles. Because they lack the characteristics of the organisms of all three domains and kingdoms, they are not included in the classification system of living organisms.

Q: How does binomial nomenclature facilitate clear communication about organisms across different languages?

A scientific name is the same all over the world and is not changed by language or region. Common names differ from place to place and language to language (onion is 'piyaz', 'ganda', 'bassal' or 'vassal' in different regions), and one common name may be used for several different organisms ('blue bell', 'black bird'). Binomial nomenclature gives every organism one unique two-part Latin name (genus + species), so scientists of all languages understand exactly which organism is meant.

mcqs.q: Biodiversity is the term used to describe:
options: The number of humans in a country
The variety of rocks in an area
The variety of living organisms in the ecosystems of the Earth
The different climates of the world
mcqs.why: Biodiversity (biological diversity) is the variety of living organisms present in the different ecosystems of the Earth, including terrestrial, marine and desert ecosystems.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a service that biodiversity provides to humans?
options: Pollination of crops and purification of water
mcqs.why: Biodiversity provides food, medicines, raw materials, clean air and water, and keeps ecosystems stable through services such as pollination of crops, purification of water and recycling of nutrients.

mcqs.q: In the Linnaean system, the broadest of the seven taxonomic ranks is:
mcqs.why: The seven ranks run from the broadest, kingdom, through phylum, class, order, family and genus to species, the narrowest and most specific rank.

mcqs.q: The scientific name of the lion, Panthera leo, shows that its genus is:
mcqs.why: In a binomial name the first part is the genus and the second the species: the lion's genus is Panthera and its species is leo; Felidae is its family and Animalia its kingdom.

mcqs.q: The cell wall of bacteria is made of peptidoglycan, while the cell wall of archaea:
mcqs.why: Both are prokaryotes, but bacteria have peptidoglycan in their walls while archaea lack peptidoglycan; their membrane lipids also differ, and archaea often live in extreme environments.

mcqs.q: One shortcoming of the old three-kingdom system was that:
options: Fungi, which lack chlorophyll and absorb food, were treated as plants
mcqs.why: In the three-kingdom system bacteria were placed with plants, fungi were also treated as plants although they absorb food and have no chlorophyll, and organisms like Euglena could not be placed satisfactorily.

mcqs.q: Which kingdom includes organisms that are multicellular and heterotrophic, and whose cells lack cell walls?
mcqs.why: Kingdom Animalia: animals are multicellular heterotrophs that ingest food, and their cells lack cell walls; fungi have walls of chitin and plants have walls of cellulose.

mcqs.q: The cell walls of fungi are made of:
mcqs.why: Fungi are eukaryotes whose cell walls are made of chitin; they lack chlorophyll, absorb food, have a body of hyphae (mycelium) and reproduce by spores.

mcqs.q: The highest level of classification, above the kingdom, is the:
mcqs.why: The three domains, Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya, encompass all living organisms, and the domain is the highest level of classification, above the kingdom.

mcqs.q: Binomial nomenclature helps scientists of different languages because:
options: Common names are translated word by word
Every organism has one unique scientific name that is the same all over the world
Each country chooses its own name
Names are written in the local script
mcqs.why: Common names differ from place to place and one name may serve several organisms, but a binomial name is unique and unchanged by language or region, so everyone knows exactly which organism is meant.

lessons.title: Detailed Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Discuss biodiversity and its significance in maintaining the health of ecosystems.

Biodiversity is the variety of species in an ecosystem, and each species has a role: producers make food, consumers transfer energy, decomposers recycle nutrients. A diverse ecosystem is stable and healthy because its food webs have many alternative pathways: if one species declines, others fill its role, so the ecosystem resists disease, pests and climate change and continues to provide clean water, fertile soil, pollination and a balanced atmosphere. Loss of biodiversity weakens these services and can collapse the ecosystem.

Q: Explain the importance of classification in biology and how it helps us understand the relationships between different organisms.

Classification arranges the millions of organisms into groups on the basis of similarities and differences. It makes the study of organisms easy and systematic, allows a new organism to be identified by comparing it with known groups, and shows relationships: organisms placed in the same group share a common ancestry and many characters, so knowing one member tells us much about the others. Classification thus reveals evolutionary relationships between organisms and is the basis of all biological research, agriculture and medicine.

Q: Describe the Linnaean system of classification in detail, stating the seven taxonomic ranks and their relationships.

The Linnaean system, given by Carolus Linnaeus, arranges organisms in a hierarchy of seven ranks (taxa), from the broadest to the most specific: Kingdom > Phylum > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species. Each higher rank contains many organisms sharing a few general characters; each lower rank contains fewer organisms sharing more characters. Species is the basic unit: members of a species are most similar and can interbreed. For example, the lion is: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Carnivora, Family Felidae, Genus Panthera, Species leo. Linnaeus also gave the system of binomial nomenclature for naming each species.

Q: Compare and contrast the domains Archaea and Bacteria, focusing on their key characteristics.

Similarities: both Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotic, unicellular, lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, and have circular DNA. Differences: (1) Cell wall: bacteria have peptidoglycan in their walls; archaea do not. (2) Membrane lipids: branched and ether-linked in archaea, unbranched and ester-linked in bacteria. (3) Habitat: archaea are famous for living in extreme environments (very hot, salty, acidic or oxygen-free); bacteria live in almost all environments. (4) Gene machinery: the ribosomes and enzymes of archaea resemble those of eukaryotes more than those of bacteria. These deep differences are why they are placed in separate domains.

Q: Describe the diagnostic characteristics of the four kingdoms within the domain Eukarya.

Domain Eukarya has four kingdoms. Protista: unicellular or simple multicellular eukaryotes; some are autotrophic (algae-like) and some heterotrophic (protozoa); they mostly live in water. Fungi: eukaryotic heterotrophs that absorb food; cell walls of chitin; body of hyphae (mycelium) or unicellular (yeast); reproduce by spores. Plantae: eukaryotic, multicellular autotrophs that make food by photosynthesis; cells have cellulose walls and chloroplasts; they have multicellular sex organs. Animalia: eukaryotic, multicellular heterotrophs that ingest food and digest it in specialized cavities; cells lack walls; most can move.

Q: Discuss the challenges of classifying viruses within the traditional three domains of life.

Viruses fit none of the three domains because they are acellular: they consist only of a nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat, with no cytoplasm, ribosomes or other organelles. They show no metabolism, growth or independent reproduction; they multiply only by hijacking a living host cell, and outside a host they are inert particles that can even be crystallised. Classification is based on cellular characters, so a non-cellular particle that is neither fully living nor non-living cannot be placed in Archaea, Bacteria or Eukarya and is kept outside the system.

Q: Explain the rules and guidelines for suggesting scientific names to organisms.

The rules of binomial nomenclature are: (1) The name is taken from Latin and has two parts: the genus name first, then the species name. (2) Every scientific name must be unique: the same name cannot be used for two different organisms. (3) The genus name begins with a capital letter; the species name begins with a small letter. (4) In print the name is written in italics. (5) When hand-written, the two parts are underlined separately. Example: Homo sapiens for man, Panthera leo for lion.

mcqs.q: A diverse ecosystem is stable and healthy mainly because:
options: Its food webs have many alternative pathways, so other species fill the role of a declining one
It has only one food chain
mcqs.why: Each species has a role in the ecosystem; with many species the food webs have alternative pathways, so the ecosystem resists disease, pests and climate change and keeps providing its services.

mcqs.q: Classification helps a biologist identify a newly found organism by:
options: Guessing its name from its size
Asking what local people call it
Comparing it with the known groups and their diagnostic characters
mcqs.why: Classification arranges organisms into groups by similarities and differences, so a new organism can be identified by comparing it with known groups, and its grouping also reveals its evolutionary relationships.

mcqs.q: Who gave the Linnaean system of classification and binomial nomenclature?
mcqs.why: The Linnaean system, given by Carolus Linnaeus, arranges organisms in seven ranks from kingdom to species, and Linnaeus also gave the system of binomial nomenclature.

mcqs.q: Archaea and bacteria are similar in that both:
options: Have peptidoglycan in their cell walls
Are prokaryotic, unicellular and lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
mcqs.why: Both domains are prokaryotic and unicellular with circular DNA and no true nucleus; they differ in wall chemistry, membrane lipids, habitat and gene machinery.

mcqs.q: Which kingdom of Eukarya is made of eukaryotic heterotrophs that absorb food and reproduce by spores?
mcqs.why: Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs that absorb food; their walls are of chitin, their body is a mycelium of hyphae (or unicellular, like yeast) and they reproduce by spores.

mcqs.q: Plantae differ from Animalia in that plants:
options: Are multicellular autotrophs whose cells have cellulose walls and chloroplasts
Ingest food and digest it in cavities
Can move from place to place
mcqs.why: Plantae make their own food by photosynthesis and their cells have cellulose walls and chloroplasts; animals ingest food, lack cell walls and mostly can move.

mcqs.q: Viruses are kept outside the three domains of life because they:
options: Consist only of nucleic acid in a protein coat, with no cytoplasm, ribosomes or metabolism
mcqs.why: Viruses are acellular particles that show no metabolism or independent reproduction and multiply only inside a living host cell, so cellular classification cannot place them in Archaea, Bacteria or Eukarya.

mcqs.q: In print, a scientific name such as Panthera leo must be written:
options: In bold, both words with capital letters
In italics, genus with a capital letter and species with a small letter
Underlined in print, both words small
In brackets after the common name
mcqs.why: The rules of binomial nomenclature require a two-part Latin name, genus capitalised and species in small letters, written in italics in print and underlined separately when handwritten.

mcqs.q: The same scientific name must never be used for two different organisms. This rule ensures that each name is:
mcqs.why: Every scientific name must be unique: the same name cannot be used for two different organisms, otherwise scientists could not tell which organism is meant.

mcqs.q: Members of a species are grouped together because they are the most similar and can:
mcqs.why: Species is the basic unit of classification: its members share the most characters and can interbreed, while each higher rank contains more organisms sharing fewer, more general characters.

lessons.title: Inquisitive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: How might placing an organism in the incorrect taxonomic group affect conservation or scientific studies?

Classification is the basis of conservation and research. If an organism is placed in the wrong group, scientists will assume it has the characters, needs and relatives of that group: its habitat requirements, food and breeding behaviour may be wrongly predicted, so conservation plans (protected areas, breeding programmes, legal protection) may fail and the species may be lost. Wrong grouping also corrupts scientific studies: data about distribution, evolution, disease relations and economic uses become unreliable, and other researchers build on the error. Correct identification and classification are therefore essential.

Q: Imagine you discover a new organism. What steps would you take to classify and name it according to the principles of binomial nomenclature?

Steps: (1) Study the organism carefully: its structure, cell type, mode of nutrition, reproduction and habitat, and compare it with known organisms. (2) Decide its domain and kingdom, then assign it step by step to phylum, class, order and family by matching its characters with the diagnostic characters of each rank. (3) Decide the genus: if it fits an existing genus, place it there; if not, propose a new genus. (4) Give it a species name following binomial nomenclature: a unique two-part Latin name, genus with a capital letter and species with a small letter, written in italics in print (underlined separately by hand). (5) Publish the description so other scientists can confirm the classification.

mcqs.q: If an organism is placed in the wrong taxonomic group, conservation plans may fail because:
options: Its habitat needs, food and breeding behaviour will be wrongly predicted from the wrong group
mcqs.why: Scientists assume a grouped organism has the characters and needs of its group; wrong grouping makes wrong predictions about habitat, food and breeding, so protected areas and breeding programmes may fail.

mcqs.q: The FIRST step in classifying a newly discovered organism is to:
options: Study its structure, cell type, nutrition, reproduction and habitat and compare it with known organisms
Give it a species name at once
mcqs.why: Classification begins with careful study of the organism's characters and comparison with known organisms; only then can its domain, kingdom and lower ranks be decided step by step.

mcqs.q: When naming a new organism, a new genus is proposed only if:
options: It is found in a new country
It is very large in size
It does not fit into any existing genus
mcqs.why: If the organism matches an existing genus it is placed there; a new genus is proposed only when its characters do not fit any known genus, as this lesson describes.

mcqs.q: After classifying a new organism and giving it a binomial name, the scientist should:
options: Publish the description so other scientists can confirm the classification
mcqs.why: Publishing the description lets other scientists check and confirm the classification and name, which is the final step described in this lesson.

mcqs.q: Wrong classification corrupts scientific studies because:
options: Data on distribution, evolution, disease relations and economic uses become unreliable and others build on the error
mcqs.why: Classification is the basis of research: a wrong group falsifies the data built on it, and other researchers then build further work on the error.

mcqs.q: In assigning a new organism to ranks, the scientist matches its characters against:
options: The climate of its country only
The diagnostic characters of each rank, from domain and kingdom down to family
mcqs.why: The organism is assigned step by step, domain and kingdom first, then phylum, class, order and family, by matching its characters with the diagnostic characters of each rank.

mcqs.q: A species placed under legal protection on the basis of wrong identification may be lost because:
options: Laws do not protect small species
The protection is designed for the wrong organism's needs
mcqs.why: Legal protection, protected areas and breeding programmes are designed around the assumed identity of the species; if the identification is wrong, the measures miss its real needs and the species may be lost.

mcqs.q: The genus part of a binomial name is written:
mcqs.why: In binomial nomenclature the genus name comes first and begins with a capital letter, followed by the species name in small letters.

mcqs.q: Correct identification and classification are described in this lesson as:
options: Essential for both conservation and scientific studies
mcqs.why: Because conservation plans and research data both rest on the grouping of the organism, correct identification and classification are essential, as this lesson concludes.

mcqs.q: To decide the kingdom of a new organism, the most useful characters include:
options: Its cell type and mode of nutrition
mcqs.why: Kingdoms are distinguished by fundamental characters such as cell type (prokaryotic or eukaryotic) and mode of nutrition (autotrophic or heterotrophic), which the scientist studies first.

lessons.notes_html:

mcqs.q: The process of cellular respiration occurs in:
mcqs.why: Cellular respiration, the release of energy from glucose, takes place in the mitochondria, the powerhouse of the cell; the nucleus controls the cell and ribosomes make proteins.

mcqs.q: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) is primarily involved in the synthesis of:
mcqs.why: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum has no ribosomes and is the site of lipid synthesis; proteins are made by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

mcqs.q: Ribosomes are composed of:
mcqs.why: Ribosomes are small particles made of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and proteins, as this chapter's list of the chemical composition of cell parts confirms.

mcqs.q: What is the primary function of ribosomes?
mcqs.why: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis: they read the instructions carried from the nucleus and join amino acids into proteins.

mcqs.q: Which cell organelle is involved in packaging and modifying proteins?
mcqs.why: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies them, sorts them and packs them into vesicles; it is the packaging organelle of the cell.

mcqs.q: Which cell organelle is responsible for breaking down waste materials?
mcqs.why: Lysosomes contain strong digestive enzymes that break down waste materials, worn-out organelles, food particles and invading bacteria.

mcqs.q: Which of the following cell structures is involved in maintaining cell shape?
mcqs.why: The cytoskeleton, a network of fibres in the cytoplasm, maintains the shape of the cell and helps in movement of materials inside it.

mcqs.q: Which specialized region of the nucleus is responsible for ribosome assembly?
mcqs.why: The nucleolus is the dense, specialized region of the nucleus where ribosomes are assembled: it makes rRNA and the ribosomal subunits.

mcqs.q: What is the main function of the nuclear pores?
options: Control of pH of the cell
mcqs.why: Nuclear pores in the nuclear envelope control the transport of molecules between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, letting mRNA out and needed materials in.

mcqs.q: Which of the following cellular structures is found in animal cells and helps in cell division?
mcqs.why: Centrioles are found in animal cells and take part in cell division by organising the spindle; higher plant cells lack centrioles.

mcqs.q: Which sub-cellular organelle plays a crucial role in energy production within the cell?
mcqs.why: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration and produce the cell's energy (ATP); that is why they are called the powerhouse of the cell.

mcqs.q: In a multicellular plant, which cell type is responsible for the production of glucose?
mcqs.why: Mesophyll cells of the leaf are packed with chloroplasts and carry out photosynthesis, producing glucose; xylem and phloem only transport materials.

mcqs.q: Which organelle can double its number by itself?
mcqs.why: Mitochondria contain their own DNA and ribosomes, so they can divide and double their number by themselves, like chloroplasts.

mcqs.q: Which of these are present on the surface of rough endoplasmic reticulum?
mcqs.why: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is 'rough' because ribosomes are studded on its surface; these ribosomes make the proteins that enter the reticulum.

mcqs.q: Which organelle is known as the powerhouse of the cell?
mcqs.why: The mitochondrion is called the powerhouse of the cell because cellular respiration there releases the energy of glucose and stores it as ATP for all cell activities.

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: What are the main functions of cell membrane?

The cell membrane (a lipid bilayer with embedded proteins) separates the cell from its surroundings and protects it; it is selectively permeable, so it controls the entry and exit of substances; it gives the cell its shape; and its surface proteins and markers help the cell recognise other cells and receive signals.

Q: What key role does the Golgi apparatus play in eukaryotic cells?

The Golgi apparatus receives proteins and lipids from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies them, sorts them and packs them into vesicles for transport to their destinations inside or outside the cell; it also makes lysosomes. It is the packaging and dispatching centre of the cell.

Q: How do lysosomes contribute to the cell's functioning?

Lysosomes contain strong digestive enzymes. They break down waste materials, worn-out organelles and food particles, and digest invading bacteria, converting complex biomolecules into simpler compounds that the cell can reuse. They keep the cell clean and recycle its materials.

Q: Which organelle detoxifies harmful substances and breaks down lipids?

The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER): it detoxifies harmful substances (especially in liver cells) and is the site where lipids are made and broken down. (Peroxisomes also break down toxic hydrogen peroxide.)

Q: What is the smooth endoplasmic reticulum responsible for?

The SER is responsible for the synthesis of lipids (including phospholipids and steroids), the detoxification of drugs and poisons, the breakdown of lipids and carbohydrates, and the storage of calcium ions in muscle cells.

Q: How do the vacuoles in plant cells differ from vacuoles in animal cells?

Plant cells have one large central vacuole filled with cell sap, which can occupy most of the cell and maintains turgor pressure. Animal cells have only small, temporary vacuoles (if any), used for storage or transport, and they do not produce turgor.

Q: What could happen if lysosomal enzymes stop working properly?

Wastes and worn-out parts would accumulate inside the cell, old organelles would not be recycled, and invading microbes would not be destroyed. The cell would become cluttered and poisoned by its own wastes, its working would be disturbed, and it could become diseased or die. (Defective lysosomal enzymes cause storage diseases in man.)

Q: Why are the cristae important for cellular respiration?

Cristae are the folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane. They greatly increase the surface area on which the reactions of cellular respiration (the electron transport chain) take place, so much more ATP (energy) can be produced. Without the folds, the mitochondrion could not meet the cell's energy needs.

Q: How are chromatin and chromosomes related?

They are two states of the same material, DNA with proteins. During interphase the genetic material exists as a loose, thread-like network called chromatin. When the cell prepares to divide, the chromatin condenses, coils and shortens into the thick, rod-shaped chromosomes that can be seen under the microscope.

Q: Which type of cell is responsible for sending nerve signals?

The neuron (nerve cell): its long fibres conduct nerve impulses (electrical signals) from one part of the body to another, linking sense organs, the brain/spinal cord and muscles.

Q: What do mesophyll cells do in plant leaves?

Mesophyll cells are the ground cells of the leaf, packed with chloroplasts. They carry out photosynthesis: they absorb light and carbon dioxide and make glucose, which is the food of the plant. (The palisade mesophyll does most of the photosynthesis; the spongy mesophyll also allows gas exchange.)

Q: How would you define a stem cell?

A stem cell is an undifferentiated (unspecialized) cell that can divide to produce more stem cells and can differentiate into specific types of cells, such as muscle, nerve or blood cells, when needed.

Q: Name the chemical compounds that make up: a. Cell membrane b. Fungal cell wall c. Plant cell wall d. Bacterial cell wall e. Ribosomes f. Chromosomes

a. Cell membrane: lipids (phospholipids) and proteins. b. Fungal cell wall: chitin. c. Plant cell wall: cellulose and hemicellulose (primary wall), with lignin in the secondary wall. d. Bacterial cell wall: peptidoglycan. e. Ribosomes: ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and proteins. f. Chromosomes: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and proteins (histones).

Q: Label the parts of these cell diagrams?

Animal cell (left diagram): 1 - Mitochondrion, 2 - Cell membrane, 3 - Cytoplasm, 4 - Endoplasmic reticulum, 5 - Lysosome, 6 - Golgi apparatus, 7 - Vacuole (small). Plant cell (right diagram): 1 - Golgi apparatus, 2 - Nucleus, 3 - Endoplasmic reticulum, 4 - Central vacuole, 5 - Mitochondrion, 6 - Cytoplasm, 7 - Chloroplast. (The plant cell is bounded outside the membrane by the cell wall.)

mcqs.q: The cell membrane is selectively permeable. This means it:
options: Allows every substance to pass freely
Controls which substances enter and leave the cell
mcqs.why: The cell membrane is a lipid bilayer with embedded proteins; being selectively permeable, it controls the entry and exit of substances and so protects the cell and keeps its internal composition steady.

mcqs.q: The Golgi apparatus is called the packaging and dispatching centre of the cell because it:
options: Modifies proteins and lipids, packs them into vesicles and sends them to their destinations
mcqs.why: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins and lipids from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies and sorts them, packs them into vesicles for transport, and also makes lysosomes.

mcqs.q: If lysosomal enzymes stopped working properly, the cell would:
options: Fill up with wastes and worn-out parts and could become diseased or die
mcqs.why: Lysosomes digest wastes, worn-out organelles and invading microbes; without their enzymes, wastes accumulate, materials are not recycled and the cell is poisoned by its own wastes.

mcqs.q: Which organelle detoxifies harmful substances and is especially active in liver cells?
mcqs.why: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum detoxifies drugs and poisons, makes and breaks down lipids and stores calcium ions in muscle cells, as this lesson states.

mcqs.q: Plant cells differ from animal cells in their vacuole because a plant cell has:
options: Many large vacuoles full of enzymes
One large central vacuole filled with cell sap that maintains turgor
mcqs.why: A mature plant cell has a single large central vacuole that can occupy most of the cell and maintains turgor pressure; animal cells have only small, temporary vacuoles or none.

mcqs.q: Cristae, the folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane, are important because they:
options: Store the DNA of the cell
Greatly increase the surface area for the reactions of cellular respiration, so more ATP is made
mcqs.why: The electron transport chain of respiration runs on the inner mitochondrial membrane; its folds, the cristae, multiply the working area so the mitochondrion can produce much more ATP.

mcqs.q: Chromatin and chromosomes are related because:
options: Chromatin is made of RNA and chromosomes of lipid
They are found in different cells
They are two states of the same material: loose chromatin condenses into chromosomes for division
mcqs.why: Both are DNA combined with proteins: during interphase the genetic material is a loose thread-like network called chromatin, which coils and shortens into rod-shaped chromosomes when the cell divides.

mcqs.q: The type of cell responsible for sending nerve signals through the body is the:
mcqs.why: The neuron (nerve cell) has long fibres that conduct nerve impulses from one part of the body to another, linking sense organs, brain and spinal cord with muscles.

mcqs.q: A stem cell is best defined as:
options: A cell found only in plant stems
A dead cell of the xylem
An undifferentiated cell that can divide and differentiate into specific cell types
A cell that can never divide
mcqs.why: A stem cell is unspecialized: it can produce more stem cells and can differentiate into specific types such as muscle, nerve or blood cells when needed.

mcqs.q: The plant cell wall is made mainly of:
mcqs.why: From this lesson's composition list: the plant cell wall is cellulose and hemicellulose (with lignin in the secondary wall); chitin makes the fungal wall and peptidoglycan the bacterial wall.

lessons.title: Detailed Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Explain the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane.

In the fluid mosaic model the cell membrane is a double layer (bilayer) of phospholipid molecules: their water-loving heads face outward and their water-hating tails face inward. Protein molecules are embedded in this bilayer like pieces of a mosaic; some pass through it and act as channels and carriers, others sit on the surfaces. The whole structure is fluid: the lipids and proteins can move sideways, so the membrane is flexible and self-sealing, and it is selectively permeable.

Q: Describe the structure and functions of the cell wall.

Structure: the cell wall lies outside the cell membrane in plant cells. The primary wall is thin and flexible, made of cellulose and hemicellulose; in woody cells a secondary wall containing lignin is laid down inside it, making it thick and rigid. Neighbouring cells are joined by the middle lamella, and plasmodesmata pass through the walls. Functions: it gives shape, strength and mechanical support to the cell and plant; it protects the cell; it prevents the cell from bursting when it takes up water; and it allows water and solutes to pass through it (it is freely permeable).

Q: Discuss the components of the nucleus.

The nucleus is a spherical or oval body bounded by a double membrane, the nuclear envelope, which has nuclear pores controlling the transport of molecules between nucleus and cytoplasm. Inside is the nucleoplasm (nuclear sap). Suspended in it is the chromatin, DNA combined with proteins, which condenses into chromosomes during division. The dense nucleolus is the region where ribosomes are assembled (it makes rRNA and ribosomal subunits). The nucleus controls all the activities of the cell and carries the hereditary information.

Q: Describe the structure and function of lysosome and endoplasmic reticulum.

Lysosome: a small spherical sac bounded by a single membrane and filled with strong digestive enzymes. It digests wastes, worn-out organelles, food particles and invading microbes, and recycles the products. Endoplasmic reticulum: a network of flattened membrane sacs and tubes continuous with the nuclear envelope. The rough ER bears ribosomes and makes and transports proteins; the smooth ER (without ribosomes) makes lipids, detoxifies harmful substances and stores calcium. Together the ER forms the cell's internal transport and manufacturing system.

Q: Describe the formation and function of the Golgi complex.

Formation: the Golgi complex (Golgi apparatus) is formed from membranes derived from the endoplasmic reticulum; vesicles from the ER fuse to build its stack of flattened sacs (cisternae). Function: it receives proteins and lipids from the ER, modifies them (e.g. adding carbohydrate to make glycoproteins), sorts them and packs them into vesicles that carry them to the cell membrane for export or to other organelles; it also produces lysosomes and, in plant cells, materials for the cell wall.

Q: Describe the structure and functions of the chloroplast.

Structure: the chloroplast is a lens-shaped organelle bounded by a double membrane. Inside is the fluid stroma, in which a system of flattened membrane sacs, the thylakoids, is stacked into grana. The thylakoid membranes carry the green pigment chlorophyll; the stroma contains enzymes, DNA and ribosomes. Function: chloroplasts are the site of photosynthesis: in the grana, light energy is trapped and converted to chemical energy, and in the stroma that energy is used to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.

Q: How does turgor pressure develop in a plant cell?

When a plant cell is placed in water (or the soil is wet), water enters the cell by osmosis and collects in the central vacuole. The vacuole swells and presses the cytoplasm against the cell wall. The wall resists this expansion, and the outward pressure of the contents against the wall is the turgor pressure. It makes the cell turgid (firm), keeps soft parts of the plant upright and helps in growth and in opening of stomata.

Q: Write any four differences between a plant cell and an animal cell.

Four differences: (1) A plant cell has a cell wall outside the membrane; an animal cell has no wall. (2) A plant cell has chloroplasts for photosynthesis; an animal cell has none. (3) A plant cell has one large central vacuole; an animal cell has small vacuoles or none. (4) An animal cell has centrioles for cell division; a (higher) plant cell lacks centrioles. (Plant cells also have a regular fixed shape, animal cells are more variable.)

Q: Describe the concept of division of labour and how it applies in multicellular organisms. Give at least three examples.

Division of labour means that different parts perform different specific tasks, so the whole work is done efficiently. In a multicellular organism the cells are specialized: each type of cell performs one function for the whole body. Examples: (1) mesophyll cells of the leaf make food by photosynthesis for the whole plant; (2) red blood cells carry oxygen to all tissues while white blood cells fight infection; (3) neurons transmit nerve impulses, while muscle cells produce movement. No single cell does everything; together the specialized cells keep the organism alive.

Q: Write a note on cell specialization.

Cell specialization (differentiation) is the process by which unspecialized cells, such as stem cells, develop the particular structures needed to perform one specific function. The specialized cell changes its shape and contents: a neuron grows long fibres to conduct impulses, a red blood cell loses its nucleus and fills with haemoglobin to carry oxygen, a mesophyll cell fills with chloroplasts to photosynthesise, and a muscle cell fills with contractile fibres. Specialization makes each task more efficient and is the basis of tissues and organs.

mcqs.q: In the fluid mosaic model, the basic framework of the cell membrane is:
options: A bilayer of phospholipids with protein molecules embedded in it
A sheet of chitin and protein
mcqs.why: The membrane is a double layer of phospholipids, heads facing outward and tails inward, with protein molecules embedded like pieces of a mosaic; the whole structure is fluid and selectively permeable.

mcqs.q: The middle lamella and plasmodesmata are features of the:
mcqs.why: Neighbouring plant cells are joined by the middle lamella of their walls, and plasmodesmata pass through the walls connecting the cells; the wall also gives shape, support and protection.

mcqs.q: The part of the nucleus that controls transport of molecules between nucleus and cytoplasm is the:
options: Nuclear pores in the nuclear envelope
mcqs.why: The nucleus is bounded by a double membrane, the nuclear envelope, whose nuclear pores control the transport of molecules between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.

mcqs.q: Rough endoplasmic reticulum differs from smooth endoplasmic reticulum in that the rough ER:
options: Bears ribosomes and makes and transports proteins
mcqs.why: The rough ER is studded with ribosomes and is the protein-making and transport system; the smooth ER, without ribosomes, makes lipids, detoxifies substances and stores calcium.

mcqs.q: The Golgi complex is formed from membranes derived from the:
mcqs.why: Vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse to build the Golgi stack of flattened sacs (cisternae), which then modifies, sorts and packs the ER's products.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplast, where the light energy is trapped in the:
options: Thylakoid membranes of the grana, which carry chlorophyll
mcqs.why: Chlorophyll sits in the thylakoid membranes stacked into grana; there light energy is converted to chemical energy, and the stroma then uses it to make glucose.

mcqs.q: Turgor pressure develops in a plant cell when:
options: Water enters by osmosis, the vacuole swells and presses the cytoplasm against the wall
The cell loses water and shrinks
mcqs.why: Water entering by osmosis collects in the central vacuole, which swells and presses the contents against the resisting cell wall; this outward pressure is turgor pressure, which keeps the cell firm.

mcqs.q: Which of these structures is present in an animal cell but NOT in a higher plant cell?
mcqs.why: Animal cells have centrioles for cell division, while higher plant cells lack them; plant cells instead have a cell wall, chloroplasts and one large central vacuole that animal cells do not have.

mcqs.q: Division of labour in a multicellular organism means that:
options: Cells divide as fast as possible
One cell controls all the others
Different specialized cells perform different specific tasks for the whole body
mcqs.why: In division of labour each cell type does one job efficiently: mesophyll cells make food, red blood cells carry oxygen, neurons conduct impulses and muscle cells produce movement.

mcqs.q: A red blood cell is specialized for carrying oxygen because it:
options: Loses its nucleus and fills with haemoglobin
mcqs.why: During specialization the red blood cell loses its nucleus and fills with haemoglobin to carry oxygen; long fibres belong to neurons and chloroplasts to mesophyll cells.

lessons.title: Inquisitive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: What impact might mitochondrial dysfunction or absence have on other organelles' ability to operate in a cell?

Almost every activity of the cell needs ATP, which the mitochondria supply by cellular respiration. If mitochondria fail, the energy supply stops: ribosomes cannot make proteins, the Golgi apparatus cannot process and pack them, active transport across membranes stops, the cytoskeleton cannot move materials, and lysosomes and other organelles slow down or stop. The whole cell is starved of energy, wastes accumulate, and the cell may die: energy failure in mitochondria is felt by every other organelle.

Q: What may happen if the coordination between the ribosomes and the nucleus were to fail, and why is it so important?

The nucleus holds the DNA and sends out messenger RNA carrying instructions for making each protein; the ribosomes read those instructions and build the proteins. If this coordination failed, ribosomes would not receive the correct instructions: needed enzymes and structural proteins would not be made (or wrong ones would), the cell could not grow, repair itself or respond to needs, and its working would break down. The coordination is vital because proteins do almost all the work of the cell, and only the nucleus knows which proteins are required.

mcqs.q: If the mitochondria of a cell fail, the first thing every other organelle loses is:
mcqs.why: Almost every activity of the cell needs ATP, which mitochondria supply by cellular respiration; if they fail, protein synthesis, packaging and active transport all slow down or stop.

mcqs.q: Active transport across the cell membrane would stop when mitochondria fail because it requires:
mcqs.why: Active transport moves substances against their gradient using ATP; with mitochondrial failure the energy supply stops, so active transport, and with it much of the cell's work, ceases.

mcqs.q: The instructions for making each protein are held in the nucleus in the form of:
options: DNA, sent out as messenger RNA
mcqs.why: The nucleus holds the DNA and sends out messenger RNA carrying the instructions for each protein; the ribosomes read those instructions and build the proteins.

mcqs.q: If coordination between the nucleus and ribosomes failed, ribosomes would:
options: Not receive the correct instructions, so needed proteins would not be made
mcqs.why: Without the mRNA instructions from the nucleus, ribosomes cannot make the needed enzymes and structural proteins, so the cell cannot grow, repair itself or respond to needs.

mcqs.q: Proteins are described in this lesson as doing:
options: Only the making of the cell wall
Almost all the work of the cell
mcqs.why: Enzymes, structural parts, carriers and signals are all proteins; because proteins do almost all the cell's work, the nucleus-ribosome coordination that produces them is vital.

mcqs.q: Energy failure in mitochondria is felt by every other organelle because:
options: All organelles depend on the ATP that mitochondria produce
Mitochondria contain the cell's DNA only
mcqs.why: Ribosomes, the Golgi apparatus, the cytoskeleton and membrane pumps all run on ATP; the whole cell is starved of energy when mitochondria fail, wastes accumulate and the cell may die.

mcqs.q: Which organelle would be unable to process and pack proteins if ATP ran out?
mcqs.why: Processing, sorting and packing proteins into vesicles in the Golgi apparatus needs energy; this lesson lists it among the activities that stop when mitochondria fail.

mcqs.q: Messenger RNA is important in the working of the cell because it:
options: Carries the protein-making instructions from the nucleus to the ribosomes
mcqs.why: The nucleus sends out messenger RNA with the instructions for each protein, and ribosomes read the mRNA to build that protein; this is the coordination this lesson describes.

mcqs.q: A cell whose mitochondria are absent would still be able to perform which of these poorly or not at all?
options: It would fail at nearly all energy-requiring activities, including growth and repair
It would only lose its colour
mcqs.why: Without mitochondrial ATP the cell cannot grow, repair itself or respond to needs; its working breaks down and it may die, as this lesson explains.

mcqs.q: The hereditary information that decides which proteins a cell makes is stored in:
mcqs.why: Only the nucleus, through its DNA, knows which proteins are required; it directs protein production by sending mRNA to the ribosomes.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: In which phase of cell cycle, maximum growth occurs in cell?

(a) M phase (b) S phase (c) G1 phase (d) G2 phase
Correct answer: G1 phase

Q: In which phase of cell cycle, the chromosomes duplicate?

(a) Mitosis (b) G1 phase (c) G2 phase (d) S phase
Correct answer: S phase

Q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of mitosis?

(a) It occurs in somatic cells. (b) It results in genetically identical daughter cells. (c) The chromosome number is halved in daughter cells. (d) It results in the formation of two daughter cells.
Correct answer: The chromosome number is halved in daughter cells.

Q: At which stage of mitosis chromosomes line up in the centre?

(a) Prophase (b) Metaphase (c) Anaphase (d) Telophase
Correct answer: Metaphase

Q: If you observe a cell in which nuclear membrane is reforming around two sets of chromosomes, what stage of cell cycle is this?

(a) Anaphase (b) Telophase (c) Prophase (d) Metaphase
Correct answer: Telophase

Q: How does the centrosome contribute to mitosis?

(a) Initiates DNA replication (b) Makes mitotic spindle (c) Forms the nuclear envelope (d) Duplicates organelles
Correct answer: Makes mitotic spindle

Q: Centrosomes make mitotic spindle in;

(a) Animal cells (b) Plant cells (c) Prokaryotic cells (d) All of these
Correct answer: Animal cells

Q: An organism has 4 pairs of chromosomes. After meiosis-I, how many chromosomes and chromatids will be present in each daughter cell?

(a) 8 chromosomes and 16 chromatids (b) 4 chromosomes and 8 chromatids (c) 4 chromosomes and 4 chromatids (d) 8 chromosomes and 8 chromatids
Correct answer: 4 chromosomes and 8 chromatids

Q: Which event is unique to meiosis but not mitosis?

(a) DNA replication (b) Chromosome alignment (c) Crossing over (d) Nuclear division
Correct answer: Crossing over

Q: Why is meiosis-II necessary after meiosis-I?

(a) To replicate chromosomes (b) To reduce chromosome number (c) To separate sister chromatids (d) To ensure genetic recombination
Correct answer: To separate sister chromatids

mcqs.q: In which phase of cell cycle, maximum growth occurs in cell?
mcqs.why: During G1 (gap 1) the cell grows in size, makes proteins, enzymes and organelles and carries out its normal activities; it is the phase of maximum growth of the cell.

mcqs.q: In which phase of cell cycle, the chromosomes duplicate?
mcqs.why: In the S (synthesis) phase DNA replication occurs: the chromosomes are duplicated, each forming two sister chromatids, so both daughter cells can receive a complete set.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of mitosis?
options: The chromosome number is halved in daughter cells.
It results in genetically identical daughter cells.
It results in the formation of two daughter cells.
mcqs.why: Halving of the chromosome number is a feature of meiosis, not mitosis. Mitosis occurs in somatic cells and produces two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number.

mcqs.q: At which stage of mitosis chromosomes line up in the centre?
mcqs.why: At metaphase the spindle fibres arrange all the chromosomes in a line at the equator (centre) of the cell, each attached to fibres from both poles.

mcqs.q: If you observe a cell in which nuclear membrane is reforming around two sets of chromosomes, what stage of cell cycle is this?
mcqs.why: A new nuclear envelope forming around each of the two sets of chromosomes at the poles is the sign of telophase, the last stage of mitosis.

mcqs.q: How does the centrosome contribute to mitosis?
mcqs.why: The centrosome organises and makes the spindle fibres of the mitotic spindle, which arrange the chromosomes and pull them to the poles during division.

mcqs.q: Centrosomes make mitotic spindle in;
mcqs.why: Centrosomes containing centrioles are found in animal cells, where they make the mitotic spindle; higher plant cells form a spindle without centrosomes.

mcqs.q: An organism has 4 pairs of chromosomes. After meiosis-I, how many chromosomes and chromatids will be present in each daughter cell?
