mcqs.why: The organism is diploid with 8 chromosomes (4 pairs). Meiosis-I halves the number, so each daughter cell has 4 chromosomes, and because sister chromatids have not yet separated, each chromosome has 2 chromatids: 8 chromatids in all.

mcqs.q: Which event is unique to meiosis but not mitosis?
mcqs.why: Crossing over, the exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes in prophase I, occurs only in meiosis; it produces new gene combinations.

mcqs.q: Why is meiosis-II necessary after meiosis-I?
mcqs.why: Meiosis-I separates homologous chromosomes, but the sister chromatids remain joined; meiosis-II is needed to separate the sister chromatids, as in mitosis, completing the formation of haploid cells.

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Enlist the events that occur during the G1 phase of interphase?

During G1 (gap 1) the cell grows in size, carries out its normal metabolic activities, and makes proteins, enzymes and organelles needed for the coming division. It is the phase of maximum growth of the cell, and it prepares the cell for DNA replication in the S phase.

Q: What is the main purpose of the S phase in the cell cycle?

The S (synthesis) phase is when DNA replication occurs: the chromosomes are duplicated, each chromosome forming two sister chromatids, so that both daughter cells can receive a complete set of genetic material.

Q: During which phase of mitosis sister chromatids separate?

Anaphase: the centromeres divide and the sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cell.

Q: How does crossing over contribute to genetic variation in meiosis?

In prophase I the non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments (crossing over). This produces new combinations of genes on the chromatids, so the gametes, and therefore the offspring, are not identical to either parent. This reshuffling is a major source of genetic variation in the next generation.

Q: What is the role of spindle fibres in mitosis?

Spindle fibres form the mitotic spindle and attach to the centromeres of the chromosomes. They arrange the chromosomes at the equator of the cell and then pull the sister chromatids (or homologous chromosomes in meiosis) to opposite poles, ensuring that each daughter cell receives the correct set of chromosomes.

Q: How is cytokinesis in animal cell different from plant cell?

In an animal cell cytokinesis occurs by cleavage: the cell membrane pinches inward at the equator, forming a furrow that deepens until the cell splits into two. In a plant cell the rigid wall cannot pinch, so a cell plate is built across the centre from vesicles; the plate becomes the new cell wall (with the middle lamella) dividing the two daughter cells.

Q: What is the difference between prophase of mitosis and prophase-I of meiosis-I?

In prophase of mitosis the chromatin condenses into chromosomes, but the homologous chromosomes do not pair and there is no crossing over. In prophase I of meiosis the homologous chromosomes come together in pairs (synapsis) and their non-sister chromatids exchange segments (crossing over), producing genetic variation; prophase I is also much longer and more complex.

Q: How does meiosis differ from mitosis in terms of chromosome number?

In mitosis the chromosome number stays the same: the diploid parent produces two diploid daughter cells with the same number of chromosomes as the parent. In meiosis the number is halved: the diploid parent produces four haploid daughter cells (gametes), each with half the number of chromosomes.

Q: What are the key events of anaphase in mitosis?

In anaphase the centromeres of the chromosomes divide; the sister chromatids separate and are pulled by the spindle fibres toward opposite poles of the cell, the chromatids (now daughter chromosomes) moving with their centromeres leading.

Q: What is the function of the centrosome during cell division?

The centrosome (containing the centrioles in animal cells) duplicates before division and the two centrosomes move to opposite poles, where they organise and make the spindle fibres of the mitotic spindle, which move the chromosomes during division.

Q: What are sister chromatids, and when do they separate in meiosis?

Sister chromatids are the two identical copies of a chromosome produced by DNA replication in the S phase, joined at the centromere. In meiosis they do not separate in meiosis I (whole homologous chromosomes separate then); they separate in anaphase II of meiosis II.

Q: How is mitosis related to the process of regeneration?

Regeneration is the regrowth of lost or damaged parts of the body, and it is carried out by mitosis: cells at the site of injury divide mitotically to produce the new cells that rebuild the tissue or part, with the same chromosome number and genetic information as the original cells. Examples: healing of wounds and regrowth of a lizard's tail.

mcqs.q: During the G1 phase of interphase, the cell:
options: Grows in size and makes proteins, enzymes and organelles needed for division
mcqs.why: G1 is the phase of maximum growth: the cell carries out its normal metabolic activities and prepares the materials needed for DNA replication in the S phase that follows.

mcqs.q: The main purpose of the S phase is:
options: Replication of DNA, duplicating each chromosome into two sister chromatids
mcqs.why: In the S (synthesis) phase the DNA is replicated so that each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids, ensuring both daughter cells receive a complete set of genetic material.

mcqs.q: Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles during:
mcqs.why: In anaphase the centromeres divide and the sister chromatids are pulled by the spindle fibres to opposite poles, moving with their centromeres leading.

mcqs.q: Crossing over contributes to genetic variation because it:
options: Produces new combinations of genes on the chromatids of homologous chromosomes
Removes harmful genes from the cell
Makes gametes identical to the parent
mcqs.why: In prophase I the non-sister chromatids exchange segments, reshuffling genes; the resulting gametes, and therefore the offspring, are not identical to either parent.

mcqs.q: The role of spindle fibres in mitosis is to:
options: Arrange the chromosomes at the equator and pull the chromatids to opposite poles
mcqs.why: Spindle fibres attach to the centromeres, line the chromosomes up at the equator and then pull sister chromatids apart, ensuring each daughter cell receives the correct set of chromosomes.

mcqs.q: Cytokinesis in a plant cell differs from that in an animal cell because the plant cell:
options: Builds a cell plate across the centre instead of pinching inward
mcqs.why: The rigid plant cell wall cannot pinch, so vesicles gather at the equator and fuse into a cell plate that becomes the new wall; animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow.

mcqs.q: Prophase I of meiosis differs from prophase of mitosis because in prophase I:
options: Homologous chromosomes pair up and crossing over takes place
mcqs.why: In mitotic prophase there is no pairing or crossing over; in prophase I the homologous chromosomes come together (synapsis) and exchange segments, producing genetic variation.

mcqs.q: After mitosis, a diploid parent cell produces:
options: Two diploid daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent
mcqs.why: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number unchanged, while meiosis halves it, producing four haploid daughter cells (gametes) from one diploid parent.

mcqs.q: Sister chromatids are:
options: The two identical copies of a chromosome, produced in the S phase and joined at the centromere
Two different chromosomes of a pair
mcqs.why: DNA replication in the S phase produces two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere; in meiosis they stay together through meiosis I and separate in anaphase II.

mcqs.q: Regeneration, such as the healing of a wound, is carried out by:
options: Mitosis, which produces new cells identical to the original ones
mcqs.why: Cells at the site of injury divide mitotically to rebuild the tissue with the same chromosome number and genetic information as the original cells; examples are wound healing and regrowth of a lizard's tail.

lessons.title: Detailed Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis.

Prophase: chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, each consisting of two sister chromatids; the nucleolus and nuclear envelope break down; centrioles move to opposite poles and spindle fibres begin to form. Metaphase: the spindle fibres attach to the centromeres and arrange all the chromosomes in a line at the equator (centre) of the cell; each chromosome is attached to fibres from both poles. Anaphase: the centromeres divide, sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles. Telophase: the chromosomes reach the poles, uncoil into chromatin, and a new nuclear envelope forms around each set, giving two nuclei; cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm.

Q: Describe cytokinesis in animal and plant cells.

Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm after the nucleus divides. In animal cells it occurs by cleavage furrow formation: a ring of proteins pinches the cell membrane inward at the equator until the cell is cut into two daughter cells. In plant cells the firm cell wall prevents pinching: vesicles from the Golgi apparatus gather at the equator and fuse to form a cell plate, which grows outward until it joins the existing wall; the plate becomes the middle lamella and new cell walls, separating the two daughter cells.

Q: Describe the significance of mitosis.

Mitosis is significant because: (1) Growth: it increases the number of cells, so a multicellular organism grows from a single zygote. (2) Cell replacement and repair: worn-out and damaged cells are replaced and wounds heal. (3) Regeneration: lost parts can be regrown in some animals. (4) Asexual reproduction: many organisms (e.g. Amoeba, yeast, and plants by cuttings) reproduce by mitosis, producing offspring identical to the parent. (5) Genetic stability: daughter cells receive exactly the same chromosomes and genes as the parent, so characters are preserved.

Q: Describe the events that occur during the phases of meiosis-I.

Prophase I: chromatin condenses into chromosomes; homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) and their non-sister chromatids exchange segments in crossing over; the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle fibres form. Metaphase I: the pairs of homologous chromosomes line up at the equator; one pair is attached to two spindle fibres from opposite poles. Anaphase I: the homologous chromosomes are pulled apart to opposite poles (the centromeres do not divide, so sister chromatids stay together). Telophase I: the spindle disappears and a new nuclear envelope forms around each set; the cell divides into two haploid cells, each with half the number of chromosomes.

Q: Describe the significance of meiosis.

Meiosis is significant because: (1) It maintains the chromosome number from generation to generation: it halves the number in gametes, so fertilisation restores the diploid number instead of doubling it each generation. (2) It produces genetic variation through crossing over in prophase I and the random separation of homologous chromosomes, so offspring differ from their parents and from each other. (3) Variation is the raw material of evolution and improves the chances of survival of the species in changing environments. (4) It is essential for sexual reproduction, forming the gametes (sperms and eggs).

mcqs.q: In prophase of mitosis, which event occurs?
options: Chromosomes line up at the equator
Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and the nuclear envelope breaks down
Sister chromatids move to the poles
mcqs.why: During prophase the chromatin condenses into chromosomes of two sister chromatids each, the nucleolus and nuclear envelope break down and spindle fibres begin to form.

mcqs.q: Cytokinesis in animal cells occurs by:
options: Building of a new cell wall first
Cleavage: the membrane pinches inward at the equator until the cell splits into two
mcqs.why: In animal cells a ring of proteins pinches the cell membrane inward, forming a furrow that deepens until the cytoplasm is cut into two daughter cells.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a significance of mitosis?
options: It replaces worn-out and damaged cells and heals wounds
mcqs.why: Mitosis brings about growth, cell replacement and repair, regeneration and asexual reproduction, while keeping the chromosomes and genes of the daughter cells exactly the same as the parent.

mcqs.q: In anaphase I of meiosis, the structures pulled to opposite poles are:
options: Whole homologous chromosomes, with sister chromatids still joined
mcqs.why: In anaphase I the centromeres do not divide, so homologous chromosomes separate as whole units and sister chromatids stay together; this is what halves the chromosome number.

mcqs.q: Meiosis maintains the chromosome number from generation to generation because it:
options: Halves the number in gametes, so fertilisation restores the diploid number
mcqs.why: Without meiosis the chromosome number would double at every fertilisation; meiosis halves it in sperms and eggs, and fertilisation restores the diploid number.

mcqs.q: Genetic variation in offspring produced by meiosis comes from crossing over and from:
options: The copying of DNA in G1
The random separation of homologous chromosomes
The formation of the cell plate
mcqs.why: Crossing over in prophase I and the random separation of homologous chromosomes reshuffle genes, so offspring differ from their parents and from each other; this variation is the raw material of evolution.

mcqs.q: At metaphase of mitosis, each chromosome is attached to:
mcqs.why: The spindle fibres attach to the centromeres and arrange the chromosomes at the equator, each chromosome connected to fibres from both poles, ready for separation.

mcqs.q: In plant cytokinesis, the cell plate is built from vesicles produced by the:
mcqs.why: Vesicles from the Golgi apparatus gather at the equator of the dividing plant cell and fuse to form the cell plate, which becomes the middle lamella and new cell walls.

mcqs.q: Asexual reproduction in Amoeba and yeast depends on mitosis, so the offspring are:
mcqs.why: Because mitosis copies the chromosomes exactly, organisms reproducing by it, such as Amoeba, yeast and plants grown from cuttings, produce offspring identical to the parent.

mcqs.q: Telophase of mitosis ends with:
options: Two nuclei, each with a new nuclear envelope around uncoiled chromatin
mcqs.why: In telophase the chromosomes reach the poles, uncoil into chromatin and a new nuclear envelope forms around each set, giving two nuclei before cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.

lessons.title: Inquisitive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: What role might mistakes in the cell cycle checkpoints play in the emergence of cancer?

Checkpoints are control points of the cell cycle where the cell verifies that DNA is complete and undamaged and that conditions are right before dividing. If the checkpoint machinery is faulty, damaged DNA is copied and cells with mutations are allowed to divide unchecked. Such uncontrolled, abnormal division produces a growing mass of cells, a tumour: this is the beginning of cancer. Faulty checkpoints also let further mutations accumulate, making the cancer more dangerous and able to spread.

Q: Why do skin cells divide continuously throughout an organism's existence, but nerve and muscle cells permanently exit the cell cycle?

Skin cells are continuously lost from the body surface by friction, washing and injury, and the skin is our first barrier against germs and water loss; so skin (epidermal) cells must keep dividing by mitosis throughout life to replace the cells shed and to repair wounds. Nerve and muscle cells, by contrast, are highly specialized for conduction and contraction; once mature they leave the cell cycle permanently (enter the G0 state) and do not divide, because their complex structures (long fibres and connections) cannot be rebuilt by division: damage to them is repaired only to a limited extent.

mcqs.q: Cell cycle checkpoints are control points where the cell:
options: Verifies that DNA is complete and undamaged before allowing division
mcqs.why: Checkpoints verify that the DNA is complete and undamaged and that conditions are right; only then is the cell allowed to pass into the next phase of the cycle.

mcqs.q: Faulty checkpoints can lead to cancer because they:
options: Allow cells with damaged DNA and mutations to divide unchecked
mcqs.why: If checkpoint machinery fails, damaged DNA is copied and mutant cells divide without control, producing a growing mass of cells, a tumour, which is the beginning of cancer.

mcqs.q: A tumour is:
options: A growing mass of abnormally dividing cells
A normal part of the skin
mcqs.why: Uncontrolled, abnormal division of cells that escaped checkpoint control produces a tumour; further accumulated mutations can make it more dangerous and able to spread.

mcqs.q: Skin cells divide continuously throughout life because:
options: Skin cells are constantly lost by friction, washing and injury and must be replaced
mcqs.why: The skin is the first barrier against germs and water loss, and its cells are shed continuously; mitosis in the skin replaces them and repairs wounds throughout life.

mcqs.q: Mature nerve and muscle cells do not divide because they:
options: Have left the cell cycle permanently (entered the G0 state) due to their specialized structures
mcqs.why: Nerve and muscle cells are highly specialized for conduction and contraction; once mature they exit the cycle into G0, and their long fibres and connections cannot be rebuilt by division.

mcqs.q: Damage to nerve tissue is repaired only to a limited extent because:
options: Mature nerve cells no longer divide to replace lost cells
mcqs.why: Since mature nerve cells permanently leave the cell cycle, lost nerve cells are not replaced by division, so repair of nerve and muscle damage is limited.

mcqs.q: Mutations become more dangerous in a cancer when faulty checkpoints allow:
options: Further mutations to accumulate in the dividing cells
mcqs.why: Failed checkpoints not only start uncontrolled division; they also let more mutations pile up in the descendants, making the cancer more dangerous and able to spread.

mcqs.q: The state in which non-dividing specialized cells rest is called:
mcqs.why: Cells that permanently exit the cell cycle, such as mature nerve and muscle cells, are said to be in the G0 state; they carry out their functions without dividing.

mcqs.q: Which cells MUST keep dividing throughout an organism's life?
mcqs.why: Epidermal cells are lost from the body surface continuously and the skin barrier must be maintained, so skin cells keep dividing by mitosis throughout life.

mcqs.q: Checkpoints protect the organism mainly by ensuring that:
options: All cells divide at the same speed
Only cells with complete, undamaged DNA go on to divide
mcqs.why: By verifying DNA and conditions before division, checkpoints prevent the copying of damaged instructions; when they fail, abnormal unchecked division and cancer can follow.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Tissues, Organs, and Organ Systems

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: A higher level of organization exhibits emergent properties when:

(a) Its parts function independently. (b) The sum of its parts is greater than the whole. (c) The individual parts are more important than the whole. (d) Its parts interact to perform more functions.
Correct answer: Its parts interact to perform more functions.

Q: Which of the following demonstrates the levels of organization of the body, from simplest to most complex?

(a) Cell -> Organ -> Tissue -> Organelle -> Organ system (b) Organelle -> Cell -> Tissue -> Organ -> Organ system (c) Tissue -> Cell -> Organelle -> Organ -> Organ system (d) Organ system -> Tissue -> Cell -> Organelle -> Organ
Correct answer: Organelle -> Cell -> Tissue -> Organ -> Organ system

Q: At which level of organization gas exchange occurs between body and environment?

(a) Organelle level in mitochondria (b) Cellular level in alveolar cells (c) Tissue level in epithelial tissues (d) Organ system level in the respiratory system
Correct answer: Organ system level in the respiratory system

Q: The epithelial tissue in the stomach wall is responsible for producing:

(a) Mucus (b) Pepsinogen (c) Hydrochloric acid (d) All of these
Correct answer: All of these

Q: In the wall of stomach, which tissue also contains blood vessels and nerves?

(a) Epithelial (b) Muscle (c) Inner connective (d) Outer connective
Correct answer: Inner connective

Q: In a leaf, which tissue is responsible for photosynthesis?

(a) Xylem (b) Mesophyll (c) Epidermis (d) Phloem
Correct answer: Mesophyll

Q: What is the primary function of the xylem tissue in a leaf?

(a) To transport sugars to other parts (b) To transport water to parts of leaf (c) To synthesize chlorophyll (d) To control the opening and closing of stomata
Correct answer: To transport water to parts of leaf

Q: Which of these is a function of the human skeletal system?

(a) Storing minerals and producing blood cells (b) Removing carbon dioxide from blood (c) Filtering blood to remove waste products (d) Breaking down food for energy
Correct answer: Storing minerals and producing blood cells

Q: Which structures are responsible for the transport of food in plant body?

(a) Xylem tissue (b) Palisade mesophyll (c) Phloem tissue (d) Spongy mesophyll
Correct answer: Phloem tissue

Q: In a plant, which of the following is the primary function of the flower?

(a) Transporting water and minerals (b) Supporting leaf growth (c) Facilitating reproduction through pollination (d) Regulating gas exchange
Correct answer: Facilitating reproduction through pollination

mcqs.q: A higher level of organization exhibits emergent properties when:
options: Its parts interact to perform more functions.
The sum of its parts is greater than the whole.
The individual parts are more important than the whole.
mcqs.why: A higher level of organization shows emergent properties when its parts interact to perform more functions than the parts alone could; the whole is more than the sum of independent parts.

mcqs.q: Which of the following demonstrates the levels of organization of the body, from simplest to most complex?
options: Cell -> Organ -> Tissue -> Organelle -> Organ system
Tissue -> Cell -> Organelle -> Organ -> Organ system
Organelle -> Cell -> Tissue -> Organ -> Organ system
Organ system -> Tissue -> Cell -> Organelle -> Organ
mcqs.why: From simplest to most complex the sequence is: organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organ system. Cells form tissues, tissues form organs and organs work together in systems.

mcqs.q: At which level of organization gas exchange occurs between body and environment?
options: Organ system level in the respiratory system
mcqs.why: Gas exchange with the environment is performed by the whole respiratory system working together, so it is an organ-system-level function, carried out at the alveoli within that system.

mcqs.q: The epithelial tissue in the stomach wall is responsible for producing:
mcqs.why: The epithelial lining of the stomach secretes gastric juice, which contains mucus, pepsinogen and hydrochloric acid: the acid kills germs and activates pepsin, and mucus protects the lining.

mcqs.q: In the wall of stomach, which tissue also contains blood vessels and nerves?
mcqs.why: The inner connective tissue of the stomach wall binds the layers together and carries the blood vessels and nerves that supply and coordinate the stomach.

mcqs.q: In a leaf, which tissue is responsible for photosynthesis?
mcqs.why: Mesophyll tissue of the leaf contains the chloroplasts and performs photosynthesis; xylem and phloem in the veins only transport water and food.

mcqs.q: What is the primary function of the xylem tissue in a leaf?
options: To transport sugars to other parts
To transport water to parts of leaf
To control the opening and closing of stomata
mcqs.why: Xylem tissue conducts water and mineral salts; in the leaf it brings water to the mesophyll cells for photosynthesis. Sugars are carried away by the phloem.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a function of the human skeletal system?
options: Storing minerals and producing blood cells
Filtering blood to remove waste products
mcqs.why: The skeletal system supports the body, protects organs, stores minerals such as calcium and produces blood cells in the bone marrow; filtering blood and removing carbon dioxide belong to other systems.

mcqs.q: Which structures are responsible for the transport of food in plant body?
mcqs.why: Phloem tissue transports prepared food (sugars) from the leaves to all parts of the plant; xylem transports water and minerals in the opposite direction.

mcqs.q: In a plant, which of the following is the primary function of the flower?
mcqs.why: The flower is the reproductive organ of the plant: it bears the male and female parts and enables pollination and fertilisation, leading to seeds and fruit.

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Enlist the levels of organization from cells to organ systems.

Organelle -> Cell -> Tissue -> Organ -> Organ system -> Organism. Cells of one kind form a tissue; different tissues form an organ; organs working together form an organ system; all the systems together form the organism. (Including the level below the cell: molecules/atoms form organelles.)

Q: What are the major roles of the epithelial tissue present in the stomach?

The epithelial tissue lines the inside of the stomach and secretes gastric juice, which contains mucus, hydrochloric acid and pepsinogen: the acid kills germs and activates the enzyme, pepsinogen (as pepsin) digests proteins, and the mucus protects the stomach lining from the acid and enzyme.

Q: How do the smooth muscles contribute to the stomach's function?

The smooth muscles of the stomach wall contract in waves (peristalsis). They churn and mix the food with gastric juice and break it into smaller pieces, turning it into a semi-liquid chyme, and push it gradually into the small intestine.

Q: What is the function of the palisade mesophyll in the leaf?

The palisade mesophyll, just below the upper epidermis, consists of column-shaped cells packed with chloroplasts. It is the main site of photosynthesis in the leaf, trapping light and making glucose.

Q: What is the role of the shoot system in plants?

The shoot system (stem, branches, leaves, flowers and fruits) grows above the ground. It supports the plant, holds the leaves up to the sunlight for photosynthesis, transports water and food between roots and leaves, and bears the flowers and fruits for reproduction.

Q: What is homeostasis, and why is it important for organisms?

Homeostasis is the body's ability to maintain a relatively stable internal environment (temperature, water, glucose, pH, etc.) despite changes in the external environment. It is important because the cells and their enzymes can work properly only within narrow limits; without homeostasis the internal conditions would fluctuate with the surroundings and life processes would fail.

Q: How does the human body maintain a stable internal temperature?

The temperature is detected by receptors and controlled by the brain (hypothalamus). When the body is too hot, blood vessels in the skin dilate and sweat glands produce sweat whose evaporation cools the body. When the body is too cold, the vessels constrict to reduce heat loss, and the muscles shiver to generate heat. Thus the internal temperature is held near 37 degrees C.

Q: Differentiate between the following: i. Tissue and organ ii. Root system and shoot system iii. Epidermal and mesophyll tissue iv. Palisade and spongy mesophyll

i. Tissue and organ: a tissue is a group of similar cells working together for one function; an organ is a structure made of more than one type of tissue performing a related function. ii. Root system and shoot system: the root system is the underground part that absorbs water and minerals and anchors the plant; the shoot system is the above-ground part (stem, leaves, flowers) that supports, photosynthesises and reproduces. iii. Epidermal and mesophyll tissue: epidermis is the protective outer layer of the leaf; mesophyll is the inner ground tissue containing chloroplasts, where photosynthesis occurs. iv. Palisade and spongy mesophyll: palisade cells are column-shaped, tightly packed with many chloroplasts, just below the upper epidermis, and do most photosynthesis; spongy cells are irregular and loosely arranged with air spaces, allowing gas exchange (and some photosynthesis).

mcqs.q: The correct sequence of levels of organization in a multicellular organism is:
options: Cell, organelle, organ, tissue, organism, organ system
Tissue, cell, organelle, organ system, organ, organism
Organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
Organ, tissue, cell, organ system, organelle, organism
mcqs.why: Similar cells form a tissue, tissues form an organ, organs form an organ system, and all the systems together form the organism; organelles lie below the cell level.

mcqs.q: The epithelial tissue of the stomach protects the stomach lining from its own acid and enzyme by secreting:
mcqs.why: The epithelium secretes gastric juice containing mucus, hydrochloric acid and pepsinogen; the mucus coats and protects the lining while the acid kills germs and activates pepsin for protein digestion.

mcqs.q: The smooth muscles of the stomach wall help digestion by:
options: Contracting in waves (peristalsis) that churn and mix food with gastric juice
Absorbing digested food into the blood
mcqs.why: Peristaltic contractions of the smooth muscle churn the food, mix it with gastric juice, break it into a semi-liquid chyme and push it gradually into the small intestine.

mcqs.q: The palisade mesophyll is the main site of photosynthesis in the leaf because its cells:
options: Form the veins of the leaf
Are packed with chloroplasts and lie just below the upper epidermis
mcqs.why: Palisade cells are column-shaped, tightly packed and rich in chloroplasts, positioned to trap the most light; the spongy mesophyll below them mainly allows gas exchange.

mcqs.q: The shoot system of a plant consists of:
options: Stem, branches, leaves, flowers and fruits growing above the ground
Only the roots and root hairs
mcqs.why: The shoot system grows above ground: it supports the plant, holds leaves to the sunlight, transports water and food and bears flowers and fruits for reproduction.

mcqs.q: Homeostasis is important for an organism because:
options: It stops the body from growing
It keeps the external environment constant
Cells and enzymes can work properly only within narrow limits of temperature, water, glucose and pH
It replaces the need for food
mcqs.why: Homeostasis maintains a stable internal environment despite external change; without it, internal conditions would fluctuate with the surroundings and life processes would fail.

mcqs.q: When the human body becomes too hot, it cools itself by:
options: Dilating skin blood vessels and producing sweat whose evaporation removes heat
mcqs.why: The hypothalamus coordinates the response: vessels in the skin dilate and sweat glands release sweat, whose evaporation cools the body back towards 37 degrees C; shivering and constriction are responses to cold.

mcqs.q: An organ differs from a tissue in that an organ is:
options: Made of only one type of cell
Made of more than one type of tissue performing a related function
mcqs.why: A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one job; an organ, such as the stomach, combines several tissues, epithelial, muscle, connective and nervous, for a larger function.

mcqs.q: Epidermal tissue of the leaf differs from mesophyll tissue in that the epidermis:
options: Is the protective outer layer, while mesophyll is the inner tissue that photosynthesises
mcqs.why: The epidermis protects the leaf and controls water loss through stomata; the mesophyll inside it contains the chloroplasts where photosynthesis occurs.

mcqs.q: Palisade and spongy mesophyll differ in that spongy cells are:
options: Irregular and loosely arranged with air spaces, allowing gas exchange
mcqs.why: Palisade cells are columnar and tightly packed for maximum photosynthesis; spongy cells are irregular with air spaces between them so gases can reach all the leaf cells.

lessons.title: Detailed Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Explain the levels of organization in multicellular organism. How does each level contribute to the overall functioning of an organism?

The levels are: organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism. Organelles perform the chemistry of the cell; the cell is the basic unit of life; tissues group similar cells for one task (e.g. muscle tissue contracts); organs combine tissues for a larger function (the stomach digests food with epithelial, muscle, connective and nervous tissues); organ systems combine organs (the digestive system takes in and processes food for the whole body); and all systems together make the organism. Each higher level shows emergent properties: it can do things its parts alone cannot.

Q: What is a tissue level? Explain plant and animal tissues.

The tissue level is the level at which a group of similar cells works together to perform a specific function. Plant tissues include: epidermal tissue (protection), mesophyll tissue (photosynthesis), and vascular tissues, xylem (transport of water and minerals) and phloem (transport of food). Animal tissues include: epithelial tissue (covering and secretion), muscle tissue (movement), connective tissue (support and connection; it contains blood vessels and nerves) and nervous tissue (conduction of impulses). Tissues are the building blocks of organs in both plants and animals.

Q: Describe the tissue composition of the stomach. How does each tissue contribute to the digestive function of the stomach?

The stomach wall contains: (1) Epithelial tissue lining the inside, which secretes gastric juice (mucus, HCl and pepsinogen): the acid kills germs and activates pepsin, which begins protein digestion, and mucus protects the wall. (2) Smooth muscle tissue, whose contractions churn and mix the food with the juice and break it down physically. (3) Connective tissue, which binds the layers together and carries blood vessels (bringing materials and taking absorbed substances) and nerves (coordinating the contractions and secretions). Working together, these tissues store food, digest it chemically and mechanically, and pass it on as chyme.

Q: Describe the tissue composition of the leaf. How does each tissue contribute to the functions of the leaf?

The leaf contains: (1) Epidermal tissue (upper and lower epidermis): a protective layer that prevents water loss and damage; its stomata, with guard cells, allow gas exchange. (2) Mesophyll tissue: palisade mesophyll with many chloroplasts performs most of the photosynthesis; spongy mesophyll, with air spaces, allows gases to reach the cells and also photosynthesises. (3) Vascular tissue in the veins: xylem brings water and minerals to the leaf cells, and phloem carries the prepared food (sugars) away to the rest of the plant. Together these tissues make the leaf an efficient food-making organ.

Q: How do the organ systems come together to form the human body?

Each organ system performs one major life function, and the systems are linked: the digestive system supplies nutrients, the respiratory system supplies oxygen, the circulatory system transports materials to every cell, the excretory system removes wastes, the nervous and endocrine systems coordinate all activities, the skeletal and muscular systems give support and movement, and the reproductive system continues the species. No system works alone: together, in coordination, they form the complete, living human body.

Q: Describe the roles of the digestive system and the excretory system in homeostasis.

The digestive system takes in food, breaks it down and absorbs nutrients and water into the blood, keeping the body's supply of energy and materials constant. The excretory system (kidneys) filters the blood, removes metabolic wastes such as urea, and adjusts the amounts of water and salts in the body. Together they keep the composition of the internal environment stable: what digestion puts into the blood, excretion balances by removing the excess and the wastes.

Q: Explain the functions of various plant organs.

Roots: absorb water and minerals from the soil and anchor the plant. Stem: supports the leaves and flowers, holds them up to light and air, and conducts water, minerals and food between roots and leaves (through xylem and phloem). Leaves: make food by photosynthesis and exchange gases through stomata; they also lose water vapour in transpiration. Flowers: the reproductive organs, producing seeds after pollination and fertilisation. Fruits: protect the seeds and help in their dispersal.

Q: Describe the structure and function of the plant root system.

Structure: the root system is the underground part of the plant. It consists of the main root and its branches, fine root hairs near the tips that greatly increase the absorbing surface, and a root cap protecting each growing tip. Function: it anchors the plant firmly in the soil; absorbs water and dissolved minerals through the root hairs and passes them to the xylem; and in some plants stores food. It is one of the two main organ systems of the plant body, the other being the shoot system.

Q: Define homeostasis and explain its importance. Discuss how different organ systems work together to maintain homeostasis.

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment despite changes outside the body. It is important because enzymes and cells work only within narrow ranges of temperature, pH, glucose and water. Organ systems cooperate to maintain it: the excretory system controls water, salts and wastes; the respiratory system controls oxygen and carbon dioxide; the digestive system supplies glucose, whose level in blood is regulated with the help of the endocrine system (insulin/glucagon); the skin and circulatory system regulate temperature; and the nervous system detects changes and coordinates the responses.

Q: Describe how the respiratory and circulatory systems work together to maintain homeostasis of oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in the body.

The respiratory system takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide at the lungs: in the alveoli, oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out. The circulatory system then does the transport: the heart pumps oxygen-rich blood to all the tissues, where oxygen is used in respiration, and carries the carbon dioxide produced back to the lungs. Breathing rate and heart rate are adjusted together (by the nervous system) according to the body's needs, e.g. both increase during exercise, keeping the levels of O2 and CO2 in the blood stable.

mcqs.q: Each higher level of organization shows emergent properties, which means it:
options: Can do things that its parts alone cannot do
mcqs.why: An organ such as the stomach digests food, something no single tissue of it can do alone; each level, organelle to organism, gains abilities beyond those of its parts.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a vascular tissue of plants?
mcqs.why: The vascular tissues are xylem, which transports water and minerals, and phloem, which transports food; epidermal tissue protects and mesophyll photosynthesises.

mcqs.q: In the stomach, the tissue that coordinates contractions and secretions through nerves is the:
options: Connective tissue, which carries the nerves (with nervous tissue)
mcqs.why: Connective tissue binds the stomach's layers together and carries blood vessels, which bring materials and remove absorbed substances, and nerves, which coordinate its contractions and secretions.

mcqs.q: Gas exchange in the leaf takes place through the:
options: Stomata, controlled by guard cells in the epidermis
mcqs.why: The epidermis bears stomata whose guard cells open and close them for gas exchange, while the spongy mesophyll's air spaces let gases reach the cells; xylem and phloem only transport.

mcqs.q: No organ system works alone; the digestive system depends on the circulatory system to:
options: Transport the absorbed nutrients to every cell of the body
mcqs.why: Digestion supplies nutrients, respiration supplies oxygen, and the circulatory system transports materials to all cells, while the nervous and endocrine systems coordinate the whole body.

mcqs.q: The kidneys help homeostasis mainly by:
options: Filtering the blood, removing wastes such as urea and adjusting water and salts
mcqs.why: The excretory system balances what digestion puts into the blood: the kidneys remove metabolic wastes and control the amounts of water and salts, keeping the internal environment stable.

mcqs.q: The plant organ that absorbs water and minerals from the soil is the:
mcqs.why: Roots absorb water and minerals and anchor the plant; the stem supports and conducts, the leaf photosynthesises and the flower reproduces.

mcqs.q: Root hairs increase the efficiency of absorption because they:
options: Greatly increase the surface area of the root in contact with the soil
mcqs.why: Fine root hairs near the tips multiply the absorbing surface; the root cap protects the growing tip and the absorbed water passes to the xylem.

mcqs.q: Blood glucose level is kept stable with the help of which system, besides the digestive system?
options: The endocrine system, through insulin and glucagon
mcqs.why: The digestive system supplies glucose, and its level in the blood is regulated by the endocrine hormones insulin and glucagon, an example of systems cooperating in homeostasis.

mcqs.q: In the alveoli of the lungs, oxygen and carbon dioxide move between air and blood by:
mcqs.why: In the alveoli oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out; the circulatory system then transports them, and breathing and heart rates are adjusted together to keep their levels stable.

lessons.title: Inquisitive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: How does the structure of epithelial tissue relate to its function in different parts of the body?

Epithelial tissue is made of closely packed cells forming continuous sheets, and its form fits its job in each place. In the stomach it is glandular and folded, secreting gastric juice and mucus. In the small intestine it has finger-like villi and microvilli, giving a huge surface for absorption. In the air passages it bears cilia and mucus to sweep dust and germs away. In the skin it is layered and tough, forming a protective barrier. In the alveoli it is a single thin layer, so gases diffuse across it rapidly.

Q: Evaluate the importance of organ systems working in harmony and predict the consequences of a failure in one system on the others.

The organ systems form one interdependent unit: each supplies what others need. If one system fails, the others suffer in a chain. For example, if the kidneys (excretory system) fail, wastes and excess water accumulate in the blood, poisoning cells, disturbing the heart and brain, and the person dies unless the blood is cleaned artificially. Failure of the circulatory system stops oxygen delivery, so the brain and all organs fail within minutes. Harmony between systems is therefore essential for homeostasis and survival; a disease of one system is a stress on the whole body.

mcqs.q: Epithelial tissue in the small intestine has villi and microvilli in order to:
options: Provide a huge surface area for absorption of digested food
Sweep dust away from the lungs
mcqs.why: The form of epithelium fits its job in each place: folds, villi and microvilli multiply the absorbing surface of the intestine, just as cilia in air passages sweep away dust and germs.

mcqs.q: The epithelium of the alveoli is a single thin layer of cells so that:
options: Gases can diffuse across it rapidly
mcqs.why: Gas exchange needs a short diffusion path: the thin, single-layered epithelium of the alveoli lets oxygen and carbon dioxide cross quickly between air and blood.

mcqs.q: Epithelium in the air passages bears cilia and mucus to:
options: Trap and sweep dust and germs away from the lungs
mcqs.why: Ciliated epithelium lining the air passages uses mucus to trap dust and germs and cilia to sweep them out, protecting the lungs; this is structure fitted to function.

mcqs.q: If the kidneys fail, the immediate danger to the body is that:
options: Wastes and excess water accumulate in the blood and poison the cells
mcqs.why: Kidney failure lets urea and excess water build up in the blood, disturbing the heart and brain; the person dies unless the blood is cleaned artificially, showing how systems depend on each other.

mcqs.q: Failure of the circulatory system is fatal within minutes because it:
options: Stops the delivery of oxygen to the brain and all other organs
mcqs.why: Every organ depends on the blood for oxygen and nutrients; if circulation stops, the brain and all organs fail within minutes, which is why harmony between systems is essential for survival.

mcqs.q: The skin's epithelium is layered and tough because its function is:
options: To form a protective barrier for the body surface
mcqs.why: Structure follows function: layered, tough epithelium protects the body surface, glandular epithelium secretes in the stomach, and thin epithelium exchanges gases in the alveoli.

mcqs.q: A disease of one organ system is a stress on the whole body because:
options: The systems are interdependent; each supplies what the others need
mcqs.why: The organ systems form one interdependent unit held stable by homeostasis; failure in one, such as the kidneys or the circulation, sets off a chain of failures in the others.

mcqs.q: Glandular, folded epithelium in the stomach is suited to its function of:
mcqs.why: In the stomach the epithelium is glandular and folded for secretion of gastric juice and protective mucus, while muscle tissue moves the food and connective tissue supplies and coordinates the organ.

mcqs.q: Artificial cleaning of blood (dialysis) becomes necessary when:
options: The kidneys fail and can no longer remove wastes and excess water
mcqs.why: This lesson's example: when the excretory system fails, wastes accumulate in the blood and the patient survives only if the blood is cleaned artificially until the kidneys recover or are replaced.

mcqs.q: The relationship between epithelial structure and function shows that in the body:
options: The form of a tissue is fitted to the job it performs in each location
Structure has no relation to function
mcqs.why: Secretory in the stomach, absorptive in the intestine, ciliated in air passages, protective in skin and thin in alveoli: everywhere the epithelium's structure matches its function.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: What is the primary function of carbohydrates?

(a) Provide energy (b) Act as enzymes (c) Regulate processes (d) Make membranes
Correct answer: Provide energy

Q: How will you differentiate between monosaccharides and polysaccharides?

(a) Monosaccharides are single sugars. (b) Polysaccharides are sweet in taste. (c) Monosaccharides are present in plant cell wall. (d) Polysaccharides dissolve easily.
Correct answer: Monosaccharides are single sugars.

Q: What is true about cellulose?

(a) It is sweet in taste. (b) It is digestible by human digestive system. (c) It provides structural support in plants. (d) It is soluble in water.
Correct answer: It provides structural support in plants.

Q: Which of the following proteins is involved in oxygen transport?

(a) Insulin (b) Haemoglobin (c) Collagen (d) Keratin
Correct answer: Haemoglobin

Q: Which component of an amino acid determines its unique properties?

(a) Amino group (b) Carboxyl group (c) R group (side group) (d) Hydrogen group
Correct answer: R group (side group)

Q: Which proteins are involved in defence against pathogens?

(a) Antibodies (b) Myosin (c) Fibrinogen (d) Haemoglobin
Correct answer: Antibodies

Q: Which of the following are the units of most lipids?

(a) Amino acids (b) Fatty acids and glycerol (c) Nucleotides (d) Simple sugars
Correct answer: Fatty acids and glycerol

Q: How do unsaturated fatty acids differ from saturated fatty acids?

(a) They have more hydrogen atoms. (b) They contain double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains. (c) They are solid at room temperature. (d) They are found only in animal fats.
Correct answer: They contain double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains.

Q: Which of the following is NOT a function of proteins?

(a) Transport oxygen in the blood. (b) Carry genetic information. (c) Help in digesting food. (d) Fight against pathogens.
Correct answer: Carry genetic information.

Q: Which components make up a nucleotide?

(a) Sugar, phosphate, nitrogenous base (b) Amino acid, sugar, nitrogenous base (c) Fatty acid, phosphate, nitrogenous base (d) Protein, sugar, nitrogenous base
Correct answer: Sugar, phosphate, nitrogenous base

Q: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA but not in DNA?

(a) Adenine (b) Thymine (c) Uracil (d) Guanine
Correct answer: Uracil

mcqs.q: What is the primary function of carbohydrates?
mcqs.why: Carbohydrates are the body's main and quickest source of energy: glucose is oxidised in respiration to release energy for all activities.

mcqs.q: What is true about cellulose?
options: It provides structural support in plants.
It is digestible by human digestive system.
mcqs.why: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide: it forms the plant cell wall and gives support. It is tasteless, insoluble and cannot be digested by the human digestive system.

mcqs.q: Which of the following proteins is involved in oxygen transport?
mcqs.why: Haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells, binds oxygen in the lungs and transports it to all the tissues; insulin is a hormone, collagen structural and keratin protective.

mcqs.q: Which component of an amino acid determines its unique properties?
mcqs.why: Every amino acid has an amino group, a carboxyl group and a hydrogen on a central carbon; only the R group (side group) differs between amino acids and gives each its unique properties.

mcqs.q: Which proteins are involved in defence against pathogens?
mcqs.why: Antibodies are proteins made by the immune system that recognise and help destroy pathogens; myosin works in muscles, fibrinogen in clotting and haemoglobin in oxygen transport.

mcqs.q: Which of the following are the units of most lipids?
mcqs.why: Most lipids (fats and oils) are built from glycerol and fatty acids: three fatty acids joined to one glycerol form a triglyceride.

mcqs.q: How do unsaturated fatty acids differ from saturated fatty acids?
options: They contain double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains.
They are solid at room temperature.
They are found only in animal fats.
mcqs.why: Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds in their hydrocarbon chains, so they hold fewer hydrogen atoms and their oils are liquid at room temperature.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of proteins?
mcqs.why: Genetic information is carried by nucleic acids (DNA and RNA), not by proteins. Proteins do transport oxygen (haemoglobin), digest food (enzymes) and fight pathogens (antibodies).

mcqs.q: Which components make up a nucleotide?
mcqs.why: A nucleotide, the building unit of nucleic acids, consists of three parts: a sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.

mcqs.q: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
mcqs.why: Uracil is found in RNA in place of thymine; DNA contains adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine, while RNA contains adenine, uracil, guanine and cytosine.

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: What are the main functions of carbohydrates in the body?

Carbohydrates are the body's main and quickest source of energy (glucose is oxidised in respiration). They also serve as stored energy (glycogen in animals, starch in plants), as structural material (cellulose in plant cell walls), and as components of other molecules such as nucleic acids (ribose and deoxyribose sugars).

Q: How do the three group of carbohydrates differ in taste?

Monosaccharides (single sugars, e.g. glucose) are the sweetest and dissolve easily in water. Disaccharides (e.g. sucrose, table sugar) are also sweet and soluble but less sweet than monosaccharides. Polysaccharides (starch, cellulose) are not sweet in taste and are mostly insoluble: taste decreases as the molecules become larger.

Q: Name two common monosaccharides and two disaccharides.

Monosaccharides: glucose and fructose. Disaccharides: sucrose (table sugar) and lactose (milk sugar). (Maltose is another disaccharide.)

Q: Which monosaccharides make a sucrose molecule?

Sucrose is made of one molecule of glucose and one molecule of fructose, joined together with the loss of a water molecule (condensation).

Q: Give an example of a storage polysaccharide in plants.

Starch: plants store glucose as starch in seeds, tubers and roots (e.g. in potato and grains). (Cellulose is a structural, not storage, polysaccharide; animals store glycogen.)

Q: Define amino acid and draw its structure.

An amino acid is the building unit (monomer) of proteins: an organic molecule containing an amino group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a hydrogen atom and a variable side group (R group), all attached to a central carbon atom. Structure in words: the central carbon has four bonds: to -NH2, to -COOH, to H, and to the R group; the R group differs in each amino acid and gives it its unique properties. (Amino acids join by peptide bonds to form proteins.)

Q: What are the basic components of lipids? Draw their structures.

Most lipids (fats and oils) are built from glycerol and fatty acids. Glycerol is a three-carbon alcohol with a hydroxyl (-OH) group on each carbon. A fatty acid is a long hydrocarbon chain ending in a carboxyl group (-COOH). In a fat molecule, three fatty acids are joined to one glycerol (a triglyceride), each link formed by condensation.

Q: What are the types of RNA? Write their functions.

Three types of RNA: (1) Messenger RNA (mRNA): carries the genetic message copied from DNA to the ribosome. (2) Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): together with proteins it forms the ribosomes, the site of protein synthesis. (3) Transfer RNA (tRNA): carries specific amino acids to the ribosome and places them in the order directed by the mRNA.

Q: Briefly describe the function of DNA.

DNA stores the genetic information of the cell: the sequence of its bases is the code for making all the proteins of the body, and hence it controls the structure and activities of the cell. It copies itself (replication) and passes the information to daughter cells and to the next generation, so characters are inherited.

mcqs.q: Plants store glucose in the form of:
mcqs.why: Starch is the storage polysaccharide of plants, kept in seeds, tubers and roots; animals store glycogen, and cellulose is a structural material of cell walls, not a store.

mcqs.q: Sucrose (table sugar) is made by joining one molecule of glucose with one molecule of:
mcqs.why: Sucrose is a disaccharide formed from glucose and fructose joined by condensation, with the loss of a water molecule, as stated in this lesson.

mcqs.q: As carbohydrates increase in size from monosaccharides to polysaccharides, their taste becomes:
options: Less sweet, and polysaccharides are not sweet at all
mcqs.why: Monosaccharides are the sweetest and dissolve easily; disaccharides are less sweet; polysaccharides such as starch and cellulose are tasteless and mostly insoluble: taste decreases as the molecules grow.

mcqs.q: Amino acids join together to form proteins by means of:
mcqs.why: An amino acid has an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and an R group on a central carbon; amino acids are linked by peptide bonds into protein chains.

mcqs.q: In a fat molecule (triglyceride), the number of fatty acids joined to one glycerol is:
mcqs.why: Glycerol is a three-carbon alcohol with a hydroxyl group on each carbon, and one fatty acid joins at each carbon by condensation, giving a triglyceride.

mcqs.q: The type of RNA that carries the genetic message from DNA to the ribosome is:
mcqs.why: mRNA carries the copied message to the ribosome; rRNA forms part of the ribosome itself, and tRNA brings the amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis.

mcqs.q: The function of DNA in the cell is to:
options: Store genetic information and control the making of proteins
mcqs.why: The base sequence of DNA is the code for making all the proteins of the body, so DNA controls the structure and activities of the cell and passes information to the next generation.

mcqs.q: Transfer RNA (tRNA) functions to:
options: Copy the DNA in the nucleus
Carry specific amino acids to the ribosome and place them in the order directed by mRNA
mcqs.why: During translation, tRNA molecules bring the amino acids specified by the mRNA codons to the ribosome, where they are joined in the correct order into a protein.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a monosaccharide?
mcqs.why: Glucose and fructose are monosaccharides (single sugars); sucrose and lactose are disaccharides, and starch is a polysaccharide of many glucose units.

mcqs.why: Disaccharides are two monosaccharides joined together; sucrose and lactose are the common examples named in this lesson, along with maltose.

lessons.title: Detailed Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Write a comprehensive note on the structures and roles of the three classes of carbohydrates.

Carbohydrates are compounds of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, built from sugar units. Monosaccharides are single sugars (glucose, fructose, galactose): sweet, soluble, and the immediate source of energy; they are the monomers of the larger carbohydrates. Disaccharides are two monosaccharides joined together (sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose; maltose): sweet and soluble, they are the transport/storage sugars in daily food. Polysaccharides are long chains of many monosaccharides: starch stores energy in plants, glycogen stores it in animals, and cellulose gives structural support in plant cell walls; they are tasteless and mostly insoluble.

Q: Discuss the functions of proteins.

Proteins perform almost every kind of work in the body. Structural: collagen in skin and tendons, keratin in hair and nails. Enzymes: all enzymes are proteins and catalyse the reactions of the cell (e.g. pepsin digests protein). Transport: haemoglobin carries oxygen. Defence: antibodies fight pathogens. Hormones: some, like insulin, regulate body processes. Movement: actin and myosin contract muscles. Storage and clotting: proteins store amino acids, and fibrinogen helps blood to clot.

Q: What are fatty acids? Explain their types.

Fatty acids are the building units of lipids: each is a long chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms (hydrocarbon chain) with a carboxyl group (-COOH) at one end. Types: (1) Saturated fatty acids have only single bonds between the carbon atoms; the chain holds the maximum hydrogen, and fats rich in them (e.g. butter, animal fat) are solid at room temperature. (2) Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds in the chain, so they hold fewer hydrogens; oils rich in them (e.g. plant oils) are liquid at room temperature and are generally healthier.

Q: Describe the basic structure of fats and oils. Explain how lipids play role in energy storage.

Fats and oils are triglycerides: one molecule of glycerol joined to three fatty acid molecules. Fats are solid at room temperature (mostly saturated, from animals); oils are liquid (mostly unsaturated, from plants). Role in energy storage: lipids contain more than twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates, and they are stored without water in the adipose tissue as a long-term energy reserve. The fat layer also insulates the body against heat loss and protects organs from shocks.

Q: Explain the double helix structure of DNA, and discuss the base pairing in this structure.

DNA is a double helix: two strands of nucleotides wind around each other like a twisted ladder. Each strand has a backbone of alternating deoxyribose sugar and phosphate groups; the nitrogenous bases project inward and form the 'rungs'. Base pairing is specific: adenine (A) always pairs with thymine (T) through two hydrogen bonds, and guanine (G) pairs with cytosine (C) through three hydrogen bonds. The two strands are complementary and run in opposite directions. This pairing explains how DNA copies itself exactly and how its base sequence stores information.

Q: Explain how the information in DNA is converted to RNA and then to proteins.

The conversion occurs in two steps. Transcription: in the nucleus, the sequence of one gene on the DNA is copied into a messenger RNA (mRNA) molecule; the mRNA base sequence is complementary to the DNA (with uracil in place of thymine). The mRNA leaves the nucleus and reaches a ribosome. Translation: the ribosome reads the mRNA sequence in groups of three bases (codons); transfer RNA molecules bring the amino acids specified by each codon, and the ribosome joins them in order by peptide bonds, forming the protein. Thus the DNA sequence determines the amino acid sequence of the protein.

mcqs.q: In DNA, adenine always pairs with thymine through:
mcqs.why: Base pairing in the double helix is specific: adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds, and guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds.

mcqs.q: The backbone of each DNA strand is made of alternating:
mcqs.why: Each strand of the double helix has a backbone of alternating deoxyribose and phosphate; the nitrogenous bases project inward and form the rungs of the twisted ladder.

mcqs.q: Transcription is the step in which:
options: Amino acids are joined into a protein
DNA makes an exact copy of itself
The sequence of a gene on DNA is copied into messenger RNA
mcqs.why: In transcription, in the nucleus, one gene's DNA sequence is copied into mRNA (with uracil in place of thymine); the mRNA then carries the message to a ribosome for translation.

mcqs.q: During translation, the ribosome reads the mRNA in groups of three bases called:
mcqs.why: The ribosome reads the mRNA sequence in codons of three bases; each codon specifies one amino acid, which tRNA delivers, and the amino acids are joined by peptide bonds into the protein.

mcqs.q: Fats are solid at room temperature while oils are liquid, because fats are mostly:
options: Saturated, with only single bonds in their fatty acid chains
mcqs.why: Saturated fatty acids have only single bonds and hold the maximum hydrogen, so animal fats rich in them are solid; unsaturated plant oils have double bonds and stay liquid.

mcqs.q: Lipids are a better long-term energy store than carbohydrates because they:
options: Contain more than twice as much energy per gram and are stored without water
mcqs.why: Fat stored in adipose tissue yields over twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate, insulates the body against heat loss and protects organs from shocks.

mcqs.q: The protein that carries oxygen in the blood is:
mcqs.why: Among the functions of proteins listed in this lesson, transport is performed by haemoglobin; collagen is structural, keratin is in hair and nails, and fibrinogen helps blood to clot.

mcqs.q: All enzymes are proteins, and their function in the cell is to:
options: Catalyse (speed up) the biochemical reactions of the cell
mcqs.why: Enzymes are protein catalysts, e.g. pepsin digests protein in the stomach; other protein roles in this lesson include structure, transport, defence, hormones and movement.

mcqs.q: The two strands of DNA are described as complementary because:
options: Both strands run in the same direction
The strands are made of different sugars
The base of one strand always matches a specific base on the other (A with T, G with C)
mcqs.why: Because of specific base pairing, knowing one strand's sequence fixes the other's; the strands run in opposite directions, and this complementarity explains how DNA copies itself exactly.

mcqs.q: Insulin is a protein whose function is to:
options: Regulate body processes as a hormone
mcqs.why: Some proteins act as hormones that regulate body processes; insulin, which controls blood glucose, is the example given in this lesson's account of protein functions.

lessons.title: Inquisitive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Evaluate the importance of water in the functioning of biomolecules.

Water is the medium of all life processes. It is the solvent in which biomolecules dissolve and move, so reactions of metabolism can occur; it takes part in reactions itself (e.g. hydrolysis breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and lipids, and condensation builds them); it transports substances in blood and sap; its high heat capacity keeps body temperature stable; and the shapes and activities of proteins and nucleic acids depend on their watery environment. Without water the biomolecules cannot function.

Q: Find the amount/ percentage of carbohydrates, Proteins, Fats and water in the following food product and compare them with each other: Roti(40gm), Burger, Cucumber, Egg, Rice(100gm), Potato fries(100gm), Carrot

Approximate composition (standard food-table values): Roti (40 g): carbohydrates about 18 g, protein about 3 g, fat about 1 g, water about 14 g. Burger (one, about 200 g): carbohydrates about 30 g, protein about 25 g, fat about 25 g, water about 100 g. Cucumber (100 g): water about 95 g, carbohydrates about 3.6 g, protein 0.7 g, fat 0.1 g. Egg (one, about 50 g): water about 38 g, protein about 6 g, fat about 5 g, carbohydrates about 0.5 g. Cooked rice (100 g): water about 68 g, carbohydrates about 28 g, protein 2.7 g, fat 0.3 g. Potato fries (100 g): carbohydrates about 41 g, fat about 15 g, protein 3.4 g, water about 40 g. Carrot (100 g): water about 88 g, carbohydrates about 10 g, protein 0.9 g, fat 0.2 g. Comparison: cucumber and carrot are mostly water with very little energy value; roti and rice are rich in carbohydrates (the main energy source); the egg has the highest proportion of protein; the burger and fries contain the most fat (fries carry much absorbed frying oil), so they are the most energy-dense and least healthy in excess.

mcqs.q: Water is the solvent in which biomolecules dissolve and move. This is essential because:
options: The reactions of metabolism can only occur when substances are dissolved and can meet
mcqs.why: Water is the medium of all life processes: dissolved biomolecules can move and react, water transports substances in blood and sap, and the shapes of proteins and nucleic acids depend on it.

mcqs.q: The breakdown of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids by water is called:
mcqs.why: Water itself takes part in reactions: hydrolysis uses water to break down large molecules, while condensation, which builds them, releases water.

mcqs.q: Water helps keep body temperature stable because of its:
mcqs.why: Water absorbs and releases large amounts of heat with little change in its own temperature, so the watery environment of cells keeps body temperature stable.

mcqs.q: From the food table in this lesson, which food is mostly water with very little energy value?
mcqs.why: Cucumber is about 95 percent water with only about 3.6 g carbohydrate per 100 g, so its energy value is very low; fries and burgers are energy-dense because of their fat.

options: Egg (about 6 g protein in one 50 g egg)
mcqs.why: The egg carries about 6 g protein and 5 g fat in 50 g, the richest protein source in the list; cucumber and carrot are mostly water and rice is mostly carbohydrate.

mcqs.q: Potato fries are energy-dense mainly because they contain much:
options: Fat absorbed from the frying oil (about 15 g per 100 g)
mcqs.why: Fries contain about 41 g carbohydrate and about 15 g fat per 100 g, much of the fat absorbed during frying; with the burger they are the most energy-dense and least healthy in excess.

mcqs.q: Roti and cooked rice are valuable in the diet chiefly as sources of:
mcqs.why: Roti (about 18 g carbohydrate in 40 g) and cooked rice (about 28 g per 100 g) are rich in carbohydrates, the body's main source of energy.

mcqs.q: The shapes and activities of proteins and nucleic acids depend on:
mcqs.why: Proteins fold and nucleic acids function correctly only in water; without water the biomolecules cannot function, as this lesson concludes.

mcqs.q: Water transports substances in plants through the:
options: Blood-like flow of sap in xylem and phloem (and in animals, the blood)
mcqs.why: Water is the transport medium of living things: it carries dissolved substances in the blood of animals and in the sap of plants, linking all parts of the organism.

mcqs.q: Carrot, like cucumber, is mostly water. Its water content per 100 g is about:
mcqs.why: From the food-table values in this lesson: carrot contains about 88 g water, 10 g carbohydrate, 0.9 g protein and 0.2 g fat per 100 g.
