Q: Primarily, all enzymes are;

(a) Nucleic acids (b) Proteins (c) Carbohydrates (d) Lipids
Correct answer: Proteins

Q: Which best defines an enzyme?

(a) A chemical that breaks down food. (b) A hormone that regulates metabolism. (c) A protein that speeds up reactions. (d) A molecule that stores energy.
Correct answer: A protein that speeds up reactions.

Q: What can happen if an enzyme is exposed to temperature that is higher than its optimal temperature?

(a) Enzyme activity rate will increase. (b) Enzyme's shape will change, potentially reducing its activity. (c) Enzyme will speed up the reaction and remain stable. (d) Enzyme will become a substrate itself.
Correct answer: Enzyme's shape will change, potentially reducing its activity.

Q: Enzymes are specific in their action because:

(a) Their active sites fit specific substrates. (b) They are always proteins. (c) They are consumed in reactions. (d) They work only at high temperatures.
Correct answer: Their active sites fit specific substrates.

Q: Prosthetic groups are;

(a) Required by all enzymes. (b) Proteins in nature. (c) Loosely attached with enzymes. (d) Tightly bound to enzyme.
Correct answer: Tightly bound to enzyme.

Q: How does increasing temperature affect enzyme activity?

(a) Increases activity to a point (b) Always decreases activity (c) Makes enzymes non-functional (d) No effect on enzyme
Correct answer: Increases activity to a point

Q: How does competitive inhibitor affect enzyme action?

(a) Attaches with the substrate. (b) Changes enzyme shape. (c) Attaches and blocks the active site. (d) Blocks the cofactors.
Correct answer: Attaches and blocks the active site.

Q: An enzyme works best at a pH of 7.4. It is placed in an acidic solution with a pH of 4.0. How will this affect the enzyme?

(a) The active site will be modified, reducing substrate binding. (b) The enzyme will catalyse reactions faster due to increased H ions. (c) The enzyme will gain additional active sites. (d) The substrate will become inactive in an acidic environment.
Correct answer: The active site will be modified, reducing substrate binding.

Q: What is TRUE according to the induced fit model of enzyme action?

(a) Enzyme's active site changes shape to bind the substrate. (b) Substrate changes shape to bind to active site. (c) No shape changes occur in active site or substrate. (d) Substrate attaches the enzyme at a site other that active site.
Correct answer: Enzyme's active site changes shape to bind the substrate.

Q: What is TRUE about the optimum pH values of the following enzymes of digestive system?

(a) Pepsin works at low pH while trypsin works at high pH (b) Both work at high pH (c) Both work at low pH (d) Pepsin works at high pH while trypsin works at low pH
Correct answer: Pepsin works at low pH while trypsin works at high pH

mcqs.q: Primarily, all enzymes are;
mcqs.why: Primarily, all enzymes are proteins: they are made of amino acids and their specific three-dimensional shape forms the active site. (A few RNA enzymes are the rare exception.)

mcqs.q: Which best defines an enzyme?
options: A chemical that breaks down food.
A protein that speeds up reactions.
mcqs.why: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up (catalyses) a biochemical reaction without being used up itself; it is neither a hormone nor an energy store.

mcqs.q: What can happen if an enzyme is exposed to temperature that is higher than its optimal temperature?
options: Enzyme's shape will change, potentially reducing its activity.
Enzyme will speed up the reaction and remain stable.
Enzyme will become a substrate itself.
mcqs.why: Above the optimum temperature the weak bonds holding the enzyme's shape break, the active site is distorted (denaturation) and activity falls, potentially to zero.

mcqs.q: Enzymes are specific in their action because:
options: Their active sites fit specific substrates.
They work only at high temperatures.
mcqs.why: Each enzyme's active site has a shape complementary to one specific substrate, so only that substrate fits: this fit is the basis of enzyme specificity.

mcqs.q: Prosthetic groups are;
mcqs.why: A prosthetic group is a non-protein part that is tightly and permanently bound to the enzyme, unlike a coenzyme, which attaches loosely and temporarily.

mcqs.q: How does increasing temperature affect enzyme activity?
mcqs.why: As temperature rises, the molecules move faster and collide more, so activity increases up to the optimum; beyond it, denaturation makes the activity fall.

mcqs.q: How does competitive inhibitor affect enzyme action?
options: Attaches and blocks the active site.
mcqs.why: A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate and competes for the active site itself, attaching there and blocking the substrate from entering.

mcqs.q: An enzyme works best at a pH of 7.4. It is placed in an acidic solution with a pH of 4.0. How will this affect the enzyme?
options: The active site will be modified, reducing substrate binding.
The enzyme will catalyse reactions faster due to increased H ions.
The enzyme will gain additional active sites.
The substrate will become inactive in an acidic environment.
mcqs.why: At pH 4.0, far from its optimum of 7.4, the charges on the active site change and its shape is modified, so the substrate binds less well and the reaction slows.

mcqs.q: What is TRUE according to the induced fit model of enzyme action?
options: Substrate changes shape to bind to active site.
No shape changes occur in active site or substrate.
Enzyme's active site changes shape to bind the substrate.
Substrate attaches the enzyme at a site other that active site.
mcqs.why: In the induced fit model the enzyme is not rigid: when the substrate approaches, the active site changes its shape slightly so that it fits the substrate closely.

mcqs.q: What is TRUE about the optimum pH values of the following enzymes of digestive system?
options: Pepsin works at high pH while trypsin works at low pH
Pepsin works at low pH while trypsin works at high pH
mcqs.why: Pepsin of the stomach works best in strongly acidic conditions (about pH 2), while trypsin of the intestine works best in alkaline conditions (about pH 8).

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Define metabolism. Differentiate between catabolism and anabolism.

Metabolism is the sum of all the biochemical reactions occurring in a living organism. Catabolism is the breaking down of larger molecules into smaller ones, releasing energy (e.g. respiration). Anabolism is the building up of large molecules from small ones, using energy (e.g. protein synthesis and photosynthesis).

Q: Which type of metabolism demands input of energy? Give an example.

Anabolism demands an input of energy, because building large molecules from small ones stores energy in their bonds. Example: the synthesis of proteins from amino acids (and photosynthesis, in which glucose is built from carbon dioxide and water).

Q: Define an enzyme. What is its role in metabolism?

An enzyme is a protein that catalyses (speeds up) a biochemical reaction without being used up itself. Its role in metabolism is to make the reactions of the cell fast enough for life: each enzyme lowers the activation energy of one specific reaction, so anabolism and catabolism proceed in an orderly, controlled way at body temperature.

Q: What is the active site of enzyme? State its importance in enzyme specificity.

The active site is the specific region (a pocket or groove) on the surface of the enzyme molecule where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place. Its shape is complementary to the substrate, so only a substrate of the matching shape can fit into it: this is the basis of enzyme specificity (lock and key).

Q: Provide an example of a specific enzyme-substrate pair.

Amylase and starch: the enzyme amylase acts only on its substrate starch, breaking it into maltose. (Another pair: pepsin and proteins in the stomach.)

Q: What is the effect of substrate concentration on enzyme activity?

As substrate concentration increases, more active sites are occupied, so the rate of reaction rises. Eventually all the active sites are busy (saturated) all the time, and adding more substrate cannot increase the rate further: the rate levels off, limited by the amount of enzyme.

Q: Provide two examples of enzymes that operate optimally at specific pH.

Pepsin, the stomach enzyme, works best in strongly acidic conditions (about pH 2). Trypsin, the intestinal enzyme, works best in alkaline conditions (about pH 8). (Salivary amylase works best near neutral, about pH 7.)

Q: What do you mean by optimum temperature and pH?

The optimum temperature is the temperature at which the enzyme works at its maximum rate (for human enzymes about 37 degrees C). The optimum pH is the pH value at which the enzyme's activity is maximum. Away from these optima the activity falls.

Q: Which type of enzyme inhibitors inhibit the enzymes without attaching to the active site?

Non-competitive inhibitors: they bind to a site on the enzyme other than the active site (an allosteric site) and change the shape of the active site so the substrate cannot fit. Examples are heavy metals and certain drugs used in cancer therapy.

Q: Differentiate between competitive and non-competitive inhibition.

A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site itself, blocking it; its effect can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration (e.g. antibiotics). A non-competitive inhibitor binds at a different site and distorts the active site, so the substrate cannot bind; adding more substrate does not remove its effect (e.g. heavy metals).

mcqs.q: Metabolism is best defined as:
options: The sum of all the biochemical reactions occurring in a living organism
The movement of substances in blood
mcqs.why: Metabolism includes both catabolism, breaking large molecules down with release of energy, and anabolism, building large molecules up using energy.

mcqs.q: Which type of metabolism demands an input of energy?
mcqs.why: Anabolism builds large molecules from small ones and stores energy in their bonds, so it demands energy input; protein synthesis and photosynthesis are examples.

mcqs.q: An enzyme speeds up a reaction by:
options: Raising the temperature of the cell
Lowering the activation energy of the reaction
mcqs.why: Each enzyme lowers the activation energy of one specific reaction, so anabolism and catabolism can proceed fast enough for life at body temperature, and the enzyme itself is not used up.

mcqs.q: The active site of an enzyme is:
options: The part that makes the enzyme a protein
The specific pocket on the enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place
The site where inhibitors must bind
mcqs.why: The active site's shape is complementary to the substrate, so only a matching substrate can fit into it; this is the basis of enzyme specificity, the lock-and-key idea.

mcqs.q: Amylase is specific for its substrate, which is:
mcqs.why: Amylase acts only on starch, breaking it into maltose; another specific pair in this lesson is pepsin acting on proteins in the stomach.

mcqs.q: When substrate concentration rises beyond the point where all active sites are busy, the rate of reaction:
options: Levels off, limited by the amount of enzyme
mcqs.why: At first more substrate fills more active sites and the rate rises; once every active site is saturated, adding more substrate cannot increase the rate further.

mcqs.q: Pepsin, the stomach enzyme, works best at about:
mcqs.why: Pepsin is adapted to the acidic gastric juice and works best near pH 2, while the intestinal enzyme trypsin works best near pH 8 and salivary amylase near pH 7.

mcqs.q: The optimum temperature for human enzymes is about:
mcqs.why: The optimum temperature is the temperature of maximum activity, about 37 degrees C for human enzymes; the optimum pH is likewise the pH of maximum activity.

mcqs.q: Non-competitive inhibitors reduce enzyme activity by:
options: Binding at a site other than the active site and distorting the active site's shape
mcqs.why: Non-competitive inhibitors attach to an allosteric site and change the shape of the active site so the substrate cannot fit; heavy metals are examples.

mcqs.q: The effect of a competitive inhibitor can be overcome by:
mcqs.why: Because a competitive inhibitor merely competes for the active site, enough extra substrate can out-compete it; this does not work for non-competitive inhibitors, which distort the site itself.

lessons.title: Detailed Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Describe the characteristics of enzymes.

Enzymes are biological catalysts with these characteristics: they are proteins; they speed up reactions enormously without being consumed, so they are needed in small amounts; they are highly specific, each acting on one substrate or one type of reaction, because of the shape of the active site; they lower the activation energy of reactions; they work best at an optimum temperature and pH and are denatured by high temperature and extreme pH; many need cofactors (metal ions, coenzymes or prosthetic groups) to be fully active; and their action can be blocked by inhibitors.

Q: Describe how temperature extremes can inhibit enzyme activity and lead to enzyme denaturation.

As temperature rises above the optimum, the increased vibration of the enzyme molecule breaks the weak bonds that hold its three-dimensional shape. The active site loses its complementary shape (denaturation), so the substrate can no longer fit and the activity falls sharply to zero. Denaturation by heat is usually permanent: cooling does not restore the shape. At very low temperatures the enzyme is not denatured but is inactive because the molecules move too slowly; warming restores activity. This is why extremes of temperature inhibit enzyme action.

Q: How does pH affect enzyme activity?

Every enzyme has an optimum pH at which its active site has the correct shape and charges to bind the substrate, and its activity is maximum. If the pH moves away from the optimum, the charges on the amino acids of the active site change, the substrate binds less well, and the rate falls; at strongly wrong pH the enzyme is denatured and stops working. Examples: pepsin works at about pH 2 in the stomach, while trypsin works at about pH 8 in the intestine; an enzyme placed in the wrong pH region is therefore almost inactive.

Q: Describe the factors that affect the activity of enzymes.

The factors are: (1) Temperature: activity rises with temperature up to the optimum, then falls as the enzyme denatures. (2) pH: each enzyme has an optimum pH; activity falls on either side. (3) Substrate concentration: rate rises with concentration until all active sites are saturated. (4) Enzyme concentration: with enough substrate, more enzyme means a faster rate. (5) Cofactors: many enzymes need metal ions or coenzymes to work. (6) Inhibitors: competitive and non-competitive inhibitors reduce or stop activity.

Q: Compare the Lock-and-Key and Induced Fit models of enzyme action.

In the lock-and-key model (Fischer), the active site has a fixed, rigid shape exactly complementary to the substrate, like a lock fitting one key; the substrate fits in and the reaction occurs. In the induced fit model (Koshland), the active site is not rigid: when the substrate approaches, the enzyme changes the shape of its active site slightly so that it fits the substrate closely and performs its function. Both models explain specificity; induced fit better explains how enzymes bind and act on substrates that are not a perfect initial fit.

mcqs.q: Enzymes are needed only in small amounts because they:
options: Are not consumed in the reactions they catalyse
mcqs.why: An enzyme emerges unchanged from its reaction and can be used again and again, so a small quantity catalyses a large amount of substrate.

mcqs.q: Denaturation of an enzyme by heat is usually:
options: Permanent: cooling does not restore the active site's shape
mcqs.why: Heat breaks the weak bonds holding the enzyme's three-dimensional shape; the active site is lost for good. Cold only makes the enzyme inactive, and warming restores activity.

mcqs.q: At very low temperatures an enzyme becomes inactive mainly because:
options: The molecules move too slowly for effective collisions
mcqs.why: Low temperature does not denature the enzyme; the molecules simply have too little kinetic energy, and activity returns when the enzyme is warmed.

mcqs.q: If the pH moves far from an enzyme's optimum, activity falls because:
options: The charges on the amino acids of the active site change and the substrate binds less well
mcqs.why: Each enzyme's active site has the correct shape and charges only at its optimum pH; at strongly wrong pH the enzyme is denatured and stops working altogether.

mcqs.q: With enough substrate present, increasing the enzyme concentration will:
mcqs.why: More enzyme molecules provide more active sites working at the same time, so, provided substrate is plentiful, the rate rises with enzyme concentration.

mcqs.q: Many enzymes need cofactors to be fully active. A cofactor may be:
options: A metal ion or a coenzyme
mcqs.why: Cofactors include metal ions, coenzymes and tightly bound prosthetic groups; without them many enzymes cannot catalyse their reactions properly.

mcqs.q: In the lock-and-key model, the active site is assumed to be:
options: Rigid, with a fixed shape exactly complementary to the substrate
mcqs.why: Fischer's lock-and-key model treats the active site as a rigid lock fitting one key (substrate); Koshland's induced fit model instead lets the site adjust its shape on binding.

mcqs.q: The induced fit model explains specificity better for substrates that:
options: Are not a perfect fit for the active site at first
mcqs.why: In induced fit the approaching substrate induces the active site to mould itself closely around it, explaining binding of substrates that are not initially a perfect fit.

mcqs.q: An enzyme placed in a pH region far from its optimum is:
mcqs.why: Pepsin works at about pH 2 and trypsin at about pH 8; an enzyme in the wrong pH region binds its substrate poorly and is therefore almost inactive.

mcqs.q: Which factor does NOT affect enzyme activity?
mcqs.why: Enzyme activity is governed by temperature, pH, substrate and enzyme concentrations, cofactors and inhibitors; the colour of the apparatus plays no part.

mcqs.why: Energy is released from ATP when its terminal phosphate bond (a P-P bond between phosphate groups) is broken, converting ATP to ADP plus phosphate.

mcqs.q: Light reactions of photosynthesis occur in;
mcqs.why: The light reactions of photosynthesis take place in the thylakoids of the chloroplasts, where the chlorophyll is located; the dark reactions occur in the stroma.

mcqs.q: Which type of chlorophyll is most common in plants?
mcqs.why: Chlorophyll a is the most common and main photosynthetic pigment in plants; chlorophyll b is an accessory pigment and c and d occur only in some algae.

mcqs.q: Which wavelengths of light are absorbed to maximum by chlorophylls?
mcqs.why: Chlorophyll absorbs light most strongly in the red and blue regions; green light is mostly reflected, which is why leaves look green.

mcqs.q: When yeast ferments glucose, the products are;
mcqs.why: In alcoholic fermentation, yeast converts glucose into ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide, with a net gain of 2 ATP; this is used in making bread and alcoholic drinks.

mcqs.q: Where do the dark reactions of photosynthesis occur?
mcqs.why: The dark reactions (Calvin cycle) occur in the stroma of the chloroplast, where carbon dioxide is reduced to glucose using the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.

mcqs.q: Which molecule donates electrons in the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis?
mcqs.why: Water is the electron donor of the light reactions: it is split (photolysis) into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen, replacing the electrons lost by chlorophyll.

mcqs.q: Which process in aerobic respiration produces the most ATP?
mcqs.why: The electron transport chain produces the largest share of ATP in aerobic respiration, far more than glycolysis or the Krebs cycle, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor.

mcqs.q: How many ATP molecules are the net profit from one glucose molecule during anaerobic respiration?
mcqs.why: Anaerobic respiration is incomplete oxidation: glycolysis alone runs, giving a net profit of only 2 ATP per glucose, compared with about 36 ATP in aerobic respiration.

mcqs.q: What is a common byproduct of anaerobic respiration in animal cells?
mcqs.why: In animal muscle cells anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid, which accumulates during intense exercise and causes fatigue and cramps until the oxygen debt is repaid.

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Write the importance of oxidation-reduction reactions.

Redox reactions transfer electrons between molecules, and this electron flow is the means by which energy is released from food molecules and captured in ATP during respiration, and by which light energy is captured in photosynthesis. Oxidation (loss of electrons) of glucose releases energy; reduction (gain of electrons) of carriers stores it. Without redox reactions, cells could not convert the energy of food or sunlight into usable form.

Q: What do ATP and ADP mean? What are the roles of these molecules for the cellular metabolism?

ATP means adenosine triphosphate and ADP means adenosine diphosphate. ATP is the energy currency of the cell: when a cell needs energy, ATP is broken to ADP + phosphate, releasing energy. When energy is available (from respiration or photosynthesis), ADP + phosphate are joined to rebuild ATP, storing the energy. This ATP-ADP cycle supplies energy for all cellular metabolism.

Q: Write down the word equation for photosynthesis.

Carbon dioxide + water --(light energy, chlorophyll)--> glucose (food) + oxygen. In symbols: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.

Q: Why is chlorophyll important for photosynthesis?

Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light energy, mainly in the red and blue regions of light. Without chlorophyll the plant cannot capture the sunlight that drives photosynthesis; the energy for making food comes entirely through chlorophyll.

Q: How is oxygen produced during photosynthesis?

The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from water. In the light reactions, water molecules are split (photolysis) into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen; the electrons and hydrogen are used further, and the oxygen is released as a by-product through the stomata.

Q: Which organisms carry out photosynthesis? Which cell organelle is responsible for the absorption of light for photosynthesis?

Photosynthesis is carried out by green plants, algae and some bacteria (the autotrophs). The organelle responsible for absorbing light is the chloroplast, whose chlorophyll in the thylakoids captures the sunlight.

Q: State the main purpose of cellular respiration.

The main purpose of cellular respiration is to release the energy stored in food (glucose) and store it in ATP, the usable energy currency, so that the cell can perform all its life activities.

Q: State the equation (in words or symbols) for aerobic respiration.

Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP). In symbols: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + ATP (energy).

Q: Write a brief note on the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration.

Oxygen is the final acceptor of electrons and hydrogen in the electron transport chain. It allows the complete oxidation of glucose: pyruvic acid is fully broken down to carbon dioxide and water, and a large amount of ATP (about 36 per glucose) is produced. Without oxygen, only glycolysis can run and very little energy is obtained.

Q: Define anaerobic and aerobic respiration.

Aerobic respiration is the complete oxidation of glucose in the presence of oxygen, producing carbon dioxide, water and a large amount of energy. Anaerobic respiration is the incomplete oxidation of glucose in the absence of oxygen, producing lactic acid (in animals) or alcohol and carbon dioxide (in yeast), with only a little energy.

Q: What are the end products of anaerobic respiration in animals and yeast?

In animals (muscle cells): lactic acid (with a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose). In yeast: ethyl alcohol (ethanol) and carbon dioxide (also a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose).

Q: How do muscles respond to oxygen deficiency during intense exercise?

During intense exercise the muscles need energy faster than the blood can supply oxygen, so they switch partly to anaerobic respiration: glucose is broken down to lactic acid, giving quick (but little) ATP. The lactic acid accumulates and causes muscle fatigue and cramps; afterwards, extra oxygen (the oxygen debt) is used to remove it.

Q: List ways in which respiratory energy is used in the body.

The energy of respiration (as ATP) is used for: muscle contraction and movement; keeping the body warm; active transport of materials across membranes; building large molecules (growth and repair); conduction of nerve impulses; and cell division. In plants it also drives the uptake of minerals and the transport of food.

mcqs.q: Oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions are important in bioenergetics because they:
options: Transfer electrons, releasing energy from food and capturing it in ATP
mcqs.why: Oxidation of glucose releases energy and reduction of carriers stores it; this electron flow is how respiration releases food energy into ATP and photosynthesis captures light energy.

mcqs.q: ATP and ADP stand for:
options: Adenine triose phosphate and adenine dual phosphate
Active transport protein and active diffusion protein
mcqs.why: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is broken to ADP (adenosine diphosphate) plus phosphate to release energy, and ADP plus phosphate are rejoined to store energy again.

mcqs.q: The word equation for photosynthesis is:
options: Carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen (using light energy and chlorophyll)
mcqs.why: In symbols: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Photosynthesis builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water and releases oxygen; the reverse equation is respiration.

mcqs.q: The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from:
options: Water, which is split in the light reactions (photolysis)
mcqs.why: In the light reactions water molecules are split into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen; the oxygen is released as a by-product through the stomata.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis is carried out by:
options: Green plants, algae and some bacteria
mcqs.why: The autotrophs, green plants, algae and some bacteria, photosynthesise; the organelle responsible for absorbing the light is the chloroplast.

mcqs.q: The main purpose of cellular respiration is to:
options: Remove carbon dioxide from the body
Release the energy of glucose and store it in ATP for the cell's activities
mcqs.why: Respiration transfers the energy stored in food into ATP, the usable energy currency, so the cell can perform all its life activities.

mcqs.q: Oxygen's role at the end of the electron transport chain is to act as:
options: The final acceptor of electrons and hydrogen, forming water
mcqs.why: Oxygen accepts the electrons and hydrogen at the end of the chain, allowing complete oxidation of glucose to carbon dioxide and water with about 36 ATP per glucose.

mcqs.q: Aerobic respiration differs from anaerobic respiration in that aerobic respiration:
options: Completely oxidises glucose in the presence of oxygen, producing much more energy
mcqs.why: Aerobic respiration gives carbon dioxide, water and a large amount of energy; anaerobic respiration is incomplete oxidation without oxygen, giving lactic acid or alcohol and carbon dioxide with little energy.

mcqs.q: During intense exercise, muscles produce lactic acid because:
options: They need energy faster than the blood can supply oxygen, so they respire anaerobically
mcqs.why: Anaerobic respiration in the muscles gives quick but little ATP; the accumulating lactic acid causes fatigue and cramps, and the oxygen debt is repaid afterwards to remove it.

mcqs.q: Respiratory energy (ATP) is used in the body for:
options: Muscle contraction, keeping the body warm, active transport and building molecules
mcqs.why: ATP powers muscle contraction, warmth, active transport, synthesis of large molecules, nerve impulses and cell division; in plants it also drives uptake of minerals and transport of food.

lessons.title: Detailed Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Explain ATP as a molecule that is the chief energy currency of all cells.

ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is a small molecule made of adenine, a ribose sugar and three phosphate groups. The bonds between its phosphate groups store energy; when the terminal phosphate is removed (ATP -> ADP + Pi), energy is released exactly where and when the cell needs it, in small usable amounts. ATP is made continuously in respiration and photosynthesis and used continuously for work, so it acts as the chief energy currency of all cells, linking energy-releasing and energy-using reactions.

Q: Outline the processes involved in photosynthesis?

Photosynthesis occurs in the chloroplasts in two stages. Light reactions (in the thylakoids): chlorophyll captures sunlight; water is split, releasing oxygen, and energy is stored as ATP and NADPH. Dark reactions (in the stroma; they do not need light directly): carbon dioxide is reduced, using the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, and built into glucose (the Calvin cycle). Overall: carbon dioxide + water, using light energy, give glucose + oxygen. The glucose is used for respiration or stored as starch.

Q: Write a note on the intake of carbon dioxide and water by plants

Plants take carbon dioxide from the air through the stomata of the leaves: the guard cells open the stomata, CO2 diffuses into the leaf and reaches the mesophyll cells. Water is taken from the soil by the root hairs by osmosis, and is carried up to the leaves through the xylem vessels (in the transpiration stream). Both raw materials thus reach the chloroplasts, where they are used in photosynthesis.

Q: Explain the types and importance of anaerobic respiration.

Anaerobic respiration is the incomplete breakdown of glucose without oxygen. Types: (1) Alcoholic fermentation in yeast and some microbes: glucose -> ethanol + carbon dioxide + 2 ATP. (2) Lactic acid fermentation in animal muscles and some bacteria: glucose -> lactic acid + 2 ATP. Importance: it supplies emergency energy to muscles when oxygen is short; it is used in industry for making bread, alcoholic drinks, yoghurt and cheese; and it allows organisms living without oxygen (e.g. in mud or the gut) to survive. Its drawback is the low energy yield and the toxic products.

Q: Outline the mechanism of aerobic respiration.

Aerobic respiration occurs in three stages. (1) Glycolysis (in the cytoplasm): glucose is broken into two molecules of pyruvic acid, with a net gain of 2 ATP. (2) Krebs cycle (in the mitochondria): pyruvic acid is completely broken down into carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions and high-energy electrons, with a small gain of ATP. (3) Electron transport chain (in the mitochondria): the electrons pass along a series of carriers, emitting energy that is used to convert ADP into ATP (the largest share of ATP); oxygen finally accepts the electrons and hydrogen to form water. Total yield is about 36 ATP per glucose.

Q: Compare the processes of respiration and photosynthesis.

Photosynthesis and respiration are opposite processes. Photosynthesis: takes in carbon dioxide and water, releases oxygen, builds glucose, stores light energy, occurs only in cells with chlorophyll and only in light, and increases the mass of the plant. Respiration: takes in oxygen, releases carbon dioxide and water, breaks glucose down, releases energy as ATP, occurs in all living cells all the time, and decreases mass. Together they balance each other in nature, cycling carbon and oxygen.

mcqs.q: ATP is made of adenine, a ribose sugar and:
mcqs.why: The bonds between ATP's phosphate groups store energy; removing the terminal phosphate (ATP -> ADP + Pi) releases energy in small usable amounts exactly where the cell needs it.

mcqs.q: The light reactions of photosynthesis produce which two energy carriers used in the dark reactions?
mcqs.why: In the thylakoids, captured light energy splits water, releasing oxygen, and is stored as ATP and NADPH, which the dark reactions in the stroma then spend to build glucose.

mcqs.q: Carbon dioxide enters the leaf for photosynthesis through the:
mcqs.why: CO2 diffuses in through the stomata and reaches the mesophyll cells, while water arrives from the roots through the xylem in the transpiration stream.

mcqs.q: Alcoholic fermentation in yeast is important in industry for making:
mcqs.why: Yeast fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide with 2 ATP; it is used for bread, alcoholic drinks, and (as lactic acid fermentation) for yoghurt and cheese.

mcqs.q: Glycolysis, the first stage of aerobic respiration, takes place in the:
mcqs.why: In glycolysis, in the cytoplasm, glucose is broken into two molecules of pyruvic acid with a net gain of 2 ATP; the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain follow in the mitochondria.

mcqs.q: The total yield of aerobic respiration from one glucose molecule is about:
mcqs.why: Glycolysis gives 2 ATP, the Krebs cycle a small gain, and the electron transport chain the largest share, totalling about 36 ATP per glucose.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis and respiration are opposite processes because photosynthesis:
options: Occurs in all cells at all times
Decreases the mass of the plant
Stores energy in glucose and releases oxygen, while respiration releases energy and uses oxygen
Takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide
mcqs.why: Photosynthesis builds glucose, stores light energy and occurs only in chlorophyll cells in light; respiration breaks glucose down in all living cells all the time. Together they cycle carbon and oxygen in nature.

mcqs.q: The drawback of anaerobic respiration is that:
options: Its energy yield is low and its products (lactic acid or alcohol) are toxic
mcqs.why: Anaerobic respiration gives only 2 ATP per glucose and leaves toxic end products, though it supplies emergency energy and is useful in industry and for organisms living without oxygen.

mcqs.q: In the Krebs cycle, pyruvic acid is completely broken down into:
options: Carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions and high-energy electrons
mcqs.why: The Krebs cycle, in the mitochondria, completes the breakdown of pyruvic acid; its electrons then pass along the electron transport chain to make most of the ATP.

mcqs.q: ATP links energy-releasing and energy-using reactions because it is:
options: Made continuously in respiration and photosynthesis and used continuously for work
mcqs.why: ATP is the chief energy currency of all cells: it is built wherever energy is released and spent wherever work is done, coupling the two kinds of reactions.

lessons.title: Inquisitive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: How does the structure of ATP enable it to store and release energy efficiently?

ATP has a chain of three phosphate groups whose bonds are energy-rich because the negatively charged phosphates repel one another: energy is stored when a phosphate is added (ADP + Pi -> ATP, during respiration) and released when the last phosphate bond is broken by hydrolysis (ATP -> ADP + Pi). The molecule is small, soluble and mobile, so it carries energy quickly from where it is made (mitochondria/chloroplasts) to where it is needed, and it can be recycled thousands of times a day: an ideal store-and-release system.

mcqs.q: The three phosphate groups of ATP store energy efficiently partly because they:
options: Are negatively charged and repel one another, so their bonds are energy-rich
mcqs.why: The repulsion between the negatively charged phosphates makes the terminal bond energy-rich: energy is stored when a phosphate is added and released when it is removed by hydrolysis.

mcqs.q: ATP can be recycled many times because after releasing energy as ADP + Pi it is:
options: Rebuilt into ATP during respiration and photosynthesis
mcqs.why: The ADP and phosphate are rejoined whenever energy is available, so the same molecule is recycled thousands of times a day, carrying energy from where it is made to where it is needed.

mcqs.q: ATP is well suited as an energy carrier because the molecule is:
options: Small, soluble and mobile within the cell
mcqs.why: Being small and soluble, ATP moves quickly from mitochondria and chloroplasts to every site of work in the cell, releasing energy in small usable amounts.

mcqs.q: Hydrolysis of ATP means:
options: Breaking ATP with water into ADP and phosphate, releasing energy
mcqs.why: Energy is released when the last phosphate bond of ATP is broken by hydrolysis (ATP -> ADP + Pi); building ATP again stores energy for later use.

mcqs.q: Energy stored in ATP is released in small usable amounts. This matters because:
options: Large amounts would be easier to use
The cell can spend exactly the energy a process needs, where and when it needs it
mcqs.why: Instead of releasing all the energy of glucose at once as heat, the cell deals in small ATP units, supplying each process with the amount it requires.

mcqs.q: Which process adds a phosphate to ADP to form ATP?
options: Respiration (and the light reactions of photosynthesis)
mcqs.why: ATP is regenerated during cellular respiration and in the light reactions of photosynthesis, completing the ATP-ADP cycle that supplies all cellular metabolism.

mcqs.q: The energy currency role of ATP is the same in:
mcqs.why: ATP is described in this chapter as the chief energy currency of ALL cells, linking energy-releasing and energy-using reactions in every living organism.

mcqs.q: If a cell could not rebuild ATP from ADP, the result would be that:
options: It would use glucose directly for everything
Its energy supply would run out and its activities would stop
mcqs.why: All cellular work is paid for in ATP; without continuous regeneration through respiration, the ATP-ADP cycle stops and metabolism cannot continue.

mcqs.q: The phosphate bond broken to release energy from ATP is the one:
options: Between the last (terminal) phosphate group and the rest of the molecule
mcqs.why: Removing the terminal phosphate converts ATP to ADP and releases the stored energy; adding it back during respiration stores energy again.

mcqs.q: ATP carries energy from where it is made to where it is needed. It is made mainly in the:
mcqs.why: Respiration in mitochondria (and light reactions in chloroplasts) produce ATP, which then diffuses to sites of work throughout the cell.

mcqs.why: In the light reactions, water is split by photolysis into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen; carbon dioxide enters the process later, in the dark reactions.

mcqs.q: The primary function of root hairs is:
mcqs.why: ATP is formed in the light-dependent reactions: as electrons pass along the chain in the thylakoid membrane, the released energy converts ADP and phosphate into ATP.

mcqs.q: Root hairs absorb salts from soil by;
mcqs.why: The dark reactions (carbon fixation) take place in the stroma, the fluid part of the chloroplast surrounding the thylakoids, where the Calvin cycle enzymes are located.

mcqs.why: C4 and CAM plants open their stomata at night (CAM) or use spatial separation (C4) so that gas exchange can happen with less water loss; C3 plants open stomata by day and lose more water.

mcqs.q: The transpiration is regulated by;

mcqs.why: In darkness there is no light energy, so the light reactions cannot run, no ATP or NADPH is made, and photosynthesis stops completely.

mcqs.why: Water moves through the xylem as a continuous unbroken column from root to leaf: the cohesion of water molecules and the pull of transpiration keep the column intact.

mcqs.q: In most plants the food is transported in the form of:

options: Water is pulled from the sink
Movement of food in phloem is due to gravity
Solutes move from low to high concentration
Water enters the source, creating pressure

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Define mineral nutrition in plants.

Mineral nutrition in plants is the taking in and use of inorganic mineral elements (nutrients) from the soil, which the plant needs for building its body substances, for growth and for its life processes. Plants obtain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from air and water; all other essential elements come as mineral salts through the roots.

Q: Define macronutrients and micronutrients and give examples.

Macronutrients are the mineral elements required in large amounts, e.g. nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur. Micronutrients are required in very small (trace) amounts, e.g. iron, zinc, boron, manganese, copper and molybdenum. Both are essential; deficiency of either group harms the plant.

Q: State the roles of nitrogen and magnesium in plants.

Nitrogen is essential for making proteins (and nucleic acids and chlorophyll), so it is needed for growth of all tissues. Magnesium is the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule, so it is essential for the formation of chlorophyll and hence for photosynthesis.

Q: Define transpiration and its types.

Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of water vapour from the aerial parts of the plant, mainly the leaves. Types: (1) Stomatal transpiration through the stomata (the largest share). (2) Cuticular transpiration directly through the cuticle of the epidermis. (3) Lenticular transpiration through lenticels in woody stems.

Q: How is the transpirational pull important in plants?

As water evaporates from the leaves, it pulls the continuous water column in the xylem upward (cohesion-tension): this transpirational pull is the main force that draws water and dissolved salts from the roots to the topmost leaves, even in tall trees, without any pump.

Q: Transpiration is the loss of water from plants. Is it a harmful phenomenon? If no, what is its importance?

No, it is not simply harmful; it is called a necessary evil. It creates the transpiration pull that lifts water and minerals to the leaves, keeps the leaf cool in hot weather, and maintains the flow needed for photosynthesis. Its harm appears only when water loss exceeds absorption, causing wilting; plants regulate it through the stomata.

Q: Differentiate between: i. Xylem and phloem ii. Transpiration and guttation iii. Hydrophytes and halophytes iv. Hydrophytes and xerophytes v. Lenticular transpiration and stomatal transpiration

i. Xylem and phloem: xylem transports water and mineral salts upward from roots to leaves and is made of dead vessels/tracheids; phloem transports prepared food (sucrose) from the leaves to all parts, in both directions, and is made of living sieve tubes. ii. Transpiration and guttation: transpiration is loss of water as vapour, mainly through stomata in the daytime; guttation is loss of liquid water droplets from the edges/tips of leaves through special pores, usually at night or early morning when transpiration is low. iii. Hydrophytes and halophytes: hydrophytes live in water or very wet places; halophytes live in salty soils (e.g. near the sea) and tolerate high salt. iv. Hydrophytes and xerophytes: hydrophytes live where water is abundant and have large air spaces and poorly developed xylem; xerophytes live in dry places and have thick cuticle, sunken stomata and water-storing tissues to reduce loss. v. Lenticular and stomatal transpiration: lenticular transpiration occurs through lenticels (pores in the bark of woody stems) and is very small; stomatal transpiration occurs through the stomata of leaves and is the main route of water loss, regulated by guard cells.

Q: How do the plants of rubber and keekar excrete their wastes?

Rubber plant excretes its waste latex in special vessels (laticifers); when the bark is cut, the latex flows out. Keekar (Acacia) gets rid of excess water and wastes through guttation and stores wastes such as gums and resins in its bark and old wood, which are shed or ooze out (keekar produces gum arabic-like gum). Such wastes are kept away from the living cells or removed with falling bark and leaves.

mcqs.q: In the light reactions, the role of NADP is to:
options: Accept hydrogen (electrons and protons) and carry it as NADPH to the dark reactions
mcqs.why: Chlorophyll absorbs the light and water is split; the hydrogen released is accepted by NADP, forming NADPH, which the dark reactions use to reduce carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: The process of photosynthesis is complete in plants, but in C3 plants it is inefficient because:
options: Rubisco can also fix oxygen (photorespiration), wasting energy
mcqs.why: In C3 plants the enzyme rubisco sometimes fixes oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, causing photorespiration, which releases CO2 and consumes energy without making sugar.

mcqs.q: CAM plants are adapted to dry conditions because they:
options: Open their stomata at night and store CO2 as an organic acid until daylight
mcqs.why: CAM plants such as cactus and pineapple take in CO2 at night, store it as malic acid, and fix it by day with stomata closed, saving water; C4 plants instead separate the steps between two cell types.

mcqs.q: A potometer is an instrument used to measure the rate of:
options: Water uptake by a plant shoot (as a measure of transpiration)
mcqs.why: As the shoot transpires it takes up water, and the movement of an air bubble in the potometer's capillary tube measures the rate of that uptake under different conditions.

mcqs.q: Transpiration is called a necessary evil because it:
options: Is essential for water transport and cooling, yet loses most of the absorbed water
mcqs.why: Plants lose most of the water they absorb through transpiration, but the pull drives the ascent of sap, brings minerals to the leaves and cools the plant; wilting occurs when loss exceeds uptake.

mcqs.q: Root pressure develops in the roots because:
options: Active pumping of minerals into the xylem draws water in by osmosis, building up pressure
mcqs.why: Mineral ions actively transported into the root xylem lower its water potential, water follows by osmosis, and the resulting root pressure pushes water a short distance up the stem.

mcqs.q: In phloem, sugars are transported from a source to a sink. A sink is:
options: A part where sugars are used or stored, such as roots, fruits or growing points
mcqs.why: Leaves that photosynthesise are sources; sinks, roots, tubers, fruits, seeds and growing points, receive the sugars, which are unloaded and used or stored as starch.

mcqs.q: Water enters the root hairs from the soil by:
options: Osmosis, because the root hair cell sap has a lower water potential than the soil water
mcqs.why: Soil water is a dilute solution with high water potential; the root hair's vacuolar sap is more concentrated, so water moves in by osmosis across the partially permeable membrane.

mcqs.q: Plants absorb minerals from the soil mainly by:
options: Active transport, using energy from respiration
mcqs.why: Minerals are often more concentrated inside the root than in the soil, so they must be pumped in against the gradient by active transport, which needs ATP; some also enter by diffusion and mass flow.

mcqs.q: The loss of water drops from the tips and edges of leaves is called:
mcqs.why: When root pressure is high and transpiration is low, xylem sap is forced out through special pores (hydathodes) as drops: this is guttation, distinct from vapour loss in transpiration.

lessons.title: Detailed Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Describe the events involved in the opening and closing of stomata.

Opening: in light, the guard cells actively take up potassium ions (K+); water follows by osmosis, the guard cells become turgid and swell. Because their inner walls (toward the pore) are thicker, the cells curve outward and the stoma opens. Closing: the K+ ions leave the guard cells, water follows out, the cells become flaccid and come together, closing the pore. This usually happens in darkness or when the plant is short of water, and it regulates both transpiration and gas exchange.

Q: Explain the internal structure of root and describe the uptake of salt and water by root.

Internal structure of root: the outer epidermis bears root hairs (extensions of epidermal cells) that absorb water and salts; inside is the cortex of loosely packed cells through which water moves; the endodermis controls entry into the central stele, which contains xylem and phloem. Uptake: water enters the root hairs by osmosis from the soil (passive absorption) and moves cell to cell into the xylem. Mineral salts are taken up both passively (with water/by diffusion where concentration allows) and by active transport, in which root cells use energy to absorb ions even against the concentration gradient.

Q: Describe temperature, wind and humidity as the factors affecting the rate of transpiration.

Temperature: higher temperature increases evaporation from the leaf and lowers the humidity of the air, so the rate of transpiration rises (until water shortage closes the stomata). Wind: moving air sweeps away the water vapour around the leaf, keeping the diffusion gradient steep, so wind increases transpiration; still air lets vapour accumulate and slows it. Humidity: humid air is already rich in water vapour, so the gradient from leaf to air is small and transpiration is slow; dry air speeds it up.

Q: Describe the mechanism of transport of water and salt in plants.

Water and salts absorbed by the root hairs pass through the cortex into the xylem vessels. The driving force is transpiration pull: evaporation from the leaves pulls the continuous water column (held together by cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to the xylem walls) upward from roots to leaves. Root pressure also pushes water up to a small extent, especially at night. In this way water and dissolved mineral salts reach every part of the plant.

Q: Explain the mechanism of food translocation by Pressure Flow Mechanism.

In the pressure flow mechanism, food moves through the phloem from a source (a leaf making sugar) to a sink (a growing or storing part). At the source, sugars are actively loaded into the sieve tubes; the high sugar concentration draws water from the xylem into the phloem by osmosis, raising the pressure. At the sink, sugars are removed and used or stored; water leaves the phloem and returns to the xylem, lowering the pressure there. The pressure difference drives the bulk flow of the sugar solution from source to sink.

Q: How do the plants excrete extra water and salts from their bodies?

Plants remove extra water by transpiration and by guttation (droplets from leaf edges through hydathodes when the air is humid). Extra salts are got rid of in several ways: they are stored in old leaves, bark or wood that is shed; some plants have salt glands that secrete salt onto the leaf surface; and halophytes store excess salt in vacuoles of special cells. Thus the internal balance of water and salts is maintained.

Q: Describe the process of gaseous exchange in plants

Plants exchange gases mainly through the stomata of the leaves: carbon dioxide diffuses in for photosynthesis and oxygen diffuses out; for respiration, oxygen diffuses in and carbon dioxide out, day and night. The spongy mesophyll has large air spaces so gases reach all the cells. In woody stems, gases pass through lenticels, and roots take up air from the spaces between soil particles. No special breathing organs are needed because the gases diffuse directly to the cells.

Q: Describe the mechanisms/adaptations in plants for excretion of wastes.

Plants have no special excretory system; they manage wastes by simple adaptations. Excess water is removed by transpiration and guttation. Oxygen, a waste of photosynthesis, leaves through the stomata. Many wastes are stored harmlessly in vacuoles, in old xylem (heartwood), in bark, or in leaves that are then shed; resins, gums and latex are kept in special ducts and vessels (e.g. gum in keekar, latex in rubber); and some wastes are deposited as crystals (e.g. calcium oxalate) in cells. Shedding of leaves and bark periodically removes the stored wastes.

Q: Explain osmotic adjustments in in hydrophytes, xerophytes and halophytes.

Osmotic adjustment means keeping the cell's water balance by adjusting solute concentration. Hydrophytes live in abundant water; their cells take up water freely and they have large air spaces and reduced xylem, with stomata on the upper leaf surface. Xerophytes live in dry habitats; they accumulate solutes to retain water, and reduce loss by thick cuticle, sunken or few stomata, rolled leaves and water-storing (succulent) tissues. Halophytes live in salty soil, where the outside solution is concentrated; they accumulate salts in vacuoles (balancing the external concentration so water can still enter), exclude salt at the roots, or secrete it through salt glands.

mcqs.q: The final product of the dark reactions of photosynthesis is:
options: Sugar (glucose), made by reducing carbon dioxide with hydrogen from NADPH
mcqs.why: In the Calvin cycle, carbon dioxide is fixed by RuBP and reduced using ATP and NADPH to carbohydrate; the cycle regenerates RuBP so fixation can continue.

mcqs.q: Photolysis in the light reactions refers to:
options: The splitting of water into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen by light energy
The joining of ADP and phosphate
mcqs.why: Light energy absorbed by chlorophyll splits water in the thylakoids; the electrons replace those lost by chlorophyll, and the oxygen is released as a by-product.

mcqs.q: C4 plants avoid photorespiration by:
options: First fixing CO2 into a 4-carbon compound in mesophyll cells, then releasing it near rubisco in bundle sheath cells
mcqs.why: By concentrating CO2 around rubisco in the bundle sheath, C4 plants such as maize and sugarcane keep oxygen away from the enzyme, so photosynthesis stays efficient in hot, dry climates.

mcqs.q: The evaporation of water from the leaves is increased by:
options: High temperature, low humidity, wind and bright light
mcqs.why: A steeper water-potential gradient and open stomata speed transpiration: hot, dry, windy, bright conditions remove vapour quickly, while humid still air slows the loss.

mcqs.q: Wilting of a plant occurs when:
options: The roots absorb too much water
The rate of transpiration exceeds the rate of water absorption and the cells lose turgor
mcqs.why: When water loss outruns uptake, cells become flaccid, the leaves droop (wilting), and the plant dies if the shortage continues; guard cells likewise lose turgor to close the stomata.

mcqs.q: In the pressure-flow model of phloem transport, pressure builds up at the source because:
options: Sugars loaded into the phloem lower its water potential, so water enters by osmosis
The sink pulls the sap by suction
mcqs.why: Active loading of sucrose into sieve tubes draws water in from the xylem by osmosis, raising hydrostatic pressure that pushes the sap towards the sink, where sugars are unloaded.

mcqs.q: Magnesium is an essential mineral for plants because it is:
options: A central part of the chlorophyll molecule
mcqs.why: Magnesium forms the centre of chlorophyll, so its deficiency yellows the leaves; nitrogen is needed for proteins and nucleic acids, potassium for enzymes and stomata, and phosphorus for ATP and membranes.

mcqs.q: A plant deficient in nitrogen shows:
options: Stunted growth and yellowing of the leaves (chlorosis)
mcqs.why: Without nitrogen the plant cannot make enough proteins and chlorophyll, so growth is stunted and leaves yellow; magnesium deficiency also causes chlorosis, especially between the veins.

mcqs.q: Water moves from the soil into the xylem of the root along the pathway:
mcqs.why: After entering the root hair, water crosses the cortex (by apoplast, symplast and vacuolar routes), passes the endodermis and enters the xylem vessels for the ascent of sap.

mcqs.q: Translocation in plants means the transport of:
options: Organic food (sugars) through the phloem from source to sink
mcqs.why: Translocation moves prepared food in the phloem to wherever it is needed, in any direction; the xylem separately carries water and minerals upward from the roots.

lessons.title: Inquisitive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Why do plants transpire more on a windy day compared to a humid one?

Transpiration is driven by the difference in water vapour concentration between the leaf and the air. On a windy day the wind continually removes the moist air surrounding the leaf and replaces it with drier air, so the gradient stays steep and evaporation is fast. On a humid day the air around the leaf is already nearly saturated with vapour, the gradient is small, and evaporation nearly stops. Hence plants transpire more on a windy day than on a humid one.

mcqs.q: Transpiration shows a positive side for the plant because the transpiration stream:
options: Makes the plant lose all its water
Carries dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves and cools the plant
mcqs.why: The same stream that lifts water also distributes minerals to all parts and keeps leaves cool; without it, minerals absorbed by roots could not reach the leaves.

mcqs.q: Insectivorous plants such as the pitcher plant catch insects mainly to obtain:
options: Nitrogen (and other minerals) lacking in their waterlogged, poor soils
mcqs.why: These plants still photosynthesise for energy; they digest insects to supplement the nitrogen and minerals their poor, acidic, waterlogged soils cannot supply.

mcqs.q: The Venus flytrap catches its prey when:
options: Trigger hairs on the leaf are touched, snapping the trap shut
Insects fall into a pool of acid
The plant releases a sweet smell only
mcqs.why: Touching the trigger hairs makes the two halves of the leaf snap shut and imprison the insect, which is then digested by enzymes; the pitcher plant instead drowns prey in a fluid-filled pitcher.

mcqs.q: By digesting insects, an insectivorous plant gains minerals that allow it to:
options: Make proteins and chlorophyll and grow healthily despite poor soil
mcqs.why: The nitrogen and minerals from prey let the plant build proteins and chlorophyll, so it competes successfully in mineral-poor bogs where other plants cannot.

mcqs.q: A similarity between insectivorous plants and ordinary green plants is that both:
options: Photosynthesise to make their own food (energy)
mcqs.why: Insectivory is only a mineral supplement: like all green plants, the pitcher plant and Venus flytrap make their energy-rich food by photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Mineral deficiency symptoms appear in plants because minerals are needed as:
options: Parts of the cell wall only
Components of essential molecules such as chlorophyll, proteins and ATP
mcqs.why: Each mineral has specific roles, magnesium in chlorophyll, nitrogen in proteins, phosphorus in ATP and nucleic acids, so a shortage of any one disrupts growth in a characteristic way.

mcqs.q: Excessive transpiration harms the plant most directly by causing:
options: Wilting and, if prolonged, death from dehydration
mcqs.why: When loss exceeds absorption the cells lose turgidity, leaves wilt, photosynthesis falls and the plant may die; that is why transpiration is called a necessary evil.

mcqs.q: The pitcher plant's modified leaf forms a:
options: Deep slippery tube of digestive fluid in which insects drown and are digested
mcqs.why: In Nepenthes the leaf blade forms a pitcher: insects slip in, drown in the fluid and are digested by enzymes and bacteria, releasing minerals the plant absorbs.

mcqs.q: Insectivorous plants typically grow in soils that are:
options: Waterlogged, acidic and poor in minerals, especially nitrogen
mcqs.why: Bogs and marshes lack available nitrogen and other minerals, which is exactly the disadvantage that insect catching overcomes for these plants.

mcqs.q: The negative side of transpiration for the plant is that:
options: It brings minerals to the leaves
About 90 percent of the water absorbed is lost, which can cause dehydration
It lifts water to the top of tall trees
mcqs.why: Most absorbed water is lost as vapour; the benefits (mineral transport, cooling, ascent of sap) come at this heavy cost, hence the term 'necessary evil'.

They produce two kinds of spores
Spores are produced to withstand harsh conditions
Spores can only grow into new fungi in dry environments
mcqs.why: In sporulation the parent produces large numbers of tiny spores, each able to grow into a new organism; bread mould (Rhizopus) reproduces this way.

options: Creation of a bud that detaches from the cell
Splitting the cell into two identical daughter cells
mcqs.why: Bryophyllum produces plantlets along the margins of its leaves, which fall and grow into new plants: vegetative propagation by leaves.

mcqs.why: The stamens (androecium) are the male parts and the carpels (gynoecium) are the female parts of a flower; sepals and petals are accessory whorls.

mcqs.q: Which plant propagates through tubers?
mcqs.why: Insect-pollinated flowers produce relatively small amounts of pollen, which is carried on the insects' bodies; wind-pollinated flowers produce huge quantities of light pollen.

mcqs.q: The horizontal aboveground stem, which produces leaves and roots at its nodes;
mcqs.why: Insect-pollinated flowers have brightly coloured petals, scent and nectar to attract insects, while wind-pollinated flowers are small, dull and lack nectar.

mcqs.why: A pollen tube grows out from a germinating pollen grain and carries the male gametes down through the style to the ovule in the ovary.

mcqs.q: Which part of the flower is responsible for producing pollen?
mcqs.why: After fertilisation the zygote develops into the embryo, the primary endosperm nucleus into the endosperm (food store), and the ovule itself into the seed.
