mcqs.why: The micropyle is the small pore in the seed coat through which water enters during germination (and through which the pollen tube entered the ovule).

mcqs.q: Which structure forms the female gametophyte in flowering plants?
mcqs.why: After fertilisation the ovary wall (pericarp) develops into the fruit wall, while the ovules inside the ovary become the seeds.

mcqs.q: The male gametophyte in flowering plants is known as:
mcqs.why: Epigeal germination is the type in which the cotyledons are carried above the ground, as in bean; in maize the cotyledon stays below ground (hypogeal).

mcqs.q: In the life cycle of flowering plants, which structure is triploid (3n)?
mcqs.why: For germination a seed needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature (warmth); light is not essential, since seeds germinate underground in darkness.

mcqs.q: Embryo sac is formed inside;
mcqs.why: In the embryo, the plumule is the part that grows upward and develops into the shoot; the radicle grows downward into the root.

mcqs.q: Double fertilization involves;
options: Fertilization of the egg by two male gametes
Fertilization of the egg and the fusion nucleus by two sperms
Fertilization of two eggs in the same embryo sac by two sperms
Fertilization of the egg and the tube cell by two sperms
mcqs.why: In a bulb (e.g. onion), the fleshy scale leaves store food around a short stem; the food sustains growth of the new plant.

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Write a short note on budding in yeast.

In budding, a small outgrowth (bud) appears on the parent yeast cell; the nucleus divides and one daughter nucleus passes into the bud. The bud grows, and finally separates as a new yeast cell, genetically identical to the parent. Under favourable conditions the buds may remain attached for a time, forming short chains.

Q: Write a short note on spore formation in fungi.

In fungi such as Rhizopus, special upright stalks (sporangiophores) bear round spore cases (sporangia) at their tips. Inside each sporangium, large numbers of tiny spores are produced asexually. When the sporangium bursts, the light spores are scattered by wind; on reaching a suitable moist food surface, each spore germinates and grows into a new fungus.

Q: What are the advantages of spore formation in fungi and bacteria?

Spores are very small, light and produced in enormous numbers, so they spread widely; they have thick walls and can remain dormant through harsh conditions (dryness, heat, cold, lack of food) for long periods, germinating when conditions improve. In bacteria, endospores even survive boiling and disinfectants. Spore formation therefore ensures survival and wide dispersal.

Q: Describe how vegetative propagation occurs through runners.

A runner (stolon) is a slender horizontal stem that grows along the surface of the ground from the parent plant (e.g. strawberry). At its nodes it produces roots downward and a new shoot upward; when the connecting stem dies or is cut, each rooted node becomes an independent new plant.

Q: State how potatoes reproduce through tubers.

The potato tuber is a swollen underground stem bearing buds in its 'eyes'. When a tuber (or a cut piece with at least one eye) is planted, the buds sprout using the stored food of the tuber and grow into new potato plants, which then form new tubers.

Q: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of vegetative propagation.

Advantages: the new plants are exact copies, so desirable qualities of the parent are preserved; they grow and bear fruit faster than seedlings; plants that produce no viable seeds (e.g. banana, seedless grapes) can still be propagated; and the method is simple and cheap. Disadvantages: there is no genetic variation, so all plants may be destroyed by the same disease or change in conditions; diseases of the parent pass to all offspring; and the plants tend to overcrowd and compete with each other.

Q: Name the four whorls present in a flower and also tell the components of each whorl.

The four whorls of a flower, from outside to inside: (1) Calyx, made of sepals (usually green, protective). (2) Corolla, made of petals (usually coloured, attracting insects). (3) Androecium, the male whorl, made of stamens; each stamen has a filament and an anther that produces pollen. (4) Gynoecium, the female whorl, made of one or more carpels; each carpel has a stigma, a style and an ovary containing ovules.

Q: Briefly describe the formation of egg cell and polar nuclei within embryo sac of a flower.

Inside the ovule, a megaspore mother cell divides by meiosis to form four haploid megaspores, of which three degenerate. The remaining megaspore divides by mitosis three times, producing eight nuclei in the embryo sac. These arrange themselves as: one egg cell (with two helper cells) at one end, three antipodal cells at the other end, and two polar nuclei in the centre, which fuse to form the fusion (primary endosperm) nucleus.

Q: Differentiate between: i. Asexual and sexual reproduction ii. Binary fission in bacteria and amoeba iii. Stolon and rhizome iv. Bulb and corm v. Cutting and grafting vi. Vegetative propagation and artificial propagation vii. Male and female gametophytes viii. Calyx and corolla ix. Stamen and carpel

i. Asexual and sexual reproduction: asexual reproduction involves one parent, no gametes and no fertilisation; offspring are genetically identical to the parent (e.g. binary fission, budding, vegetative propagation). Sexual reproduction involves two parents (or two gametes), gamete formation by meiosis and fertilisation; offspring show variation (e.g. seed formation in flowering plants). ii. Binary fission in bacteria and amoeba: in bacteria the single circular DNA replicates and the cell divides into two equal cells, with no mitotic spindle or nucleus involved. In Amoeba (a eukaryote) the nucleus first divides by mitosis and then the cytoplasm divides into two. iii. Stolon and rhizome: a stolon (runner) is a horizontal stem growing above the ground (strawberry); a rhizome is a horizontal stem growing under the ground that stores food (ginger). iv. Bulb and corm: a bulb is a short underground stem surrounded by fleshy leaves that store food (onion); a corm is a swollen, solid underground stem without fleshy leaves (e.g. Colocasia/taro). v. Cutting and grafting: in cutting, a detached piece of stem or root is planted and grows into a whole new plant; in grafting, a shoot (scion) of one plant is joined to the rooted stem (stock) of another so they grow as one plant. vi. Vegetative propagation and artificial propagation: vegetative propagation is the natural production of new plants from roots, stems or leaves of the parent; artificial propagation is done by man using methods such as cutting, layering, grafting and tissue culture. vii. Male and female gametophytes: the male gametophyte is the pollen grain, which produces the male gametes (sperms); the female gametophyte is the embryo sac inside the ovule, which contains the egg cell. viii. Calyx and corolla: the calyx is the outer whorl of green sepals that protects the bud; the corolla is the inner whorl of usually brightly coloured petals that attract pollinators. ix. Stamen and carpel: the stamen is the male part (filament + anther, producing pollen); the carpel is the female part (stigma + style + ovary, containing the ovules).

Q: Label the given diagram of flower.

The parts indicated by the lines in the printed diagram (top to bottom) are: Stigma (the top of the carpel, which receives pollen); Anther (on its filament, producing pollen); Petal (one of the large coloured lobes of the corolla); Style (the neck of the carpel); Filament (the stalk of the stamen); Ovary (the swollen base of the carpel containing the ovules); Sepal (one of the green leaf-like parts of the calyx); and Pedicel with the thalamus/receptacle (the green stalk and base on which the flower parts sit). (The diagram's leader lines are unnumbered in the book.)

mcqs.q: Asexual reproduction differs from sexual reproduction in that it:
options: Involves only one parent and no gametes, producing identical offspring
mcqs.why: Asexual reproduction needs one parent, involves no gamete fusion and gives genetically identical offspring; sexual reproduction combines gametes from two parents and produces variation.

mcqs.q: Rhizopus (bread mould) reproduces asexually by:
mcqs.why: In favourable conditions Rhizopus forms sporangia that release large numbers of spores; each spore germinates into a new mould. Bacteria use binary fission and Hydra uses budding.

mcqs.q: Vegetative propagation by stem cuttings is used for:
mcqs.why: A piece of stem with nodes is planted and roots develop from the nodes; roses and sugarcane are raised this way. Potato uses stem tubers and sweet potato uses root tubers.

mcqs.q: Grafting joins the shoot of one plant (scion) to the rooted stock of another so that:
options: A new hybrid seed is produced
The good fruiting qualities of the scion combine with the strong roots of the stock
mcqs.why: In grafting the scion keeps its own variety's qualities while the stock provides a strong, disease-resistant root system; it is widely used for mango and citrus varieties.

mcqs.q: The part of the flower that receives pollen during pollination is the:
mcqs.why: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma; the anther produces the pollen, and fertilisation happens later inside the ovule.

mcqs.q: Cross-pollination is transfer of pollen to the stigma of:
options: A flower on a different plant of the same species
Another flower on the same plant
A flower of a different species
mcqs.why: Self-pollination occurs within the same flower or plant; cross-pollination between different plants brings variation and is carried by insects or wind.

mcqs.q: Wind-pollinated flowers typically have:
options: Small dull petals, no nectar, light smooth pollen and feathery stigmas
mcqs.why: Wind pollination needs huge amounts of light, dry pollen and large feathery stigmas to catch it; insect-pollinated flowers instead attract insects with colour, scent and nectar.

mcqs.q: Double fertilisation in flowering plants means that:
options: One male gamete fuses with the egg (forming the zygote) and the other with the polar nuclei (forming the endosperm)
Fertilisation happens twice in one ovule
Two pollen tubes enter one ovule
mcqs.why: The pollen tube releases two male gametes: one fuses with the egg cell (syngamy) to form the diploid zygote, and the other fuses with the two polar nuclei (triple fusion) to form the triploid endosperm.

mcqs.q: The structure in the seed that stores food for the embryo in castor and maize is the:
mcqs.why: In endospermic seeds such as maize and castor the endosperm stores food; in bean and gram the food is stored instead in the fleshy cotyledons.

mcqs.q: Seeds of bean show epigeal germination, in which:
options: The hypocotyl elongates and carries the cotyledons above the ground
mcqs.why: In epigeal germination (bean, castor) the hypocotyl grows fast and pulls the cotyledons out of the soil; in hypogeal germination (maize, gram) the epicotyl grows and cotyledons stay below.

lessons.title: Detailed Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Explain the process of binary fission in bacteria and describe how it leads to the formation of two daughter bacteria.

In binary fission the bacterial cell first copies its single circular DNA molecule, so two identical DNA molecules are present. The cell elongates, the two DNA molecules move apart, and a cross-wall (septum) grows inward across the middle of the cell. The wall completes the division and the two parts separate as two daughter bacteria, each with one complete DNA molecule and the same genetic material as the parent. Under favourable conditions the process repeats about every 20 minutes, producing a rapidly growing population.

Q: What do you mean by vegetative propagation? Differentiate among different plant structures modified for vegetative propagation.

Vegetative propagation is asexual reproduction in which a new plant grows from a vegetative part (root, stem or leaf) of the parent, without seeds. Structures modified for it: runners/stolons are horizontal stems above ground that root at the nodes (strawberry); rhizomes are horizontal underground stems storing food (ginger); tubers are swollen stem tips full of stored food with buds (potato); bulbs are short stems with fleshy storage leaves (onion); corms are swollen solid underground stems (taro); and suckers are shoots arising from the base of the stem (e.g. mint, banana). Runners spread quickly over the surface, rhizomes and corms persist and store food underground, tubers and bulbs store food for the new shoot.

Q: Describe the ways by which humans can grow new plants by using the vegetative parts of the parent plants?

Humans grow new plants from vegetative parts by artificial propagation. Cutting: a piece of stem (rose, sugarcane) or root is planted and roots to form a new plant. Layering: a branch is bent and covered with soil while still attached; it roots at the covered part and is then separated (jasmine). Grafting: a scion (shoot with desired qualities) is joined to a hardy rooted stock so they unite (mango, citrus, apple). Budding: a single bud is grafted onto a stock (rose, citrus). Tissue culture (micropropagation): small pieces of tissue are grown on a sterile nutrient medium to produce many identical plantlets. These methods preserve the parent's qualities and give fruit much earlier than seedlings.

Q: Define sporophyte and gametophyte. State their roles in the life cycle of plants.

The sporophyte is the diploid (2n) generation: the main plant body in flowering plants. It produces spores by meiosis in the anthers and ovules. The gametophyte is the haploid (n) generation: the pollen grain (male gametophyte) and the embryo sac (female gametophyte); it produces the gametes by mitosis. Their roles alternate: the sporophyte makes spores, the spores grow into gametophytes, the gametophytes make gametes, and fertilisation restores the diploid sporophyte in the seed.

Q: Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.

The life cycle of a flowering plant shows alternation of generations. The familiar plant is the diploid sporophyte. In its flowers, meiosis in the anthers produces pollen grains (male gametophytes) and meiosis in the ovules produces embryo sacs (female gametophytes). The pollen produces male gametes and the embryo sac the egg. After pollination and double fertilisation, the zygote grows into the embryo (the new sporophyte) inside the seed, and the ovary becomes the fruit. On germination the embryo grows into a new sporophyte plant, completing the cycle: sporophyte (2n) -> spores (n) -> gametophyte (n) -> gametes (n) -> zygote (2n) -> sporophyte.

Q: Describe how the female gametophyte (embryo sac) develops within the ovule of a flower.

The ovule is attached inside the ovary and contains a megaspore mother cell (2n). This cell divides by meiosis to give four haploid megaspores; three of them degenerate. The surviving megaspore enlarges and its nucleus divides by mitosis three times, forming eight haploid nuclei within the enlarging embryo sac. The nuclei arrange themselves: three at one end (the middle one becomes the egg cell, flanked by two synergids), three at the opposite end (antipodal cells), and two polar nuclei in the centre, which fuse to form the diploid fusion nucleus. This mature embryo sac is the female gametophyte, ready for fertilisation.

mcqs.q: Artificial vegetative propagation is preferred by farmers and gardeners because it:
options: Produces new plants quickly, all identical to the parent and bearing fruit earlier
mcqs.why: Cutting, layering, grafting and budding copy a proven parent exactly, give disease-free plants of the desired variety and bring earlier fruiting than seed-grown plants.

mcqs.q: Tissue culture (micropropagation) can produce:
options: Large numbers of identical, disease-free plants from a small piece of tissue in a short time
mcqs.why: A small explant grows on a sterile nutrient medium into many plantlets, all clones of the parent and free of disease; it is used for orchids, banana and potato.

mcqs.q: The disadvantage of asexual reproduction is that:
options: All offspring are identical, so a disease or change of environment can destroy the whole population
mcqs.why: Lack of variation is the main drawback: clones share the parent's weaknesses, whereas sexual reproduction's variation lets some offspring survive new conditions.

mcqs.q: A hermaphrodite (bisexual) flower is one that contains:
options: Both stamens and carpels in the same flower
mcqs.why: Mustard, rose and hibiscus have bisexual flowers with both male and female parts; unisexual flowers have only one, as in corn and cucumber.

mcqs.q: The embryo sac of the ovule contains the:
options: Egg cell and the two polar nuclei that take part in fertilisation
mcqs.why: At fertilisation one male gamete fuses with the egg cell in the embryo sac and the other with the two polar nuclei, the double fertilisation unique to flowering plants.

mcqs.q: After fertilisation, the ovary develops into the:
options: Fruit, with its wall forming the pericarp
mcqs.why: The ovary becomes the fruit and its wall the pericarp, while each ovule becomes a seed, the zygote the embryo and the primary endosperm nucleus the endosperm.

mcqs.q: Germination cannot start until the seed absorbs water because water:
options: Activates the enzymes that digest stored food and softens the seed coat
mcqs.why: Imbibed water swells and ruptures the testa, activates enzymes that convert stored food into soluble form, and lets respiration release energy for the growing embryo; oxygen and suitable warmth are also needed.

mcqs.q: During germination, the first structure to emerge from the seed is the:
options: Radicle, which grows downward into the soil
mcqs.why: The radicle emerges first through the micropyle and establishes the root system to absorb water, after which the plumule grows upward into the shoot.

mcqs.q: Dormancy of seeds is useful to the plant because it:
options: Delays germination until conditions are favourable, helping survival and dispersal
mcqs.why: A dormant seed can survive unfavourable seasons and be dispersed far from the parent before germinating when water, oxygen and temperature are right.

mcqs.q: Natural vegetative propagation by runners occurs in:
options: Strawberry and grasses, whose horizontal stems root at the nodes
mcqs.why: Runners are horizontal stems that grow along the ground and produce new plants at their nodes; bulbs, tubers and rhizomes are other natural methods, in onion, potato and ginger respectively.

lessons.title: Inquisitive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Why are spores considered an adaptation for survival n harsh environmental conditions?

A spore is a tiny, single-celled reproductive unit with a thick, resistant wall and very little stored water or metabolism. It can survive heat, dryness, cold and lack of food in a dormant state for months or years, and it is so light that wind carries it far away. When it lands where moisture and food are available, it germinates and grows into a new organism. Thick wall, dormancy, small size and huge numbers make spores an ideal survival adaptation for fungi and bacteria.

Q: How do asexual and sexual reproduction contribute differently to genetic diversity of plant populations?

Asexual reproduction produces offspring genetically identical to the single parent, so it adds no new genetic diversity to the population (except by rare mutation); it is fast and useful for spreading in a stable environment, but the whole population may fail if conditions change. Sexual reproduction mixes genes from two parents through meiosis (crossing over, independent assortment) and fertilisation, producing varied offspring; this diversity allows populations to adapt to changing environments and diseases, at the cost of more time and energy.

Q: How does the pollen tube facilitate the process of fertilization in flowering plants?

Flowering plants cannot move their gametes directly: the pollen is delivered to the stigma, which may be far from the ovule. The pollen grain germinates on the stigma and grows a pollen tube down through the style; the tube is guided to the micropyle of the ovule and enters the embryo sac, where it releases the two male gametes. In this way the pollen tube carries the non-motile sperms safely across the tissues of the carpel and makes double fertilisation possible.

mcqs.q: Plants that reproduce only asexually, like the seedless banana, risk extinction from disease because:
options: All plants are genetically identical, so one disease can attack every plant
mcqs.why: Variation is a population's insurance: in a clone, a pathogen or environmental change that harms one plant harms all, as the lesson's examples of uniform crops show.

mcqs.q: Pollination by insects benefits plants because insects:
options: Carry pollen directly from flower to flower, making cross-pollination efficient
mcqs.why: Insects visiting for nectar brush against anthers and stigmas and transfer pollen precisely between plants, so less pollen is wasted than in wind pollination.

mcqs.q: If pollinating insects disappeared, the most immediate effect on insect-pollinated crops would be:
options: Little or no fruit and seed set, because pollination would fail
mcqs.why: Without insect visitors the pollen never reaches the stigmas of these flowers, so fertilisation, seed formation and fruit set collapse, a serious threat to food crops.

mcqs.q: A farmer who wants every new mango tree to bear exactly the fruit of one excellent parent tree should use:
options: Grafting or budding from that parent tree
mcqs.why: Seeds are produced sexually and vary; only asexual methods such as grafting copy the parent's exact qualities in every new tree.

mcqs.q: Dispersal of seeds away from the parent plant is important because it:
options: Reduces competition for light, water and minerals and colonises new areas
mcqs.why: Seeds scattered by wind, water, animals or explosive fruits escape overcrowding and competition with the parent and siblings, and spread the species to new habitats.

mcqs.q: Fruits eaten by animals help the plant because the seeds:
options: Pass unharmed through the gut and are dropped far away in droppings
mcqs.why: Fleshy fruits attract animals; the tough-coated seeds survive digestion and are deposited at a distance with a supply of manure, aiding germination.

mcqs.q: Self-pollination, though it ensures seed set, is disadvantageous in the long run because it:
options: Reduces genetic variation in the offspring
mcqs.why: Self-pollination combines gametes of the same plant, so offspring resemble the parent closely and variation, the raw material for adaptation, is reduced.

mcqs.q: Wind-pollinated plants must produce enormous quantities of pollen because:
options: Each flower needs many pollen grains
Most pollen is wasted and only a tiny fraction reaches a stigma by chance
mcqs.why: Wind transfer is random: producing vast amounts of light, smooth pollen raises the chance that some grains land on the feathery stigmas of the same species.

mcqs.q: Humans benefit from plant reproduction knowledge most directly in agriculture by:
options: Propagating improved varieties asexually and breeding new varieties sexually
mcqs.why: Grafting and cuttings preserve proven varieties, while controlled cross-pollination in breeding produces new varieties with better yield and resistance.

mcqs.q: Germination of a seed in complete darkness underground is possible because the embryo:
options: Uses food stored in the cotyledons or endosperm until the shoot reaches light
mcqs.why: Light is not a condition for germination; the embryo lives on stored food, digesting it with enzymes activated by absorbed water, until the plumule emerges and can photosynthesise.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: What is the primary purpose of biostatistics?

(a) To analyse financial data (b) To apply statistical methods to biological sciences (c) To design engineering models (d) To study historical events
Correct answer: To apply statistical methods to biological sciences

Q: In biostatistics, which method is used to predict future outcomes based on current data?

(a) Designing experiments (b) Drawing charts (c) Taking average (d) Analysing data
Correct answer: Analysing data

Q: Which of the following best describes the mean of a data set?

(a) The most frequently occurring value (b) The middle value when data is ordered (c) The sum of all values divided by the number of values (d) The difference between the highest and lowest values
Correct answer: The sum of all values divided by the number of values

Q: If the data set is 5, 8, 12, 15, 20, what is the median?

(a) 8 (b) 12 (c) 15 (d) 20
Correct answer: 12

Q: What is the mean of the data set: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11?

(a) 7 (b) 8 (c) 9 (d) 10
Correct answer: 9

Q: When the number of values in a data set is even, how is the median calculated?

(a) By choosing the middle value (b) By taking the average of the two middle values (c) By selecting the most frequent value (d) By adding all values and dividing by the total number of values
Correct answer: By taking the average of the two middle values

Q: In a data set with values 3, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, what is the mode?

(a) 3 (b) 6 (c) 7 (d) Both 3 and 9
Correct answer: Both 3 and 9

Q: If a data set has no repeated values, what is the mode?

(a) The highest value (b) The average of the data set (c) There is no mode (d) The median value
Correct answer: There is no mode

Q: In a bar chart, what does the height or length of each bar represent?

(a) The total number of categories (b) The value of the corresponding category (c) The average of all values (d) The difference between the highest and lowest values
Correct answer: The value of the corresponding category

Q: When constructing a bar chart, which axis usually represents the categories?

(a) Vertical axis (y-axis) (b) Horizontal axis (x-axis) (c) Both axes equally represent the categories (d) Neither axis represents the categories
Correct answer: Horizontal axis (x-axis)

mcqs.q: What is the primary purpose of biostatistics?
options: To apply statistical methods to biological sciences
mcqs.why: Data of two kinds: quantitative data (numbers, e.g. height) and qualitative data (descriptive, e.g. blood groups). Mass, measured in kilograms, is quantitative.

mcqs.q: In biostatistics, which method is used to predict future outcomes based on current data?
mcqs.why: Biostatistics handles variability: it collects, organises, summarises, analyses and interprets biological data, which are naturally variable, so conclusions can be drawn from them.

mcqs.q: Which of the following best describes the mean of a data set?
options: The sum of all values divided by the number of values
The middle value when data is ordered
The difference between the highest and lowest values
mcqs.why: For the 9 values 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16, the middle (5th) value is 10, so the median is 10; the median depends only on position, not on the extreme values.

mcqs.q: If the data set is 5, 8, 12, 15, 20, what is the median?
mcqs.why: The range is the difference between the maximum and minimum values in a data set; it is the simplest measure of spread (dispersion).

mcqs.q: What is the mean of the data set: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11?
mcqs.why: For the even set 3, 6, 7, 10, 12, 15 there are two middle values, 7 and 10; the median is their average, (7 + 10) / 2 = 8.5.

mcqs.q: When the number of values in a data set is even, how is the median calculated?
options: By taking the average of the two middle values
By selecting the most frequent value
By adding all values and dividing by the total number of values
mcqs.why: The mode is the most frequently occurring value in the data; a set may have one mode, several modes or no mode at all.

mcqs.q: In a data set with values 3, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, what is the mode?
mcqs.why: In a symmetrical distribution the three measures coincide: mean = median = mode. (The mean is the average value, not a measure of position in that sense.)

mcqs.q: If a data set has no repeated values, what is the mode?
options: The average of the data set
mcqs.why: Bar charts, histograms and pie charts present data visually; a frequency table only lists values and frequencies in rows and columns, so it is not a graph.

mcqs.q: In a bar chart, what does the height or length of each bar represent?
options: The value of the corresponding category
The difference between the highest and lowest values
mcqs.why: The mean uses every value in the data set, so one extremely large or small value pulls it strongly: the mean is the measure most affected by extreme values (outliers).

mcqs.q: When constructing a bar chart, which axis usually represents the categories?
options: Both axes equally represent the categories
mcqs.why: A histogram displays continuous data in adjacent bars whose areas represent frequencies; a bar chart, with separated bars, is used for discrete or categorical data.

lessons.title: Short Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Define biostatistics.

Biostatistics is the branch of statistics that applies statistical principles and methods to biological sciences: it is the collection, organisation, analysis and interpretation of data related to living organisms, used to draw conclusions and make decisions in biology, medicine and public health.

Q: What is the median of a data set?

The median is the middle value of a data set when the values are arranged in increasing (or decreasing) order. Half the values lie below it and half above it; for an even number of values it is the average of the two middle values.

Q: How is the mean calculated?

The mean is calculated by adding all the values of the data set and dividing the sum by the total number of values. Formula: Mean = (Sum of all values) / (Number of values).

Q: What does the height of a bar in a bar chart represent?

The height (or length) of a bar represents the value (amount, frequency or quantity) of the category to which the bar belongs, read against the scale of the value axis.

Q: What is the mode of a data set?

The mode is the value that occurs most frequently in a data set. A data set may have one mode, more than one mode, or no mode at all if no value repeats.

mcqs.q: Data collected directly by the investigator himself is called:
mcqs.why: Primary data are gathered first-hand, e.g. by observing or measuring; secondary data are taken from existing records or publications.

mcqs.q: Qualitative data are data that:
options: Describe qualities or categories and cannot be measured numerically, e.g. blood groups
mcqs.why: Qualitative data classify observations into categories such as blood group or flower colour; quantitative data are numerical measurements such as height and mass.

mcqs.q: A frequency distribution table organises data by:
options: Listing each value (or class) together with how often it occurs
mcqs.why: The frequency of a value is the number of times it appears; the table of values and frequencies is the first step in summarising a data set.

mcqs.q: The mean of the numbers 4, 8, 6, 10, 2 is:
mcqs.why: Mean = sum of values / number of values = (4 + 8 + 6 + 10 + 2) / 5 = 30 / 5 = 6.

mcqs.q: For the data 5, 7, 9, the median is:
mcqs.why: Arranged in order, 5, 7, 9, the median is the middle value, 7; the sum 21 would be used for the mean (21 / 3 = 7 also, in this symmetric case).

mcqs.q: The mode of the data 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 3, 9 is:
mcqs.why: The value 3 occurs three times, more often than any other value, so 3 is the mode of this data set.

mcqs.q: The range of the data 12, 7, 25, 9, 18 is:
mcqs.why: Range = maximum - minimum = 25 - 7 = 18; it gives the spread of the data in a single number.

mcqs.q: Grouped data are used when:
options: There are many values, so they are collected into class intervals
mcqs.why: For large sets, values are grouped into classes (e.g. heights 140-145 cm) and the frequency of each class is counted, making the data manageable.

mcqs.q: A pie chart shows data as:
options: Sectors of a circle, each sector's angle proportional to its share of the total
mcqs.why: In a pie chart the whole circle is the total and each category gets a sector sized by its proportion; bar charts use bars and histograms use adjacent bars for continuous data.

mcqs.q: Continuous data differ from discrete data in that continuous data:
options: Can take any value within a range, e.g. height or mass
mcqs.why: Discrete data are counted in whole numbers (e.g. number of petals); continuous data are measured and can fall anywhere in a range, such as a height of 152.4 cm.

lessons.title: Detailed Answer Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Explain the importance of biostatistics in the field of public health. Provide examples of how it is used to inform public health decisions.

Biostatistics provides the evidence on which public health decisions are made. It is used to measure how common a disease is (incidence and prevalence), to identify its risk factors, to test whether a new medicine or vaccine works, and to plan health services. Examples: data on polio cases guided vaccination campaigns until the disease was nearly eliminated; statistics on smoking and lung cancer led to warnings and bans on tobacco advertising; during the COVID-19 pandemic, daily case and death statistics decided lockdowns, hospital capacity and vaccine priorities; and figures on child malnutrition guide nutrition programmes.

Q: Discuss the differences between mean, median, and mode. Include examples where each measure is most appropriate to use.

Mean: the sum of all values divided by the number of values; it uses every value but is pulled by extreme values, so it is best for fairly even data (e.g. average marks of a class). Median: the middle value of the ordered data; it is not affected by extreme values, so it is best when data are skewed (e.g. incomes of a town, where a few very rich people would distort the mean). Mode: the most frequent value; it is best for finding the most common category (e.g. the most common blood group in a hospital, or the most sold shoe size).

Q: Describe the steps involved in creating a bar chart using Excel. Include a discussion on how to customize the chart for better visualization and interpretation of data.

Steps in Excel: (1) Enter the data in two columns, e.g. categories in column A and values in column B, with headings. (2) Select the data range. (3) Go to Insert > Charts > Column or Bar chart and choose the style; the chart appears on the sheet. (4) Customise: add a clear chart title, label both axes (category axis and value axis) with titles and units, adjust the scale of the value axis, and change bar colours if needed. (5) Check that bar heights match the values. A well-labelled chart lets the reader see at once which category is largest and how the values compare, making the data easy to interpret.

Q: Provide a detailed example of how to calculate the mean, median, and mode of a data set. Use the following data set for your calculations: 12, 15, 22, 8, 19, 25, 15.

Data set: 12, 15, 22, 8, 19, 25, 15. MEAN: Step 1, add all values: 12 + 15 + 22 + 8 + 19 + 25 + 15 = 116. Step 2, count the values: n = 7. Step 3, apply the formula: Mean = 116 / 7 = 16.57 (approximately). MEDIAN: Step 1, arrange in order: 8, 12, 15, 15, 19, 22, 25. Step 2, with 7 values the middle one is the 4th value. Median = 15. MODE: Step 1, count the frequency of each value: 15 occurs twice, all others occur once. Mode = 15. So for this data set: mean 16.57, median 15, mode 15.

Q: You are given the following data set, create a bar chart to represent the number of different types of fruits sold at a market in one week: Apples: 30, Bananas: 45, Oranges: 20, Grapes: 25, Mangoes: 15. Ensure to label the axes and provide a title for the chart.

The bar chart (described in full, as it is drawn on graph paper or in Excel): Title: "Number of different types of fruits sold at a market in one week". Horizontal axis (x-axis): Type of fruit (Apples, Bananas, Oranges, Grapes, Mangoes). Vertical axis (y-axis): Number of fruits sold, with a scale of 0 to 50 in steps of 5. Bars (height = number sold): Apples 30, Bananas 45, Oranges 20, Grapes 25, Mangoes 15. Reading the chart: bananas sold the most (45) and mangoes the least (15); the five bars, drawn to the same width with equal gaps, make the comparison immediate.

mcqs.q: From the worked example in this chapter: 20 seeds germinated out of 25 sown. The percentage germination is:
mcqs.why: Percentage germination = (seeds germinated / seeds sown) x 100 = (20 / 25) x 100 = 80 percent, the measure used to test seed viability.

mcqs.q: If a data set has two values occurring with the same highest frequency, the data are:
mcqs.why: A set with two modes is bimodal; the chapter's own data 3, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9 are bimodal with modes 3 and 9.

mcqs.q: The median is preferred to the mean when the data contain:
options: Extreme values (outliers) that would distort the mean
mcqs.why: The median depends only on the middle position, so a few very large or small values cannot pull it; the mean, which uses every value, is strongly affected by outliers.

mcqs.q: A class interval of 140-145 cm for heights means the class includes heights:
options: From 140 cm up to (but not including) 145 cm
mcqs.why: Continuous data are grouped into classes with stated limits so that every measurement falls into exactly one class and frequencies can be counted.

mcqs.q: Standard deviation is a measure of:
options: The middle value of the data
How widely the values are spread around the mean
mcqs.why: Measures of dispersion describe spread: the range is the simplest, and the standard deviation measures the average distance of values from the mean.

mcqs.q: In the chapter's plant-height data (14 plants), most heights clustered around 15-17 cm. This clustering is described by the:
options: Measures of central tendency (mean, median and mode)
mcqs.why: Mean (about 16.6 cm), median (15 cm) and mode (15 cm) each summarise the centre of the distribution; the worked example uses all three to describe the same data set.

mcqs.q: A sample in biostatistics is:
options: A smaller part of the population, studied to draw conclusions about the whole population
mcqs.why: Studying every individual is usually impossible, so a representative sample is measured and statistics from it are used to infer the properties of the whole population.

mcqs.q: The sum of the frequencies in a frequency table equals:
options: The total number of observations in the data set
mcqs.why: Each observation is counted once in exactly one class, so adding all the class frequencies gives N, the total number of observations.

mcqs.q: Which graph is most suitable for showing how a quantity changes over time, e.g. growth of a plant each week?
mcqs.why: A line graph joins points plotted against time, making trends such as steady growth easy to see; pie charts show proportions and bar charts compare categories.

mcqs.q: Biostatistics is important in biology because it allows the researcher to:
options: Summarise variable biological data and draw reliable conclusions from experiments
mcqs.why: Biological measurements always vary; statistics organises that variation into tables, graphs and averages so that experiments and surveys can be interpreted objectively.
